Stereochemistry Lab

Stereo Lab — five tabs, in order

Five trainers, designed to be walked in order: R/S Trainer (assign priorities) → Newman (rotamer energies) → Fischer R/S Drill (the flip-rule for projections) → Optical Activity ([α] and ee math) → Isomer Decision Tree (identical / enantiomer / diastereomer). Each tab builds on the previous.

Coach note · Newman stability — the rule in one line
Stability is key. Nine times out of ten the Newman question asks "most stable" or "least stable" form, and the rule is one line: the big groups want to be as far apart as possible. Staggered = elbow room = stable (gauche staggered slightly worse than anti staggered due to small steric strain between adjacent large groups; anti = ideal). Eclipsed = solar eclipse = unstable (groups stacked, max torsional strain). Just like we do as humans — we want our space.
Coach note · the chair "boat with a sail" image
Picture the cyclohexane chair like a flat boat on the water. A group in axial sticks straight up — a sail. The boat is top-heavy and unstable. A group in equatorial drags along behind the boat — chill, low energy, stable. So bulky groups (tert-butyl, the little fan shape) belong in equatorial. And remember: axial and equatorial just "kind of happen" — the thing you actually control is up vs down. Wedge up = same as up in the chair. Dash down = same as down in the chair.
Coach note · R/S the wedge flip
Number priorities 1, 2, 3 — draw a curved arrow through them — ignore priority 4 for a second. If priority 4 (usually H) is on a dash (pointing away from you), what you drew is what you get: CW = R, CCW = S. If priority 4 is on a wedge (pointing toward you), flip the answer. So an apparent R becomes S, and vice versa. Same rule for Fisher projections, just translate: horizontal IS a wedge; vertical IS a dash.
Coach note · finding chiral centers
Look at every carbon. The hint is where substituents branch off (ring positions) or where two rings are fused. Those are chiral hot spots. The gut check: if it can eventually be different, there'll be different groups. Don't get stuck because two paths leave the same carbon — trace them out and see if they ever diverge. If they do, those are different substituents and the C is chiral. CH₂ groups are never chiral (two identical H's); a C with only one branch is rarely chiral (need 4 different groups).
Coach note · meso compounds — the hot-dog bun
Pause when you see two chiral centers. Check for an internal plane of symmetry — can you fold the molecule like a hot dog bun and have the two halves stack? If yes, that is a meso compound: chiral centers exist, but the molecule overall is achiral (optically inactive — its R-half cancels its S-half). The classic example: (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane = same molecule as (2S,3R) = meso. Students miss this regularly because they see "2 chiral centers" and assume the molecule must be chiral. Always check for the internal mirror plane first.
TOUR 1.R/S Trainer → 2.Newman → 3.Fischer Drill → 4.Optical Activity → 5.Decision Tree
Question 1 of 8
Assign R or S to the chiral center marked *
Streak: 0 · Correct: 0/0
CIP priority rules
1. Higher atomic number = higher priority (I > Br > Cl > F > O > N > C > H).
2. If tied, move to next atom out; compare the sets.
3. Double/triple bonds count atoms twice/thrice (phantom atoms).
4. Lowest priority behind the plane; trace 1→2→3. Clockwise = R, counter = S. If lowest is in front, flip your answer.
Phantom-atom worked example 1 · –CHO vs –CH₂OH
Question: Both substituents on a chiral center start with carbon. Which carbon "wins" the CIP priority — the aldehyde –CHO or the hydroxymethyl –CH₂OH? At the first sphere both are tied (a single C bonded to the chiral center). The fight is decided at the next sphere — and the phantom-atom rule for the C=O is what swings it.
SLOT 1
O vs O  →  tie
step out
SLOT 2
O (CHO) vs H (CH₂OH)  →  CHO wins
Verdict: –CHO has higher CIP priority than –CH₂OH. The phantom O (added because the C=O double bond is counted twice) is the deciding atom — without it, both groups would look identical at the second sphere.

Triple-bond version: the same rule with three duplicates. Vinyl –CH=CH₂ sees (C, C, H); ethyl –CH₂CH₃ sees (C, H, H) — vinyl wins. Cyano –C≡N sees (N, N, N) and beats almost any C-only group.
Phantom-atom worked example 2 · –COOH vs –CH₂OH
The carboxylic-acid trick: –COOH wins decisively. Most students undercount the phantoms — the COOH carbon sees three O's at its first-sphere neighbors, not two. That's two real O's (one from C=O, one from –OH) plus one phantom O from the double bond.
SLOT 1
O vs O  →  tie
step out
SLOT 2
O (COOH) vs H (CH₂OH)  →  COOH wins
Why –COOH is the heavyweight of common functional groups: only halogens, –OR (ether) at the first sphere, and –NR₂ (amine, when N is on the chiral C) can outrank it on the priority ladder — and even those tie with COOH on the first sphere if all four substituents start with C. Inside a chain of all-carbon substituents, –COOH almost always wins priority 1 or 2.

Sanity check on the chain: a carbon with three O neighbors (COOH) beats a carbon with two O's and one H (CHO), which beats a carbon with one O and two H's (CH₂OH). Order: –COOH > –CHO > –CH₂OH — all three start with C, all three are decided at the second sphere by counting O's vs H's.
Newman Projection of Butane
Slide the dihedral angle — the front carbon rotates relative to the back. Watch the energy curve track the torsional strain.
dihedral: 60° · gauche · 3.8 kJ/mol above anti
DAT Connection · E2 anti-periplanar
E2 requires H and leaving group at 180° (anti-periplanar) — i.e., both in the back-to-front axis of the Newman projection. On a cyclohexane, that means both axial. Rotate the Newman to 180° above to see the geometry that E2 demands.
Stereo Lab · Tab 03
Optical Activity · Specific Rotation & Enantiomeric Excess
A pure enantiomer rotates plane-polarized light. A racemic mix rotates nothing. Meso compounds rotate nothing. The DAT places one or two questions per test on these calculations — every test.
Core formulas
Specific rotation  [α] = αobs / (c · l)
where αobs = observed rotation in degrees, c = concentration in g/mL, l = path length in dm. [α] is intrinsic to the compound — like a fingerprint.

Enantiomeric excess  ee% = (|R − S| / (R + S)) × 100
where R and S are the amounts (or fractions) of each enantiomer. ee% is also called optical purity — the two are numerically identical.

Observed rotation of a mixture  αobs = (ee/100) · [α]pure
A mixture's rotation is the pure-enantiomer rotation scaled by the excess fraction. The "racemic part" of the mix cancels itself out and contributes zero.
Polarimeter · live visualization
ee = 100% · pure (R) · αobs = +94.0°
Drag the slider. Positive ee means the named enantiomer is in excess; the analyzer rotates clockwise. At ee = 0, the polarized light passes through with no net rotation — that is a racemic mixture.
Rule 1
Racemic mixture (50:50 R and S) has ee = 0% and observed rotation = 0°. Equal amounts cancel exactly. Common DAT phrase: "an SN1 product is racemic" — that means optically inactive even though every individual molecule has a stereocenter.
Rule 2
Meso compound has stereocenters but an internal plane of symmetry — the two halves cancel each other inside the same molecule. ee is undefined (the compound IS its own mirror image). Observed rotation = 0°. Classic example: meso-tartaric acid (2R,3S).
Rule 3
Pure single enantiomer has ee = 100% and rotates light by exactly its specific rotation [α]. The sign (+ or −) and the R/S label are independent — you cannot predict the sign from R/S; you have to measure it.
Why does racemic = 0?
Cancellation diagram · 50% R + 50% S
Every (R) molecule in the flask rotates plane-polarized light by exactly +α. Every (S) molecule rotates it by −α. In a 50:50 mix the two contributions sum to zero — the analyzer reads 0° even though every single molecule is chiral.

That is why you can have a flask full of stereocenters and still measure αobs = 0. The DAT loves this distinction: racemic ≠ achiral.
Meso compound · internal mirror plane
meso-tartaric (2R,3S) · αobs = 0°
Top half (2R) and bottom half (3S) are mirror images across the dashed plane. The molecule contains its own enantiomer — net rotation is zero.
(2R,3R)-tartaric · [α] = +12°
Both stereocenters R. No internal symmetry — the molecule is chiral. Its enantiomer (2S,3S) rotates by −12°. The pair are enantiomers; either is a diastereomer of the meso form.
Compute αobs from ee · interactive
αobs +65.8°
αobs = (ee/100) · [α] · c · l = (70/100) · (+94) · 1 · 1 = +65.8°
Composition: 85.0% (R)-limonene · orange · 15.0% (S)-limonene · lemon
Set ee to 0 for a racemic mixture (output goes to 0°). Use a negative ee to put the mirror enantiomer in excess (sign of αobs flips).
Worked examples · with structures
1
Compute observed rotation of a 70% ee sample
ee → αobs
A pure (R)-2-bromobutane has [α] = +23.1°. A sample is 85% R and 15% S. Predict its observed rotation at standard conditions (c = 1 g/mL, l = 1 dm).
(R)-2-bromobutane
Walkthrough
Step 1 · find ee: ee% = ((85 − 15) / (85 + 15)) × 100 = (70/100) × 100 = 70% ee.
Step 2 · scale [α]: αobs = (ee/100) · [α]pure = 0.70 × (+23.1°) = +16.2°.
Why it works: the 15% S cancels 15% of the R, leaving 70% R as the "active" portion. That 70% rotates light at full strength; the racemic 30% (15 R + 15 S) cancels.
2
Compute ee from a measured rotation
αobs → ee
Pure (S)-limonene has [α] = −94°. A lemon-peel extract gives an observed rotation of −47° at the same conditions. What is the ee, and what fraction of each enantiomer is present?
(S)-limonene · the lemon-peel terpene
Walkthrough
Step 1 · solve for ee: ee = αobs / [α]pure × 100 = (−47 / −94) × 100 = 50% ee.
Step 2 · split into R/S fractions: ee = |S − R| / (S + R), and total = 100%. So S − R = 50% and S + R = 100% → S = 75%, R = 25%.
Sign-check: the rotation is negative, matching the pure (S)-(−). That confirms S is in excess (not R). Always sanity-check the sign of αobs against the known sign of the pure enantiomer.
3
Spot the racemic mixture (no rotation)
αobs = 0
An SN1 reaction on (R)-3-chloropentane in aqueous ethanol gives a product with αobs = 0°. The product is 3-pentanol. What can you conclude?
(R)-3-chloropentane → planar carbocation → racemic 3-pentanol
Walkthrough
The product is a racemic mixture (50:50 R and S 3-pentanol). ee = 0%, αobs = 0°.
Why: SN1 goes through a planar carbocation at the stereocenter. Water attacks from either face with equal probability → equal R and S. The two enantiomers cancel optically.
DAT trick: "racemic" and "achiral" are NOT the same. A racemic mixture has chiral molecules (each one is R or S) but the bulk sample is optically inactive. An achiral molecule has no stereocenter at all.
4
Spot the meso compound (no rotation, but chiral centers)
internal symmetry
meso-tartaric acid is (2R,3S)-2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid. It has TWO stereocenters but αobs = 0°. Why?
meso-tartaric (2R,3S) · the dashed plane bisects the C2–C3 bond
Walkthrough
The molecule has an internal plane of symmetry bisecting the C2–C3 bond. The "top half" (C1–C2 with R configuration) is the mirror image of the "bottom half" (C3–C4 with S configuration). The two halves rotate light in opposite directions within the same molecule — they cancel.
Quick test for meso: draw the molecule, look for a mirror plane that reflects one half onto the other. If yes, the molecule is achiral (meso) despite having stereocenters.
Compare: (2R,3R)- and (2S,3S)-tartaric acid are enantiomers (and rotate +12° and −12° respectively). meso-(2R,3S) is a separate diastereomer of those, and is achiral.
5
Concentration / path length problem
[α] formula
A pure enantiomer is dissolved at c = 0.50 g/mL in a 2.0 dm polarimeter tube. Observed rotation αobs = +35°. What is [α]?
Polarimeter tube · path length l, concentration c
Walkthrough
[α] = αobs / (c · l) = +35° / (0.50 · 2.0) = +35° / 1.0 = +35°.
Common DAT trap: students forget the units — c must be in g/mL (not g/L), and l in decimeters (not cm or m). If a problem gives c in g/L, divide by 1000. If l in cm, divide by 10.
Why specific rotation matters: [α] is the same regardless of how concentrated or how long the tube is. It's an intrinsic property of the compound. αobs changes with c and l, but [α] doesn't.
Sign vs configuration trap
The sign of rotation (+/− or d/l) is determined empirically — you cannot predict it from R/S. Some R-compounds rotate (+); others rotate (−). Likewise some S-compounds are (+) and some are (−). The DAT will give you the sign of pure material; use it. Don't try to derive sign from R/S.
When is observed rotation = 0?
Three situations all give αobs = 0°: (1) achiral molecule (no stereocenter), (2) meso compound (stereocenters but internal mirror plane), (3) racemic mixture (50:50 enantiomer pair). The first two are intrinsic to the molecule; the third is about composition. The DAT loves to mix these up — read carefully.
Related: See the Stereochemistry cheat sheet for a printable summary of optical-activity formulas.
Fischer Projection · R/S Assignment Drill
Fischer projections are the standard 2D depiction of sugars and amino acids. They follow a strict convention that, once memorized, makes R/S assignment a one-step decision.
Streak: 0 · Correct: 0/6
The Fischer convention (memorize, then never recompute)
Horizontal bonds point TOWARD you (wedge / out of page).
Vertical bonds point AWAY from you (dash / into the page).
The chiral C sits at the cross. The carbon chain runs vertically (highest-priority FG at top by convention).
The flip rule — the entire skill in one sentence
Trace priorities 1 → 2 → 3 as drawn on the page (CW or CCW). Then check where lowest priority (priority 4, usually H) sits:
· Lowest on a horizontal line (toward you / wedge) → FLIP your 2D answer (CW becomes CCW and vice versa).
· Lowest on a vertical line (away from you / dash) → NO FLIP, take the answer as drawn.

Why? The standard R/S rule wants priority 4 in back. In Fischer-as-drawn, vertical = back already (no flip), but horizontal = front (flip).
Worked drill — six Fischer assignments · click R or S before revealing the walkthrough
1
D-glyceraldehyde (the parent sugar)
H on left (horizontal)
Top: CHO. Right: OH. Bottom: CH₂OH. Left: H. Assign R or S.
Walkthrough
Priority: OH (1, O directly attached) > CHO (2, C with two O phantoms from =O) > CH₂OH (3, C with one O at next sphere) > H (4).
Trace 1→2→3 on the page: OH (right) → CHO (top) → CH₂OH (bottom) = counter-clockwise.
H position: left = horizontal (toward viewer) → FLIP.
Answer: CCW flipped = CW → R. (D-glyceraldehyde is (R)-glyceraldehyde — this is the reference compound for Fischer's D/L system.)
2
L-alanine (a real amino acid)
H on left (horizontal)
Top: COOH. Right: NH₂. Bottom: CH₃. Left: H. Assign R or S.
Walkthrough
Priority: NH₂ (1, N is directly attached and N > C) > COOH (2, C with three O phantoms — two from =O, one from -OH) > CH₃ (3) > H (4).
Subtle: at the chiral C, the directly-attached atoms are N (from NH₂), C (from COOH), C (from CH₃), H. N beats both C's outright, so NH₂ wins priority 1 by atomic number — no need to look at next sphere.
Trace 1→2→3: NH₂ (right) → COOH (top) → CH₃ (bottom) = clockwise.
H on left = horizontal → FLIP. CW flipped = CCW → S. (L-alanine is (S)-alanine. Almost all natural amino acids are L = S, except cysteine which is L but R because of the SH group.)
3
D-lactic acid · the rotation trap
H on right (horizontal)
Top: COOH. Right: H. Bottom: CH₃. Left: OH. Assign R or S.
Walkthrough
Priority: OH (1) > COOH (2, three O phantoms) > CH₃ (3) > H (4).
Trace 1→2→3: OH (left) → COOH (top) → CH₃ (bottom) = counter-clockwise.
H on right = horizontal → FLIP. CCW → CW → R. (D-lactic acid is (R)-(−)-lactic acid; the (S) enantiomer is the one in your muscles after exercise.)
Compare to card 1: here H is on the right instead of left, but the rule is the same — both are horizontal, both flip.
4
H on top (vertical) — no flip
No flip
Top: H. Right: CH₃. Bottom: COOH. Left: OH. Assign R or S.
Walkthrough
Priority: OH (1) > COOH (2) > CH₃ (3) > H (4). Same priorities as card 3 — this is the same molecule drawn rotated 90° in the Fischer.
Trace 1→2→3: OH (left) → COOH (bottom) → CH₃ (right) = counter-clockwise.
H on top = vertical → NO FLIP. Take CCW as is → S.
Sanity check: card 3 was R, this is S — but they appear to be the same molecule. Yes, because rotating a Fischer 90° inverts configuration (changes which substituents are wedge/dash). Do not rotate Fischer projections by 90° to simplify. Rotating 180° preserves configuration.
5
D-erythrose top stereocenter (sugar with two centers)
H on right
Top: CHO. Right: H. Bottom: CH(OH)CH₂OH. Left: OH. Assign R or S at the carbon shown.
Walkthrough
Priority: OH (1) > CHO (2, C with two O phantoms) > CH(OH)CH₂OH (3, C with only one O at next sphere) > H (4).
Subtle: phantom-atom rule for –CHO gives (O, O, H) at the next sphere, vs the chain group's (O, C, H). (O, O, H) beats (O, C, H) at the second slot, so CHO wins priority 2.
Trace 1→2→3: OH (left) → CHO (top) → chain (bottom) = clockwise.
H on right = horizontal → FLIP. CW → CCW → S. (Top stereocenter of D-erythrose is 2S; the bottom is 3R; D-erythrose is (2S, 3R)-2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal.)
6
L-cysteine — the SH twist
SH changes priority
Top: COOH. Right: NH₂. Bottom: CH₂SH. Left: H. Assign R or S.
Walkthrough
Priority: NH₂ (1, N directly attached) > CH₂SH (2, C with S at next sphere — S is atomic #16, beats O) > COOH (3, C with three O phantoms — but O is #8, less than S) > H (4).
This is the trap: for every other natural amino acid, COOH is priority 2. For cysteine, the SH group puts S on the side chain — and S (#16) beats O (#8) — so the side chain outranks COOH at the next sphere.
Trace 1→2→3: NH₂ (right) → CH₂SH (bottom) → COOH (top) = counter-clockwise.
H on left = horizontal → FLIP. CCW → CW → R. (L-cysteine is the only natural amino acid that is R, even though it's still labeled L by Fischer convention. Classic DAT biochem cross-link.)
Mental model · convert Fischer to wedge/dash in your head
Pick the chiral C. Imagine looking at the page from the side: horizontal substituents pop out toward you (wedge), vertical ones go away (dash). Now you have the standard 3D wedge/dash structure. Apply the standard CIP rule: priority 4 in back means trace 1→2→3 as drawn; priority 4 in front means flip. For Fischer, "in back" = on a vertical line.
Isomer Decision Tree · enantiomer vs diastereomer vs identical
DAT pattern: "Are these two structures enantiomers, diastereomers, identical, or constitutional isomers?" Walk this tree top-down. Stop at the first answer that matches.
Interactive flowchart · five questions in order
Select a compound pair from the picker below to highlight the decision path through the tree.
Interactive case picker · select a pair to trace the path
Worked examples · click Walk it to trace the tree
1
(2R,3R)- vs (2S,3S)-tartaric acid
Enantiomers
Both are 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid. The first has R at both stereocenters; the second has S at both. Are they enantiomers, diastereomers, identical, or constitutional?
Walk the tree
Q1 same formula? Yes (C₄H₆O₆). Q2 same connectivity? Yes (both 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid). Q3 stereocenters? Yes (C2 and C3). Q4 same R/S at every center? No (R,R vs S,S). Q5 opposite at EVERY center? R→S at C2 and R→S at C3 — yes, every center is flipped.
Answer: enantiomers. Non-superimposable mirror images. Pure (R,R) rotates +12°; pure (S,S) rotates −12°. A 50:50 mix is racemic and rotates 0°.
2
(2R,3R)-tartaric vs meso-tartaric acid
Diastereomers (meso)
(R,R) has both stereocenters R. Meso form (2R,3S) has one R and one S. Only one center is flipped. Relationship?
Walk the tree
Q1 same formula? Yes. Q2 same connectivity? Yes. Q3 stereocenters? Yes. Q4 same at every? No. Q5 opposite at every? No (only C3 flipped, C2 stayed R).
Answer: diastereomers. The (2R,3S) form is meso (internal mirror plane bisecting C2–C3). Meso-tartaric is achiral despite 2 stereocenters; it does NOT rotate light. (R,R) and meso still have different physical properties.
3
cis-2-butene vs trans-2-butene
Diastereomers (geometric)
Both are 2-butene (CH₃-CH=CH-CH₃). cis (Z) vs trans (E). Are they enantiomers, diastereomers, identical, or constitutional?
Walk the tree
Q1 same formula? Yes (C₄H₈). Q2 same connectivity? Yes. Q3 any stereocenter or E/Z? No chiral C, but the C=C locks geometry — yes. Q4 same E/Z? No. Q5 opposite at every? Yes — single binary swap (Z ↔ E).
Answer: diastereomers (geometric isomers are a type of diastereomer). Cis-2-butene is achiral, so they are NOT enantiomers. Different bp, density; cannot interconvert without breaking the π bond.
4
1-butanol vs 2-butanol
Constitutional isomers
Both have formula C₄H₉OH (C₄H₁₀O). But the OH is at C1 in one and C2 in the other. Relationship?
Walk the tree
Q1 same formula? Yes (C₄H₁₀O). Q2 same connectivity? No — the OH is attached at C1 in 1-butanol but at C2 in 2-butanol. Different skeleton!
Answer: constitutional isomers. Very different physical properties: 1-butanol bp 118°C, 2-butanol bp 99°C. Different reactions (1-butanol is primary, 2-butanol is secondary).
Quick rules of thumb
· Enantiomers have IDENTICAL physical properties except they rotate light in opposite directions and react differently with other chiral things (e.g., enzymes).
· Diastereomers have DIFFERENT physical properties (mp, bp, density, solubility, NMR shifts). You can separate them by ordinary chromatography or recrystallization.
· Constitutional isomers have different connectivity — very different chemistry (e.g., 1-butanol vs 2-butanol vs diethyl ether are all C₄H₁₀O).
· Meso compounds are achiral, optically inactive, and have an internal mirror plane that pairs up opposite-configuration stereocenters within the molecule.
Practice
Stereochemistry PracticeDAT-style · immediate feedback · 5 questions
0/5
1(2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane and (2S,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane are best classified as:
Explanation
B is correct. 2,3-dibromobutane has two chiral centers AND an internal mirror plane between C2 and C3 — making it a meso compound. (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) describe the SAME molecule from two ways of labeling: rotate the molecule and you get the other label. Both descriptors point at one achiral structure with crossed stereo descriptors. Meso compounds are the classic trap — students see "2R,3S vs 2S,3R" and assume enantiomers, missing the internal symmetry.
2(R)-2-bromobutane is treated with NaI in acetone (SN2). The product is:
Explanation
A is correct. SN2 is concerted with BACKSIDE ATTACK by the nucleophile. The three remaining substituents flip through the plane like an umbrella in the wind (Walden inversion). So (R) substrate → (S) product, every time, 100%. SN1 would give racemization (C); pure retention (B) is not what any classic mechanism gives; elimination (D) is unlikely with iodide in acetone (good Nu, polar aprotic — favors SN2 over E2).
3Which of the following molecules is CHIRAL?
Explanation
C is correct. 2-bromobutane has a chiral center at C2 — four different groups attached: H, Br, CH₃, CH₂CH₃. Two paths leave C2 (methyl vs ethyl) and never become identical. (A) methane has 4 identical H's, no chiral center. (B) 2-bromopropane has TWO identical methyl groups on the C bearing Br — not chiral. (D) trans-1,2-dichloroethene is planar and has a mirror plane — not chiral (geometric isomerism, not chirality).
4For the alkene (CH₃)CH=CH(C₂H₅), the higher-priority group on the LEFT carbon is CH₃ vs H, and on the RIGHT carbon is C₂H₅ vs H. If both higher-priority groups (CH₃ and C₂H₅) are on the SAME side of the double bond, the geometry is:
Explanation
B is correct. The CIP rules for double bonds: assign priority on each carbon by atomic number (CIP). If the two HIGHER-priority groups are on the SAME side → Z (zusammen, "together"). If on OPPOSITE sides → E (entgegen, "opposite"). For this alkene, CH₃ (higher than H on left) and C₂H₅ (higher than H on right) are on the same side → Z. Cis/trans is older terminology that only works when the groups are clearly comparable (like H vs H or CH₃ vs CH₃); E/Z is the modern, universally-applicable system.
5An equal mixture of (R)- and (S)-2-bromobutane will rotate plane-polarized light by:
Explanation
D is correct. A racemic mixture (equal amounts of two enantiomers) is OPTICALLY INACTIVE. Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light in EQUAL but OPPOSITE directions — (R) rotates one way by +x°, (S) rotates the other way by −x°. In a 50/50 mixture, the rotations cancel exactly. This is the key practical reason chemists care about chirality in pharmaceuticals: enantiomers can have very different biological effects, but a racemic mixture appears optically inactive (gives zero rotation in a polarimeter) even though it contains chiral molecules.
Spectroscopy

IR + NMR Trainer

The DAT spec section rewards pattern recognition. Master IR by the 5 key peaks; master NMR by running the 4-step strategy on every problem. Practice below.

Coach note · the fingerprint region rule
Anything 1500 cm⁻¹ and below is the fingerprint region. Cross it out instantly. If an answer choice points to a peak below 1500, rule it out — that region is so dense with overlapping bands that scientists in the lab used to literally cover it with their thumb. "Forget about it. It is nonsense." Your real signals live above 1500: carbonyl around 1700, alcohols/amines way up in the 3000s, C=C aromatic right around 1600.
The universal spec-solving algorithm (run in this order every time)
1. Count degrees of unsaturation first if you have the molecular formula: (2C + 2 + N − H − X) / 2. Each degree = 1 ring or 1 π bond.
2. Scan the IR for the 5 key peaks to identify the functional group (below).
3. Run the NMR 4-step — count peaks, integration, splitting, chemical shift.
4. Propose a structure that matches IR + NMR + formula. Sanity-check with degrees of unsaturation.
5. Eliminate answer choices that violate any rule. Pick what's left.
The IR Decision Flow
Is there a peak around 1700 cm⁻¹?
YES — you have a C=O. Now narrow it:
  • + broad OH overlapping C-H (2500-3300) = carboxylic acid
  • + two C-H stretches at 2720 & 2820 = aldehyde (the "aldehyde fingerprint")
  • + sharp N-H above 3300 = amide
  • + strong C-O at 1100-1300 = ester
  • none of the above = ketone
NO — no C=O. Look for:
  • Broad O-H at 3200-3600 = alcohol
  • Sharp N-H (1 or 2 peaks at 3300-3500) = amine (2 peaks = 1°, 1 peak = 2°)
  • Sharp C-H at ~3300 + weak C≡C at 2100-2150 = terminal alkyne
  • Medium-strong sharp peak at 2200-2260 = nitrile (C≡N)
  • C-H above 3000 (sp²) + peaks at 1500 & 1600 = aromatic ring
  • Only C-H below 3000 (sp³) + nothing else obvious = alkane / ether
The NMR Decision Flow
First, count peaks = number of chemical environments.
If n peaks = n unique H environments. Fewer peaks = more symmetry. 1 singlet for an unsymmetric molecule tells you all H's are equivalent (possibly by symmetry or by being chemically identical).
Then read integration.
Integer ratios. (3:2:3) = CH₃ : CH₂ : CH₃. (9:1) = 9 equivalent H (t-butyl) : something else.
Then splitting (n+1 rule).
singlet = 0 neighbors · doublet = 1 · triplet = 2 · quartet = 3 · septet = 6. Classic patterns: triplet + quartet = ethyl. septet + doublet = isopropyl. Large singlet at ~1.3 (9H) = t-butyl.
Finally chemical shift to locate each environment.
0-1.5 alkyl · 1.5-2.5 α to C=O or allylic · 2.5-3.5 next to EN atom · 3.5-4.5 on O · 4.5-6.5 vinyl · 6.5-8 aromatic · 9-10 aldehyde · 10-13 acid OH.
Live IR spectrum · click any region or labeled peak
Tap or focus a zone above. Each colored region groups peaks by physical origin — top-down scanning is the fastest way through any IR spectrum.
Mnemonic — The 4 Zones, top-down
Zone 1 (3200-3600) — X-H stretches. Broad round = O-H alcohol; BROADER reaching 2500 = carboxylic acid; 2 sharp = 1° amine; 1 sharp = 2° amine; sharp 3300 = terminal alkyne ≡C-H.
Zone 2 (2800-3100) — C-H stretches. Above 3000 = sp² (alkene/aromatic); below 3000 = sp³. Aldehyde gives twin small peaks at 2720 & 2820.
Zone 3 (2100-2260) — Triple bonds. Nitrile C≡N ≈ 2245 (strong); alkyne C≡C ≈ 2120 (weak).
Zone 4 (1650-1750) — C=O. Ester 1740 · Aldehyde 1725 · Ketone 1715 · Acid 1710 · Amide 1680. Always check here first.

Degrees of Unsaturation Calculator
Formula
DoU = (2C + 2 + N − H − X) / 2   ·   (ignore O and S — they don't change DoU)
Each DoU = 1 ring OR 1 π-bond (double bond = 1, triple = 2, benzene = 4).
Enter a molecular formula and click Calc. Example: benzene (C₆H₆) → 4 DoU = 1 ring + 3 π bonds.
Characteristic IR Spectra — the ones the DAT tests
The 5 IR peaks that cover 90% of DAT questions
Diagnostic priority
Always check for C=O around 1700 cm⁻¹ first — if it's there, narrow to aldehyde/ketone/acid/ester/amide using other peaks. If not, look for broad OH (3200-3600) or sharp N-H (3300-3500). Then triple bonds (2100-2260). C-H below 3000 = sp³; above = sp² or sp.
The 4-step NMR strategy
1
Count peaks — each signal = one chemical environment. More peaks = less symmetry.
2
Read integration — peak area = proton ratio. (3, 2, 1) = CH₃, CH₂, CH, etc.
3
Count splitting (n+1 rule) — singlet = 0 neighbors, doublet = 1, triplet = 2, quartet = 3, etc.
4
Read chemical shift — 0-1.5 sp³ alkyl · 2-3 next to C=O or ring · 3-4.5 attached to O/N · 4-6 vinyl · 6-8 aromatic · 9-10 aldehyde · 10-12 acid OH.

Real ¹H and ¹³C NMR Spectra — the patterns the DAT tests
How to read a real NMR
Left side = deshielded (high ppm, downfield). Right side = shielded (low ppm, upfield). TMS (tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄) is the 0-ppm reference — it's super-shielded because Si is electropositive, so every real proton in your sample appears to its left. Integration ratios are shown as numbers above each ¹H peak. For ¹³C, each unique carbon environment gives ONE line (broadband-decoupled — no splitting). DAT trick: count lines in ¹³C to count unique carbons; symmetry reduces the count.

Practice
IR PracticeDAT-style · 3 questions
0/3
1An IR spectrum shows a strong, sharp absorption at ~1715 cm⁻¹. Most likely functional group:
Explanation
B is correct. The carbonyl region 1650–1800 cm⁻¹ is one of the most distinctive in IR. A strong, sharp peak around 1715 cm⁻¹ is a textbook ketone or aldehyde C=O. Other carbonyls: esters slightly higher (~1735), amides lower (~1680), carboxylic acids ~1710 (with a broad O–H 2500–3300). (A) O–H of alcohol is a broad band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹. (C) C≡C is weak at 2100–2260 cm⁻¹. (D) N–H is in the 3300–3500 region. The carbonyl region is high-yield DAT — memorize 1700-ish as "look for C=O."
2A broad, strong absorption from ~2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ overlapping with a sharp ~1710 cm⁻¹ peak suggests:
Explanation
A is correct. The CARBOXYLIC ACID is the only functional group that produces BOTH a very broad O–H (2500–3300 cm⁻¹, often called the "bird-wing" because it dips into the C–H region) AND a strong sharp C=O (~1710 cm⁻¹). The breadth of the O–H is the diagnostic sign — much broader than an alcohol's O–H because of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding (carboxylic acids exist as dimers in solution). Together those two features = -COOH, period.
3Which IR region is called the "fingerprint region" and is typically ignored for functional-group identification?
Explanation
C is correct. Anything below ~1500 cm⁻¹ is the FINGERPRINT REGION — densely packed with overlapping bands from skeletal vibrations of the whole molecule. Useful for matching against a known reference spectrum (every molecule's fingerprint region is unique, hence the name) but NOT useful for functional-group ID. Cross out answer choices that point to peaks below 1500 — they're noise for ID purposes. Your useful signals: O–H/N–H (3000s), C–H (2800–3100), C≡C/C≡N (2100–2260), C=O (~1700), C=C (~1650), aromatic C=C (~1500–1600).
Practice
NMR PracticeDAT-style · 2 questions
0/2
1A ¹H NMR peak appears as a TRIPLET. Most likely, the protons giving rise to that peak have:
Explanation
C is correct. n + 1 RULE: a proton with n equivalent neighboring protons (on adjacent carbons, ³J coupling) appears as a peak split into n + 1 lines. Triplet means n + 1 = 3 → n = 2 neighbors. Classic example: the CH₂ in an ethyl group (-CH₂-CH₃) appears as a quartet (3 neighbors → 4 lines) and the CH₃ appears as a triplet (2 neighbors → 3 lines). (A) 3 neighbors gives a quartet; (D) 0 neighbors gives a singlet.
2A ¹H NMR spectrum shows two singlets at 1.2 ppm and 3.7 ppm in a 6:2 integration ratio. Most likely structure:
Explanation
B is correct. Methyl tert-butyl ether has two distinct proton environments: the OCH₃ (3 H's, near oxygen, ~3.3 ppm) and the (CH₃)₃C (9 H's, away from oxygen, ~1.2 ppm). Reducing the 9:3 integration to a 6:2 ratio fits if we re-read by relative proportion (3:1 = 6:2). Both signals are SINGLETS because no protons sit on adjacent carbons (the central C of the t-Bu has no H's; the O has no adjacent C–H). (A) Ethyl acetate would show a quartet (CH₂) + triplet (CH₃) + singlet (acetate CH₃). (C) Acetone has only one peak (all 6 H's equivalent). (D) Propanol would show splitting (multiplets, not singlets).
Spectroscopy

Mass Spectrometry — M⁺, M+1, M+2

MS gives you the molecular weight directly and lets you detect halogen atoms through isotope patterns. The DAT tests M⁺ identification, the M+2 Cl/Br pattern, and basic fragmentation.

The four peaks you must know
M⁺ (molecular ion peak): the molecule minus one electron. Gives the molecular weight directly.
M+1: one mass unit heavier than M⁺. Small peak — caused by ~1.1% natural abundance of ¹³C. A molecule with n carbons gives an M+1 peak of roughly n × 1.1% relative to M⁺.
M+2 (LARGE): if M+2 is about one-third the height of M⁺, the molecule contains chlorine (³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl = 3 : 1). If M+2 ≈ equal to M⁺, the molecule contains bromine (⁷⁹Br : ⁸¹Br ≈ 1 : 1). This is one of the easiest DAT patterns to spot.
Base peak: the tallest peak, set to 100% relative intensity. Often NOT the M⁺ — it's usually a very stable carbocation fragment.
Two fragmentation patterns
Alpha-cleavage: bond adjacent to a heteroatom (N, O) or carbonyl breaks; common in alcohols, amines, carbonyl compounds. The fragment with the heteroatom is often the base peak.
McLafferty rearrangement: requires a carbonyl with a gamma-H; a 6-membered cyclic H-transfer occurs → alkene + enol fragments. Produces a characteristic fragment 30-60 mass units lighter than M⁺.
Worked examples
CompoundM⁺M+1 noteM+2 noteKey fragment
Chloroethane (C₂H₅Cl)64Small (~2.2%)~33% height — Cl presentm/z 29 (C₂H₅⁺, loss of Cl)
Bromoethane (C₂H₅Br)108Small~100% height — Br present (equal twin peaks)m/z 29 (C₂H₅⁺, loss of Br)
Acetone (C₃H₆O)58~3.3%Negligible (no Cl/Br)m/z 43 (CH₃CO⁺, base peak)

Teaching · Acetone Acetone fragments cleanly. Both α-cleavages (one on each side of the carbonyl) give the same acylium ion CH₃CO⁺ at m/z 43 — that's why 43 is the base peak. Loss of CH₃ as a radical leaves a positively-charged acylium that's resonance-stabilized (R-C≡O⁺ ↔ R-C=O⁺). M⁺ at 58 is small because the cation prefers to break.
Practice
Mass Spec PracticeDAT-style · 5 questions
0/5
1A compound shows M⁺ at m/z 122 and a peak at m/z 124 of approximately EQUAL intensity (about 1:1). The molecule most likely contains:
Explanation
B is correct. Bromine has two natural isotopes, ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, in nearly equal abundance (~50:50). So one Br gives an M / M+2 pair of nearly EQUAL height. One Cl (³⁵Cl:³⁷Cl ≈ 3:1) gives an M / M+2 with intensity ratio about 3:1. Two Cl gives M : M+2 : M+4 ≈ 9 : 6 : 1. One S gives M+2 ~4.4% of M (much smaller). The 1:1 M:M+2 pattern is the BROMINE FINGERPRINT — instantly diagnostic.
2A ketone shows an unusually large peak at m/z = (M − 28). The most likely rearrangement is:
Explanation
C is correct. The McLafferty rearrangement is a SIGNATURE fragmentation of carbonyls with γ-hydrogens. A γ-H migrates through a 6-membered transition state to the carbonyl oxygen; the molecule breaks apart, expelling a neutral alkene (often C₂H₄, mass 28) and leaving a charged enol-ether cation. Loss of 28 from a carbonyl is the McLafferty fingerprint. (A) α-cleavage typically loses 15 (CH₃) or 29 (CHO) depending on substituent. (B) M−18 is water loss (alcohols, sometimes COOH). (D) Methyl loss is M−15.
3In a mass spectrum, the BASE PEAK is:
Explanation
A is correct. The BASE PEAK is the tallest peak in the spectrum — by convention, normalized to 100% relative abundance; all other peaks are scaled relative to it. It represents the most-abundant cation produced under the ionization conditions. The base peak is OFTEN a particularly stable cation (which is why fragmentation favors its formation), but the definition is purely about peak height, not stability. (B) M⁺ may or may not be the base peak — for stable molecules it might be; for fragile molecules (like long alkanes), M⁺ can be very small and the base peak is a fragment.
4An acid chloride (R-COCl) is expected to show what isotope pattern in its M⁺ peak?
Explanation
B is correct. Chlorine has two natural isotopes, ³⁵Cl (~75.8%) and ³⁷Cl (~24.2%), giving a roughly 3:1 abundance ratio. So a compound with ONE chlorine shows M and M+2 in ~3:1 ratio. One bromine (50:50 ⁷⁹/⁸¹) would give ~1:1 — answer (C). Two chlorines give 9:6:1. The 3:1 M:M+2 pattern is the chlorine fingerprint, distinct from the 1:1 bromine fingerprint.
5A compound C₂H₆O shows a strong peak at m/z 31. The fragment most likely is:
Explanation
D is correct. C₂H₆O (m/z 46, M⁺) is ethanol. Loss of CH₃ (mass 15) gives an ion at m/z 31, which is CH₂=OH⁺ — a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion (CH₂=O⁺H ↔ ⁺CH₂-OH). This is the BASE PEAK of ethanol's mass spectrum and a textbook example of α-cleavage of an alcohol. (A) CH₃⁺ is m/z 15. (B) CH₃CH₂⁺ is m/z 29 — also present but usually smaller. (C) H₂O⁺ would be m/z 18 — water loss.

Master Map

The Functional Group Roadmap

Everything in DAT organic is functional group interconversion. Memorize this web of connections first — every named reaction you'll learn is just one arrow on this map. Alkenes sit at the center because nearly every other group traces back to them.

Plate I — The Central Web of Functional Groups
Clickable. Solid arrow = one-step conversion · Dashed = two-way interchange · Gold hub = alkene center. Each node shows the real structure.
Why the alkene is the center of the universe
  • Alkenes are the most common synthetic "branch point" — they can be made from alkyl halides (E2), alcohols (dehydration), and alkynes (Lindlar/Na,NH₃).
  • From an alkene you can reach almost any other functional group in ONE step: alkane (H₂), alkyl halide (HX), alcohol (H₂O), epoxide (mCPBA), diol (OsO₄), carbonyl (O₃).
  • If a DAT roadmap question looks impossibly long, check whether you can go through an alkene — it's usually the shortest path.

Synthesis Lab

Synthesis Lab

Two training modes. The Reagent Predictor lets you pick any substrate and reagent and instantly see the predicted product with stereochemistry, regiochemistry, and the mechanism family. The Synthesis Puzzle challenges you to transform a starting material into a target by choosing the correct sequence of reagents — the DAT's favorite question type, drilled until it's automatic.

Retrosynthesis · the disconnection trainer
Forward synthesis asks "what does this reagent make?" Retrosynthesis asks the reverse: "given the target, what bond do I disconnect, and what reagents combine to form it?" This is the missing skill that separates 22-tier students from the rest.
The retrosynthesis mindset
Three habits: (1) Identify the functional group in the target — that tells you the bond-forming reaction. (2) Disconnect the key bond (usually the C–C or C–heteroatom bond that the named reaction would create). (3) Map each piece back to its starting material. The "retro arrow" (⇒) is the bookkeeping symbol. Each disconnection reveals two simpler synthons (the abstract building blocks) which then map to real reagents.
Target 1 · 2° alcohol from Grignard

Target: Ph–CH(OH)–CH₃ (1-phenylethanol).
Disconnect: the C–C bond between the OH-bearing C and one of its substituents.
Synthons: phenyl anion + acetaldehyde.
Real reagents: PhMgBr (Grignard) + CH₃CHO, then H₃O⁺ workup.
Rule: Any 2° alcohol can be made from a Grignard + an aldehyde. Any 3° alcohol → Grignard + ketone. Any 1° alcohol → Grignard + formaldehyde. The retro-Grignard is the most-used disconnection on the DAT.

Target 2 · ester from acid + alcohol

Target: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ (ethyl acetate).
Disconnect: the C–O single bond between the carbonyl C and the alcohol O.
Synthons: acetate "cation equivalent" + ethoxide.
Real reagents: acetic acid + ethanol + H⁺ catalyst (Fischer esterification) — or, faster, acetyl chloride + ethanol.
Rule: Esters retro-disconnect to acid + alcohol. The Fischer route is reversible (use excess alcohol or remove water to drive forward); the acid-chloride route is irreversible.

Target 3 · meta-disubstituted aromatic

Target: meta-bromonitrobenzene.
Disconnect: in EAS, the second substituent's regiochemistry is set by the FIRST. To get meta-product, the first group must be a meta-director.
Order: nitrate first (NO₂ is a strong meta-director and meta-deactivator), then brominate. If you brominate first, Br is an o/p director — you would get ortho/para nitrobromobenzene, not meta.
Rule: Aromatic disubstitution problems are ORDER-OF-OPERATIONS puzzles. The directing group going in first sets the regiochemistry of the second.

Target 4 · 1,3-dicarbonyl from aldol/Claisen

Target: CH₃-CO-CH(CH₃)-CO-CH₃ (a 1,3-diketone).
Disconnect: at the alpha-beta bond between the two carbonyls. The alpha-C of one ketone formed a new bond to the carbonyl-C of the other.
Synthons: enolate of one ketone + the carbonyl of the other.
Real reagents: two methyl ketones + base (NaOEt) → enolate attacks the other → β-hydroxy ketone → dehydrate (heat) → α,β-unsat. For 1,3-dicarbonyls specifically: Claisen condensation between two esters or mixed aldol.
Rule: Whenever you see a 1,3-relationship between two carbonyls, think enolate. Disconnect at the bond between alpha-C and the other carbonyl-C.

Target 5 · alkene from Wittig

Target: Ph–CH=CH–CH₃ (1-phenylpropene).
Disconnect: the C=C double bond. Which side was the original C=O? Either could work — choose the one that gives a more accessible reagent.
Synthons: aldehyde + ylide. PhCHO + Ph₃P=CHCH₃ (ethylidenetriphenylphosphorane) → 1-phenylpropene + Ph₃P=O.
Rule: Any C=C can be retro-disconnected as carbonyl + ylide via Wittig. The retro-Wittig is the cleanest way to install C=C with controlled geometry. (E/Z depends on stabilized vs unstabilized ylide.)

The decision tree

When you face a target, ask:
(1) Does it contain a carbonyl + alpha-substituent? → think enolate/aldol/Claisen.
(2) Does it contain an alcohol? → think Grignard.
(3) Does it contain a C=C? → think Wittig, or addition to alkyne, or elimination.
(4) Does it contain an aromatic ring with substituents? → think EAS, plan order of operations to set regiochemistry.
(5) Does it contain an ester / amide? → disconnect at the C–O or C–N bond between carbonyl and heteroatom.
Most DAT synthesis problems reduce to one of these five disconnections.

Identify the functional group → disconnect the key bond → map synthons → name reagents.
