Tier I · Foundation

Bonding, resonance & molecular geometry

Every later hub leans on this one. Hybridization tells you geometry. Sigma vs pi tells you what rotates. Resonance tells you where the electrons actually live (a hybrid of all valid contributors). Newman and chair conformers tell you which 3D shape costs the least energy. Master the four interactives below and the rest of OChem reads like a story.

Coach lock Count electron domains. Read off the table. 2 / 3 / 4 → sp / sp² / sp³ → 180° / 120° / 109.5°. The rest is bookkeeping.
Plate I — The Hybridization Table
Three carbons. Three hybridizations. Three geometries. Memorize this once and bonding is solved.
Tool 1 — The Hybridization Decoder
Click 2, 3, or 4 to set the electron-domain count. Geometry, bond angle, and hybridization update live. Lone pairs count as a domain — that's why H₂O is sp³ not sp².
Tool 2 — Sigma vs Pi
Single = 1σ. Double = 1σ + 1π. Triple = 1σ + 2π. Pi bonds prevent rotation — that's why alkenes have cis/trans isomers but alkanes do not.
Single bond · 1σ · rotates freely
Double bond · 1σ + 1π · NO rotation (cis/trans)
Triple bond · 1σ + 2π · linear · sp
Tool 3 — Resonance Arrow Pusher
Pi electrons and lone pairs move; atoms stay. Click Push to flip acetate's electron arrangement. The real molecule is the average of both contributors — both C–O bonds are equivalent, charge spread over two oxygens. That delocalization is why –COOH (pKa 5) is way more acidic than –OH (pKa 16).
Rules of the road
1. Only π and lone-pair electrons move — never sigma bonds, never atoms.
2. You can push electrons INTO an atom that lacks an octet (carbocation).
3. If destination already has full octet, push electrons OUT the other side simultaneously.
4. Most stable contributor: full octets, fewest charges, − on most electronegative.
Tool 4 — Newman Conformer Flip
Drag the slider to rotate the back carbon. Energy curve shows you that anti (180°) is most stable, gauche (60°) costs ~3.8 kJ/mol, eclipsed (0°) is the worst. Big groups want to be far apart.
Energy curve · gauche bumps + eclipsed peaks
Tool 5 — Cyclohexane Chair Flip
Cyclohexane sits in the chair conformation (every C at 109.5°, no strain). Each ring C has one axial bond (perpendicular) and one equatorial (~horizontal). A ring flip swaps axial ↔ equatorial. Bigger groups want equatorial — 1,3-diaxial repulsions cost ~7.6 kJ/mol per axial methyl.
Methyl currently equatorial — most stable.
1
Hybridization · the 2/3/4 rule
Geometry
▾
Count electron groups on a central atom (lone pairs included). 2 → sp / linear / 180°. 3 → sp² / trigonal planar / 120°. 4 → sp³ / tetrahedral / 109.5°. The unhybridized p-orbitals make the π bonds of double and triple bonds.
Examples: CO₂ → 2 groups → sp · linear
BF₃ → 3 groups → sp² · trigonal planar
CH₄, NH₃, H₂O → 4 groups → sp³ · tetrahedral (water "looks bent" because lone pairs are invisible — geometry is still tetrahedral)
2
Sigma vs pi · what rotates
Bond order
▾
Single = 1σ (head-on overlap, rotates freely). Double = 1σ + 1π (side-on p overlap, no rotation → cis/trans isomers possible). Triple = 1σ + 2π (linear, sp).
Counting σ + π in a molecule:
Each bond contributes exactly 1σ.
Each double bond adds 1π. Each triple bond adds 2π.
Acetic acid (CH₃COOH): 7σ + 1π.
3
Resonance · push electrons, never atoms
Delocalization
▾
Only π and lone-pair electrons move. Sigma bonds and atom positions stay fixed. The real molecule is a hybrid (weighted average) of all valid contributors. Best contributor: all atoms have full octets · fewest formal charges · negative on the most electronegative atom · positive on the least.
Why it matters: resonance stabilizes anions → makes their conjugate acids stronger. Carboxylate (2 equivalent O contributors) makes RCOOH (pKa 5) about 10¹¹× more acidic than ROH (pKa 16).
4
Newman conformers · anti > gauche > eclipsed
Conformer
▾
For n-butane: anti (180°) is lowest energy. Gauche (60°) costs ~3.8 kJ/mol from a single methyl-methyl gauche interaction. Eclipsed varies (15–20 kJ/mol) depending on what aligns; totally eclipsed methyl-methyl is the worst.
Energy ladder (n-butane):
Anti = 0 kJ/mol
Gauche = +3.8
Eclipsed H-CH₃ = +6 (per pair)
Eclipsed CH₃-CH₃ (totally eclipsed) = +20
5
Cyclohexane chair · big = equatorial
Ring
▾
Chair conformation puts every C at 109.5° (no strain). Each ring C has one axial bond (perpendicular to the ring's average plane) and one equatorial (~horizontal). 1,3-diaxial repulsions cost ~7.6 kJ/mol per axial methyl. Bigger groups always prefer equatorial.
Trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane: both methyls can sit equatorial in one chair → most stable diastereomer. cis-1,4: one must be axial → higher energy.
Tier I · Foundation

Nomenclature — IUPAC for every functional group

Every DAT shows up with at least two pure-naming items and a dozen reagents identified by name. Find the longest chain that contains the highest-priority FG, number to give that FG the lowest locant, and alphabetize substituents. Below: the priority chart, a structure-to-name speed game, and a name-to-structure builder.

Coach lock Highest-priority FG owns the suffix. Everything else becomes a prefix. Carboxylic acid wins everything.
The Priority Ladder
Top of the list = parent suffix. Lower-priority groups become prefixes (oxo-, hydroxy-, amino-, methoxy-, halo-, nitro-).
01Carboxylic acid-oic acid(carboxy-)
02Ester-oatealkoxycarbonyl-
03Amide-amideamido-
04Nitrile-nitrilecyano-
05Aldehyde-aloxo- (or formyl-)
06Ketone-oneoxo-
07Alcohol-olhydroxy-
08Amine-amineamino-
09Alkene-ene—
10Alkyne-yne—
11Alkane-anealkyl-
12Ether—alkoxy-
13Halide—fluoro/chloro/bromo/iodo-
14Nitro—nitro-
Name-That-Molecule · live drill
A random structure each round. Pick the IUPAC name. Diagnostic feedback shows you why the wrong choices fail.
Trap 1
Numbering for the wrong end. Highest-priority FG must take the lowest locant — even if other substituents are forced to higher numbers.
Trap 2
Cis/trans where E/Z is required. If both alkene carbons have non-H substituents and they're different, cis/trans is ambiguous — use E/Z (CIP priority).
Trap 3
Ignoring the parent-chain choice. If two chains tie for length, pick the one with MORE substituents. Length first; on a tie, branch count breaks it.
E/Z Assignment · CIP on each alkene carbon
The E/Z protocol
1. Take the C=C. Look at the two substituents on the LEFT alkene carbon. Rank them by CIP priority — call the higher-priority one "L1" (the lower one "L2").
2. Same on the RIGHT carbon → R1 (higher) and R2 (lower).
3. If L1 and R1 are on the same side of the double bond → Z (zusammen, German for "together").
4. If L1 and R1 are on opposite sides → E (entgegen, "opposite").

Memory: "Zame zide" / "Epposite". Or: Z is the one with priorities cuddled up.
Ex 1
2-bromo-2-butene · simple case
Br on top-left, CH₃ on top-right
Br on the top of the left alkene carbon, CH₃ on the bottom; CH₃ on the top of the right alkene carbon, H on the bottom. What is the E/Z designation?
Z
L1 (Br, top) and R1 (CH₃, top) sit on the same side of the C=C → Z (zusammen). Full name: (Z)-2-bromo-2-butene.
Walkthrough
Left C: substituents are Br and CH₃. Higher priority = Br (atomic #35 vs C's 6). L1 = Br, on top.
Right C: substituents are CH₃ and H. Higher priority = CH₃ (C #6 vs H #1). R1 = CH₃, on top.
Compare positions: L1 (Br, top) and R1 (CH₃, top) are on the same side → Z.
Full name: (Z)-2-bromo-2-butene.
Note: "cis" would also work here colloquially, but Z is the formal answer because the two top substituents (Br and CH₃) are different identities.
Ex 2
cis/trans fails · 4 different substituents
cis/trans undefined; E/Z required
Cl on the top of the left alkene carbon, F on the bottom; Br on the top of the right alkene carbon, CH₃ on the bottom. All four substituents differ — cis/trans is undefined, so E/Z is required.
Z
L1 (Cl, top) and R1 (Br, top) sit on the same side → Z. Note: cis/trans is undefined here because no two of the four substituents are identical.
Walkthrough
cis/trans? All four substituents are different identities → cis/trans is meaningless. Must use E/Z.
Left C: Cl (#17) vs F (#9). L1 = Cl, on top.
Right C: Br (#35) vs CH₃ (C #6). R1 = Br, on top.
Same side (both on top) → Z.
Notice the trap: the "heavier" substituent on each carbon doesn't have to be on the same side just because they're heavy — it's about which side the highest-priority of each carbon ends up on. If Br were on the bottom right instead, R1 would be on the bottom, L1 still on the top, and the answer would flip to E.
Ex 3
Phantom atoms decide it · vinyl vs ethyl, CHO vs CH₂OH
Same first atom, different next sphere
Vinyl (–CH=CH₂) on the top of the left alkene carbon, ethyl (–CH₂CH₃) on the bottom; aldehyde (–CHO) on the top of the right alkene carbon, hydroxymethyl (–CH₂OH) on the bottom. Every substituent starts with C — the priority is decided at the second sphere by phantom atoms.
Phantom-atom expansion · why second sphere differs
Z
L1 (vinyl, top) and R1 (CHO, top) sit on the same side → Z. Both winners are decided by phantom atoms — vinyl by the doubled C, –CHO by the doubled O.
Walkthrough
Left C: both substituents start with C → must look at next sphere.
· –CH=CH₂ (vinyl): the directly-attached C is double-bonded to another C → the second sphere is (C, C, H) because CIP duplicates the double bond, adding a phantom C.
· –CH₂CH₃ (ethyl): the second sphere is (C, H, H).
(C, C, H) beats (C, H, H) at the second slot. L1 = vinyl, on top.

Right C: both start with C → next sphere.
· –CHO (aldehyde): second sphere = (O, O, H) — phantom O from the C=O.
· –CH₂OH: second sphere = (O, H, H).
(O, O, H) beats (O, H, H). R1 = CHO, on top.

L1 (vinyl, top) and R1 (CHO, top) are on the same side → Z.
Why this is on the DAT: the phantom-atom rule for double bonds is the single most-tested CIP subtlety. Memorize: a doubly-bonded atom counts twice at the next sphere; triply-bonded counts three times.
Ref
CIP quick reference · the 4 rules in order
Walk top-to-bottom; stop at first decisive rule
Apply these in order. The first rule that distinguishes two substituents wins — never skip ahead. On the DAT, Rule 1 settles most cases; Rule 3 settles the rest; Rules 2 and 4 are rare but tested.
RULE 1 · ATOMIC NUMBER
Higher atomic number wins. Compare at the first sphere; whichever atom's Z is larger is higher priority.
I > Br > Cl > S > F > O > N > C > H
RULE 2 · ATOMIC MASS (ISOTOPES)
If atomic numbers tie (i.e., same element), the heavier isotope wins.
D (²H) > H  ·  ¹³C > ¹²C
Rare on DAT — but every few exams a deuterium-labeled stereocenter appears.
RULE 3 · STEP OUT TO NEXT SPHERE
If the first atoms tie, compare the set of atoms one bond further out. Sort each set high-to-low; compare slot-by-slot.
–CH₂OH: (O, H, H)
–CH₃  : (H, H, H)
slot 1: O > H → CH₂OH wins
RULE 4 · DOUBLE / TRIPLE BONDS = PHANTOMS
Each multi-bonded atom is counted multiple times. A=B becomes A–(B) and B–(A); A≡B becomes A–(B)–(B) and B–(A)–(A).
–CHO  : (O, (O), H)
–CH₂OH: (O, H, H)
slot 2: (O) > H → CHO wins
How to walk the rules
1. Look at the four atoms directly attached to the chiral C. Apply Rule 1 (atomic number). If you can rank all four, you're done.
2. If two atoms are the same element but different isotopes, apply Rule 2. (Rare. Only matters when D or ¹³C is explicitly drawn.)
3. If two substituents are still tied, step out one bond and compare the second-sphere atom sets. This is Rule 3.
4. Anywhere you see a double or triple bond inside a substituent, apply Rule 4 first — duplicate the multi-bonded atoms — then compare second-sphere sets.

Mantra: Z first, then mass, then step out, then count phantoms. Stop at the first rule that decides.
Tier I · Foundation

Acid-Base CARDIO — the 5-factor pKa ranking

The single highest-leverage skill on the OChem section. CARDIO ranks any pair of acids by walking five factors in priority order — stop at the first one that differentiates. The ranking drives reactivity (nuc/base strength), mechanism (SN1 / SN2 / E1 / E2), stability arguments, and biology (which form predominates at physiological pH). Master CARDIO and pKa stops being a memorization problem; it becomes a 2-second priority walk.

Coach lock Charge → Atom → Resonance → Dipole/Induction → Orbital. Walk in order. Stop at the first factor that differs. Always look at the conjugate base — most acidic = whose anion is most stable.
Jump to: pKa Ladder 5-Factor Priority CARDIO Wizard Worked Factors
Foundational — Acid strength = conjugate-base stability
When HA loses its proton, the negative charge lands on whatever atom held the H. The more stable that resulting anion (A⁻), the further right the equilibrium sits, and the lower the pKa. Every CARDIO factor is just a different way that A⁻ can be made more stable. When asked "which is more acidic?", redraw both conjugate bases, then walk CARDIO until one factor decides.
Acid-Base Ranker · drag-to-rank by pKa
The highest-yield DAT drill. Drag each compound into the ladder by acid strength — strongest acid (lowest pKa) at the top. The acidic H is highlighted in red on every tile. Don't memorize pKa values; reason about conjugate-base stability (CARDIO walks). Reveal explains why each compound sits where it does.
Round 1 Drag 8 compounds into the pKa ladder 0 / 8 placed
stronger acid · low pKa
weaker acid · high pKa
Score: 0 / 8
Plate I-A — The pKa Landmark Ladder
Nine anchors span 60 pKa units (10⁶⁰ in Keq). Lock these compounds in spatial memory; every pKa question reduces to "which landmark is it next to?". Lower pKa = stronger acid = more stable conjugate base.
Plate I-B — The CARDIO Priority Walk
Each row owns a domain. The question to ask at each step is on the right; if both species look the same on that question, drop down to the next factor.
CARDIO Wizard · pick the more acidic species
Each round shows two acids with their hand-drawn structure and pKa range. Pick the more acidic one. The wizard then walks CARDIO step-by-step and highlights the factor that decided.
8 rounds · cycles
How to read the feedback bar
The five letters under "factor walk" are CARDIO. Skipped factors are dimmed; the one that decided lights up in gold. After 5–10 rounds, you'll start predicting which factor will fire before clicking — that's the goal. The Wong palette (teal-green = confirmed, orange = let's revisit) is color-blind-safe.
The 5 factors · worked examples with conjugate-base diagrams
C
Charge — start positive, end neutral
CARDIO 1
When two acids differ in net charge, charge always wins. A cation acid (H₃O⁺, NH₄⁺, ROH₂⁺) yields a neutral conjugate base — losing charge is hugely stabilizing. Same atom, same orbital, same neighbors: doesn't matter. Charge dominates.
H₃O⁺  ⇌  H₂O + H⁺   (pKa = −1.7)   ||   H₂O ⇌ HO⁻ + H⁺   (pKa = 16)
winner
H₃O⁺  (hydronium)
pKa −1.7 · A⁻ = H₂O (neutral, very stable)
vs
loser
H₂O  (water)
pKa 16 · A⁻ = HO⁻ (anion, less stable than neutral)
Why this happens
Removing a proton from H₃O⁺ removes a charge (+1 → 0). Removing a proton from H₂O creates a charge (0 → −1). Going from +1 to 0 is downhill (−ΔG). Going from 0 to −1 is uphill (+ΔG). The charge gap alone is worth ~17 pKa units (~10¹⁷× difference in Keq).
Verdict: H₃O⁺ wins by 17 pKa units. The same logic explains why NH₄⁺ (pKa 9) beats NH₃ (pKa 35), and why RNH₃⁺ (pKa 10) beats RNH₂ (pKa 35) — at physiological pH 7.4, an amine is mostly protonated. Cross-link → Hub 10 · amine basicity.
A
Atom — electronegativity (across) and size (down)
CARDIO 2
When the H sits on different atoms, two periodic-table rules fire. Across a row: more electronegative atoms hold negative charge better → CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF. Down a column: bigger atoms diffuse the charge over a larger volume → HF < HCl < HBr < HI. Size beats electronegativity when both pull in opposite directions.
HF  ⇌  F⁻ + H⁺  (pKa 3)  ||  HCl ⇌ Cl⁻ + H⁺  (pKa −7) · across-period vs down-column
across · HF wins vs CH₄
HF
pKa 3 · vs CH₄ pKa 50 → HF wins by 47
vs
down · HCl wins vs HF
HCl
pKa −7 · vs HF pKa 3 → HCl wins by 10
When EN and size compete
Size always wins down a column. F is more electronegative than I (4.0 vs 2.7), but I⁻ is so much larger that the negative charge is spread over a far bigger volume — and HI (pKa −10) is a stronger acid than HF (pKa 3) by 13 pKa units. The same logic explains thiols vs alcohols: RSH (pKa 10) is more acidic than ROH (pKa 16) because S is bigger than O.
Verdict: Same row → trust EN. Same column → trust size. Different row and column → think about which axis dominates (usually size). The classic CARDIO-A pair is HF vs CH₄ (47-unit gap, all from EN).
R
Resonance — spread the charge, stabilize the anion
CARDIO 3
When the conjugate base can delocalize the negative charge across multiple atoms, A⁻ becomes far more stable. The classic CARDIO-R pair is the carboxylic acid vs alcohol gap: same O, same row, same column — but RCOO⁻ has two equivalent oxygens sharing the charge (50% on each), while RO⁻ keeps it all on one atom. ~11 pKa units of stabilization from one π system.
RCOOH ⇌ RCOO⁻ + H⁺ (pKa 5)  ||  ROH ⇌ RO⁻ + H⁺ (pKa 16)
winner · resonance-stabilized
RCOO⁻  (carboxylate)
pKa 4–5 (acetic acid 4.76)
vs
loser · localized
RO⁻  (alkoxide)
pKa 16 (ethanol 15.9)
Phenol (pKa 10) is the famous middle case
Phenoxide (PhO⁻) delocalizes the negative charge into the ring at the ortho and para positions — so charge spreads to 4 atoms instead of 2. Cyclohexanol (no ring resonance) has pKa 16. Phenol has pKa 10. Six pKa units (~10⁶× more acidic) earned by aromatic ring resonance. This is also why para-nitrophenol (pKa 7) beats phenol — the NO₂ at para extends resonance to the nitro O.
Verdict: Whenever you see a C=O, NO₂, or aromatic ring next to the acidic H, draw the conjugate base and look for delocalization. Cross-link → Hub 09 · carboxylic acids.
D
Dipole / Induction — σ-bond electron pull at a distance
CARDIO 4
Electron-withdrawing groups (F, Cl, NO₂, CF₃, C=O at distance) drain electron density through σ-bonds, helping stabilize a developing negative charge. Effect is cumulative (more EWGs → bigger effect) and distance-dependent (drops sharply with each carbon between EWG and acidic site). The classic D pair: chloroacetic acid series.
CH₃COOH (pKa 4.76)  >  ClCH₂COOH (2.86)  >  Cl₂CHCOOH (1.29)  >  Cl₃CCOOH (0.65)
winner · 3 EWGs adjacent
CCl₃COOH  (TCA)
pKa 0.65 (~10,000× more acidic than acetic)
vs
loser · no EWGs
CH₃COOH  (acetic)
pKa 4.76
Trap — distance kills induction fast
Inductive effect roughly halves with each σ-bond. Cl on the α-carbon (next to COOH) shifts pKa by ~2 units. Cl on the β-carbon shifts it by ~0.3. Cl on γ → barely measurable. The DAT loves to ask "which Cl-substituted acid is most acidic?" — answer is always the one with Cl closest to the carboxyl.
Verdict: Count EWGs. Closer beats more. F > Cl > Br > I for inductive pull (EN order, opposite of size). Resonance always beats induction — which is why CARDIO puts R above D.
O
Orbital — s-character of the carbanion
CARDIO 5
The s-orbital sits closer to the nucleus than p-orbitals. More s-character in a hybrid means electrons are held tighter — more electronegative behavior. So an sp carbanion (50% s) is far more stable than sp² (33%) or sp³ (25%). This is the only factor that ranks C–H acidities of pure hydrocarbons, and it's the reason terminal alkynes have a synthetically useful pKa (25).
HC≡C–H (pKa 25)  ≪  H₂C=CH–H (pKa 44)  ≪  H₃C–CH₂–H (pKa 50)
winner · sp 50% s
HC≡CH  (acetylene)
pKa 25 · NaNH₂ (pKaH 38) deprotonates cleanly
vs
loser · sp³ 25% s
CH₃CH₃  (ethane)
pKa 50 · no common base reaches it
Why we use NaNH₂ for terminal alkynes
A base deprotonates an acid only when its conjugate acid has a higher pKa than the substrate. NaNH₂ (pKaH = 38) clears HC≡CR (pKa 25) by 13 units → quantitative deprotonation. NaOH (pKaH 16) cannot deprotonate a terminal alkyne — the equilibrium sits all the way left. Match the base to the acid using the pKa ladder.
Verdict: Orbital is the tiebreaker. It only fires when charge, atom, resonance, and induction all match. Most often: when comparing C–H acidities across sp / sp² / sp³.
Applying CARDIO · basicity is acidity-in-reverse
Decision widget
Acidity ↔ Basicity — the same factors, mirrored
memorize once
Most acidic HAlow pKa
Conjugate base A⁻ is most stable — it doesn't want the H back
Walk CARDIO downward through HA → A⁻
HCl (pKa −7) → Cl⁻ is the worst base ever
Strong acid ⇒ weak conjugate base
↔
Most basic Bhigh pKaH
Conjugate acid BH⁺ is most stable — wants its electron pair back as a bond
Walk CARDIO backwards from B → BH⁺ (lone pair holds the H tightly)
R₃N (pKaH 10) is the best amine base; aniline (pKaH 4.6) is weak — N lone pair in resonance with ring
Strong base ⇒ weak conjugate acid
The flip: "most acidic" and "most basic" use the same 5 factors — you just look at the opposite side of the equilibrium. To rank a set of amines by basicity, draw the protonated form (RNH₃⁺) and ask: which conjugate acid has the highest pKa? That amine is the strongest base. → Hub 10 · amines.
Physiological pH — predict the predominant form
Blood is buffered at pH 7.4. The Henderson-Hasselbalch rule of thumb: when pH > pKa, the deprotonated form dominates. So carboxylic acids (pKa 5) are deprotonated at pH 7.4 → carry a negative charge (RCOO⁻). Amines (pKaH 10) are protonated → carry a positive charge (RNH₃⁺). This explains why amino acids exist as zwitterions, and why histidine (pKaH 6) flips state across the physiological window — the only standard amino acid that does. CARDIO ranks pKa; pKa predicts charge state; charge state predicts biology.
CARDIO takeaways
  • Strongest acid = most stable conjugate base. Always redraw A⁻ before judging.
  • Walk in order: C → A → R → D → O. Stop at the first row that differs.
  • Charge wins by ~17 units (e.g. NH₄⁺ vs NH₃). Atom (across) is worth ~10–47 units. Resonance worth ~6–11 units. Induction worth 1–4 units per group. Orbital is a tiebreaker.
  • For basicity, run CARDIO in reverse on the protonated form. Strongest base = highest pKaH.
  • At physiological pH 7.4: RCOOH is deprotonated (RCOO⁻, anionic); RNH₂ is protonated (RNH₃⁺, cationic).
Hub 01

Alkanes — the inert starting material

Alkanes are sp³ and saturated. They're famously unreactive — the DAT essentially tests two reactions: free-radical halogenation and combustion. Their real job on the test is as the product of hydrogenation, not as a reactant.

Plate II — The Alkane Hub
Starting material: propane. Only two reactions radiate out — everything else enters the alkane (via hydrogenation).
1
Free-Radical Halogenation
Radical
▾
UV or heat replaces an alkane H with a halogen. Selectivity: Br₂ is picky (3° >> 2° > 1°); Cl₂ is sloppy.
R–H + X₂  →hν  R–X + HX
Substrate: alkane (or benzylic / allylic) Reagent: Br₂ or Cl₂ + UV light (hν) or Δ Output: most-stable C-H replaced (Br) · or random (Cl)
Worked example 2-methylpropane + Br₂/hν → 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Br• selectively abstracts the 3° H (lowest C-H BDE, most stable resulting radical). The 3° alkyl radical then grabs Br from Br₂, giving the 3° alkyl bromide and a fresh Br• that continues the chain.
Why is Br₂ selective and Cl₂ sloppy?
Hammond's postulate: Br• abstraction is endothermic, so the TS resembles the radical product → radical stability dominates → 3° >> 2° > 1°. Cl• abstraction is exothermic, so the TS resembles the reactants → C-H bond strength matters less, all H's compete → roughly statistical.
Practice
Toluene + Br₂/hν gives mainly:
Answer: benzyl bromide · the benzylic C-H is super-stable (resonance into ring), so Br• grabs that H first. Use Br₂/hν for benzylic bromination, NOT Br₂/FeBr₃ (which would give EAS on the ring).
Benzylic / allylic beat 3°
If a benzylic or allylic H is present, it wins over 3° (resonance stabilizes the radical). Always check the substrate for π-systems next to C-H before predicting.
Play mechanism · 5 frames Tier 2
Step Mode
Radical Halogenation · Full Chain MechanismInitiation → Propagation → Termination · Br₂ with 2-methylpropane · watch the radical count
1/5
Deep dive · radical stability + Hammond Tier 3
Why 3° H wins — hyperconjugation stabilizes the radical
Each α-H (a hydrogen on the carbon adjacent to the radical center) donates electron density from its σC-H bond into the half-empty orbital on the radical carbon. More α-H = more donors = more stable radical. Counts: methyl 0, 1° has 3, 2° has 6, 3° has 9. That's the entire reason for the 3° > 2° > 1° regioselectivity ladder. Bromination respects this ladder almost perfectly because Hammond says the TS for an endothermic step looks like the product radical (see panel below).
Fishhook vs regular arrows
The single-barbed fishhook arrow means "one electron moves." Contrast with the two-barbed arrow used in polar mechanisms (SN, EAS, carbonyl addition) which means "a pair of electrons moves." This is the only DAT mechanism where you exclusively see fishhooks.
Regioselectivity
3° > 2° > 1° (most stable radical wins)
Stereochem
Planar radical → racemic at new stereocenter
Br vs Cl
Br = very selective; Cl = sloppy (kinetic)
Why Br is selective and Cl isn't — Hammond's postulate
Br abstraction is endothermic — the C-H bond is stronger than the new H-Br bond. Hammond says the TS resembles the higher-energy side, so the product radical's stability dominates the activation energy. 3° vs 1° is a big gap → big rate difference → highly selective.

Cl abstraction is exothermic — the new H-Cl bond is stronger than the C-H bond it replaces. The TS resembles the reactants, so the C-H bond strength matters more than the radical's stability. The C-H BDE difference between 1°/2°/3° is small → all sites compete → product mixture is roughly statistical.

Mnemonic: Br is picky, Cl is careless.
DAT Trap — benzylic and allylic beat 3°
The benzyl radical's unpaired electron delocalizes into the aromatic ring across three carbons (ortho, para, ortho) + the original benzylic carbon — four resonance contributors total. The allylic radical does the same trick over a smaller π-system (two contributors). This makes both ~13 kcal/mol more stable than even a 3° tertiary radical.

DAT trap: if you see Br₂/hν on a substrate with both a 3° H and a benzylic/allylic H, the halogen lands on the benzylic/allylic carbon every time — never the 3°.
2
Combustion
Redox
▾
Complete oxidation of an alkane to CO₂ and H₂O with excess O₂. Rare on DAT as a reaction, common on the general chemistry balancing questions.
CnH2n+2 + (3n+1)/2 O₂ → n CO₂ + (n+1) H₂O
Balancing shortcut
Balance C first, then H, then O last. For C₅H₁₂: 5 CO₂ needs 10 O; 6 H₂O needs 6 O → total 16 O → 8 O₂.
Alkane takeaways
  • Only two alkane reactions you need: radical halogenation and combustion.
  • Radical stability: benzylic ≈ allylic > 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.
  • Br is selective (gives the most stable product); Cl is not (product distribution close to statistical).
  • Alkanes matter most as products of hydrogenation — when you see H₂/Pt, you're landing on this hub.
Practice
Alkane PracticeRadical halogenation + selectivity · 5 questions
0/5
12-methylbutane is treated with Br₂ and hν (1 equiv). The major monobromination product is:
Explanation
B is correct. Br is highly selective (3° >> 2° > 1°). The single 3° H at C2 gets abstracted fastest because the resulting 3° radical is most stable. Cl₂ would give a sloppy mix; Br₂ picks the winner.
2Ethylbenzene is treated with Br₂/hν (or NBS/hν). Where does bromination occur?
Explanation
D is correct. Benzylic C-H bonds are abstracted preferentially because the resulting benzylic radical is resonance-stabilized into the ring (more stable than any plain 1°/2°/3° radical). Ring bromination needs Br₂/FeBr₃ (an entirely different, electrophilic mechanism).
3The rate-determining propagation step of Br₂/hν with an alkane is:
Explanation
A is correct. H abstraction is the slow (rate-determining) propagation step — its transition state closely resembles the alkyl radical (Hammond's postulate), which is why radical stability controls selectivity so strongly. The second propagation (R• + Br-Br) is fast and non-selective.
4Complete combustion of propane (C₃H₈) requires how many O₂ molecules per propane?
Explanation
C is correct. C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O. Check: 3 C needs 3 O₂ (→ 3 CO₂); 8 H needs 2 O₂ (→ 4 H₂O). Total = 5 O₂. Formula for any CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: need (3n+1)/2 O₂.
5Why does Cl₂/hν give a messy distribution of monochlorination products but Br₂/hν gives a clean one?
Explanation
B is correct. Hammond's postulate: endothermic steps have TS resembling products → radical stability matters a lot → high selectivity. Cl's H-abstraction is exothermic → TS resembles reactant → little selectivity. This is a favorite DAT "why" question.
Hub 02 · Central

Alkenes — the center of the universe

The π bond is a nucleophile looking for an electrophile. Almost every reaction here is electrophilic addition: something electrophilic attacks the π bond first, then a nucleophile closes in. Master regioselectivity (Markovnikov vs anti-Markovnikov) and stereoselectivity (syn vs anti) and you own this hub.

Pattern shortcuts for this hub
Jump to: Atlas 3-Bucket Classifier 11 Reactions Hydroboration Mechanism Regio/Stereo Summary
Plate III — The Alkene Hub
Starting material: propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂). Ten branches show the actual product of each reagent. Stereo wedges are drawn where relevant.
Foundational — Markovnikov's Rule
In acid-catalyzed addition of HX or H₂O, the H adds to the carbon with more H's (the less substituted carbon) so that the resulting carbocation lands on the more substituted carbon. In short: "the rich get richer" — the carbon that already has H's gets another H, and X/OH lands on the more substituted carbon. Driven by carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1°.
Coach note · carbocation stability vs alkene stability — two different ranking ladders
Two different stability rules, do not mix them up. Carbocation stability: primary < secondary < tertiary < allylic < benzylic. Allylic and benzylic only count when there is an actual adjacent C=C double bond or aromatic ring providing resonance stabilization. Alkene stability: monosubstituted < disubstituted < trisubstituted < tetrasubstituted. When you see a Zaitsev question, you are picking the MOST SUBSTITUTED ALKENE — not the most stable carbocation. When you see a Markovnikov question, you are picking the MOST STABLE CARBOCATION as the intermediate (which then drives where the X/OH lands). Two different ladders, two different prompts — match the ladder to the question.
The 3-Bucket Mechanism Classifier
Bucket #1
Carbocation
  • Follows Markovnikov
  • Rearrangements YES
  • Stereo: racemic (planar cation)
Reactions in this bucket:
HX H₃O⁺ / H₂SO₄
If you see an open carbocation in the mechanism → this bucket.
Bucket #2
3-Membered Ring
  • Can be Markov or anti-Markov
  • Rearrangements NO
  • Stereo: anti (backside attack)
Reactions in this bucket:
X₂ X₂ / H₂O Hg(OAc)₂ / NaBH₄ mCPBA
If the intermediate is a 3-membered cyclic cation → this bucket.
Bucket #3
Concerted
  • Often anti-Markov (or no regio)
  • Rearrangements NO
  • Stereo: syn (same-face)
Reactions in this bucket:
H₂ / Pt BH₃ → H₂O₂/OH⁻ OsO₄ (syn diol)
If both new atoms add to the same face in one step → this bucket.
How to use the 3-Bucket Classifier
Instead of memorizing 11 alkene reactions as separate facts, classify each by its mechanism type. When the DAT shows you an unfamiliar reagent, you ask: "which bucket does this fall into?" — and the regiochemistry, stereochemistry, and rearrangement risk all follow automatically. HBr/ROOR is the one outlier (radical mechanism, anti-Markov) that doesn't fit the three buckets.
1
Hydrohalogenation (HX addition)
Markov
▾
HCl, HBr, or HI adds across the π bond. The halogen lands on the more substituted carbon. Goes through an open carbocation, so rearrangements are possible (hydride or methyl shifts if a more stable cation is adjacent).
R₂C=CHR' + H–X  →  R₂C(X)–CH₂R'
Mechanism — 2 steps
1
π bond attacks H of HX
The alkene's π electrons form a new C–H bond on the less substituted carbon. The H–X bond breaks heterolytically, releasing X⁻. Net: one sp² carbon becomes sp³ with a new H; the other becomes a carbocation on the more substituted carbon.
2
X⁻ attacks cation
X⁻ attacks the carbocation from either face → racemic at that carbon. Bond formation gives the final alkyl halide.
Regio
Markovnikov (X on more substituted C)
Stereo
Not stereospecific → racemic
Rearr.
YES — if a more stable cation is adjacent
Trap — Rearrangement
If an adjacent carbon has a H or methyl that can shift to convert a 2° cation into a 3° cation, it will. On an exam, any 2° cation adjacent to a quaternary center is a rearrangement red flag.
2
HBr + Peroxides (anti-Markov)
Radical
▾
Only HBr (not HCl, not HI) flips to anti-Markovnikov with peroxides. Mechanism is radical, not cation, so there's no rearrangement.
R₂C=CH₂ + HBr / ROOR  →  R₂CH–CH₂Br
Mechanism — radical chain
1
Initiation
Peroxide homolysis → 2 RO•. RO• + HBr → ROH + Br•.
2
Propagation
Br• adds to the less substituted carbon (so the resulting carbon radical is the more stable tertiary/secondary one). That alkyl radical abstracts H from HBr → final product + new Br•.
Why only HBr?
HCl: C–Cl BDE too high → Cl• can't abstract H efficiently. HI: H–I too weak → I• won't add to the alkene. Only HBr has the right energy match for both propagation steps.
3
Acid-Catalyzed Hydration (H₂O/H⁺)
Markov
▾
H₂O adds across the π bond with H₂SO₄ catalyst. Gives the Markovnikov alcohol. Same cation mechanism as HX → rearrangements possible.
R₂C=CHR' + H₂O / H⁺  →  R₂C(OH)–CH₂R'
1
Protonation
π bond grabs H⁺ → carbocation on more substituted C.
2
Water attacks cation
H₂O (weak nucleophile, but in excess) attacks the cation → oxocarbenium (R–OH₂⁺).
3
Deprotonation
A second water removes H⁺ → neutral alcohol. Regenerates catalyst.
4
Oxymercuration–Demercuration
Markov · no rearr.
▾
Hg(OAc)₂ / H₂O, then NaBH₄. Gives the same Markovnikov alcohol as H₂O/H⁺ but without rearrangement because the intermediate is a bridged mercurinium ion, not an open cation.
R₂C=CHR'  →1. Hg(OAc)₂/H₂O · 2. NaBH₄  R₂C(OH)–CH₂R'
1
Mercurinium formation
Hg²⁺ (from Hg(OAc)₂) bridges across the π bond → 3-membered mercurinium ion. Partial positive charge is larger on the more substituted carbon.
2
Water opens the ring
H₂O attacks the more substituted carbon (Markov) from the side opposite Hg → anti addition.
3
NaBH₄ demercuration
Replaces –HgOAc with –H. Net: Markovnikov alcohol, no rearrangement.
When to pick this over H₂O/H⁺
Whenever the problem hints that rearrangement would give a better carbocation. Oxymercuration is your "clean Markov" reagent.
5
Hydroboration–Oxidation
anti-Markov · syn
▾
BH₃·THF adds across the alkene with B (electrophile) on the less hindered carbon. Oxidation with H₂O₂/NaOH replaces B with OH with retention → anti-Markovnikov alcohol, syn addition, no rearrangement.
R₂C=CHR'  →1. BH₃/THF · 2. H₂O₂/OH⁻  R₂CH–CH(OH)R'
Step Mode
Hydroboration–Oxidation MechanismConcerted syn addition · then oxidative migration with retention · 4 steps
1/4
Regio
anti-Markovnikov
Stereo
Syn (both add to same face)
Rearr.
No — concerted
Why anti-Markovnikov — H lands on the more substituted C
Two effects, same answer:

Steric: the BR₂ end of the TS is bulky. Putting it on the less hindered alkene carbon avoids clashing with substituents on the more substituted C. ~6 kcal/mol penalty for the wrong orientation.

Electronic: in the partially-formed 4-membered TS, the more substituted C develops a partial + (alkyl groups stabilize positive character — same logic as Markovnikov for HBr). H delivers there because B–H acts hydridically, with H going to the most + center.

Both effects align → strong, clean regioselectivity. No carbocation ever forms (the TS is concerted), so no rearrangement — that's the synthetic killer feature: hydroboration installs the OH exactly where you predict, without skeletal scrambles.
6
Catalytic Hydrogenation
syn
▾
H₂ over Pt, Pd/C, or Ni delivers both H's from the same face of the alkene → syn addition. Reduces alkene to alkane. Can be poisoned (Lindlar) to stop at cis-alkene for alkynes.
R₂C=CHR' + H₂ / Pt  →  R₂CH–CH₂R'
Selectivity
Carbonyls and aromatic rings are not reduced by standard H₂/Pt (you need more aggressive conditions). Useful for selectively hydrogenating alkenes in a polyfunctional molecule.
7
Halogenation (X₂)
anti
▾
Br₂ or Cl₂ in an inert solvent (CCl₄, CH₂Cl₂) gives a vicinal dihalide with anti stereochemistry via a bridged halonium intermediate.
R₂C=CHR' + Br₂  →  R₂CBr–CHBrR'
1
Halonium ion
π bond attacks Br₂ → 3-membered cyclic bromonium ion + Br⁻.
2
Backside Br⁻ attack
Br⁻ attacks from the opposite face → anti vicinal dihalide. On a cyclic alkene, this gives a trans-dihalide.
Visual test
Red-brown Br₂ in CCl₄ decolorizes on mixing with an alkene. Classic qualitative test for unsaturation.
8
Halohydrin Formation (X₂/H₂O)
Markov · anti
▾
Same halonium intermediate, but water (present in excess) attacks instead of X⁻. OH ends up on the more substituted carbon, X on the less substituted, anti.
R₂C=CH₂ + Br₂ / H₂O  →  R₂C(OH)–CH₂Br
Why OH lands on the more substituted C
The bromonium ion is asymmetric: the more-substituted carbon carries more + charge, so H₂O (nucleophile) attacks there. Still backside → anti.
9
Epoxidation (mCPBA)
syn
▾
A peroxy acid (mCPBA most common) transfers one oxygen to the alkene in a concerted, syn step → epoxide. Retains alkene geometry (cis-alkene → cis-epoxide).
R₂C=CHR' + mCPBA  →  epoxide (R₂C–CHR' bridged by O)
Follow-up
Open with H₃O⁺ (acid) → anti-Markov diol, trans. Or open with nucleophile/base → anti diol again, but nucleophile attacks the less hindered carbon.
10
Syn Dihydroxylation (OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄)
syn diol
▾
OsO₄ (or cold, dilute KMnO₄/OH⁻) adds two OH groups to the same face of the alkene → syn (cis) diol.
R₂C=CHR'  →OsO₄ then NaHSO₃  R₂C(OH)–CH(OH)R' (cis)
Cold vs hot KMnO₄
Cold dilute KMnO₄ = syn diol. Hot concentrated KMnO₄ = cleavage (like ozonolysis; terminal CH₂ becomes CO₂, other side gives acid or ketone). The DAT loves this distinction.
11
Ozonolysis (O₃)
Cleavage
▾
O₃ cleaves the C=C completely through an ozonide intermediate. The workup determines the oxidation level of the product fragments — and the DAT tests this distinction directly.
R₂C=CHR'  →1. O₃ · 2. workup  two carbonyl fragments
Two workups on the same alkene — reductive vs oxidative
Same starting 2-methyl-2-butene in both columns. Mild reductant (Zn/H₂O or Me₂S) caps the ozonide at carbonyls — you see exactly where the C=C lived. Peroxide drives the aldehyde C–H one rung higher to a carboxylic acid; a terminal =CH₂ is lost entirely as CO₂.
The workup matters
Reductive vs Oxidative
three reagents · two outcomes
ReductiveZn/H₂O or Me₂S (DMS)
Stops at carbonyl.
Disubstituted side → ketone
Monosubstituted side → aldehyde (the H stays)
Terminal =CH2 → formaldehyde (HCHO)
Use when: you want to see the carbonyls cleanly to map the original C=C.
vs
OxidativeH2O2
Pushes aldehydes one step further.
Disubstituted side → ketone (no C-H to oxidize)
Monosubstituted side → carboxylic acid
Terminal =CH2 → CO2 + H2O (loses a carbon!)
Use when: a synthesis needs the acid endpoint without a separate oxidation step.
The DAT trap: "Which workup converts the alkene to two acids?" → H2O2. "Which gives one ketone + one aldehyde?" → Zn/H2O or Me2S. Hot concentrated KMnO4 behaves like the oxidative workup (also cleaves to acids/ketones, terminal CH2 → CO2) — different reagent, same logic.
Retrosynthesis tool
Ozonolysis is the #1 tool for locating a double bond in an unknown alkene — the positions of the resulting carbonyls mark exactly where the C=C was. If you see "compound X (C10H20) gave two ketones after ozonolysis," draw the two ketones and connect their carbonyl C's with a double bond — that's your alkene.
Regiochemistry at a glance
ReagentRegioStereoRearr.?
HXMarkovRacemicYes
HBr / ROORanti-MarkovMixNo (radical)
H₂O / H₂SO₄MarkovRacemicYes
Hg(OAc)₂ / NaBH₄MarkovAntiNo (bridged)

H₂ / Pt—SynNo
X₂—AntiNo

Alkene master takeaways
  • Anything with a free carbocation (HX, H₂O/H⁺) → Markov + possibility of rearrangement.
  • Anything with a bridged intermediate (Hg²⁺, BH₃, X₂, mCPBA) → no rearrangement, anti or syn depending on whether the nucleophile comes in from opposite or same face.
  • Peroxides (ROOR) with HBr only flip regiochem to anti-Markovnikov.
  • Ozonolysis and hot KMnO₄ cleave the alkene — the rest just modify it.
  • Master four stereo words: syn, anti, Markov, anti-Markov. Every alkene question tests two of them.
Practice
Alkene PracticeDAT-style · immediate feedback · 5 questions
0/5
1What is the major product when 1-methylcyclohexene is treated with HBr?
Explanation
B is correct. HBr addition is Markovnikov: the H adds to the carbon with more H's (the less substituted one) so the more stable tertiary carbocation forms on the more substituted carbon. Br then traps that cation → 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane. No peroxides are mentioned, so this is NOT anti-Markov.
2Which reagent sequence converts 2-methyl-1-butene to 2-methyl-1-butanol (a 1° alcohol)?
Explanation
C is correct. To get OH on the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov), you need hydroboration–oxidation. BH₃ adds with B on the less hindered C; H₂O₂/NaOH replaces B with OH with retention → 1° alcohol. Options A and B give Markov (2°) alcohols; D gives an anti-Markov alkyl bromide, not alcohol.
3When cis-2-butene reacts with Br₂ in CCl₄, the product is:
Explanation
A is correct. Br₂ adds anti via a bridged bromonium ion. For a cis-alkene + anti addition, the result is the racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair. If it were trans-2-butene + anti addition, you'd get the meso (2R,3S) product. This is the classic "cis → racemic, trans → meso" rule for anti addition.
4Which reagent pair gives different products when applied to 2-methyl-2-butene?
Explanation
D is correct. Cold dilute KMnO₄ gives a syn diol (just like OsO₄); hot concentrated KMnO₄ cleaves the alkene to give two carbonyls (like ozonolysis with oxidative workup). A, B, and C give effectively the same products (Markov alcohols, syn diols, and vicinal dihalides respectively).
5Ozonolysis of an unknown alkene followed by Zn/H₂O gives exactly one compound: cyclopentanone. The original alkene must be:
Explanation
B is correct. Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C to give two carbonyl fragments. If one compound is obtained (cyclopentanone), both halves of the alkene must be identical cyclopentane rings joined by the C=C. That's bicyclopentylidene. Cyclopentene (A) would give a diacid (open chain); 2-pentene (C) gives two aldehydes; 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene (D) gives a single diketone (different product).

DAT rarely tests endo vs exo specifically — know that DA is concerted, stereospecific, and syn. Don't memorize the endo orbital rationale.

DAT scope · what to actually memorize about Diels-Alder
The DAT rarely asks endo vs exo specifically — that's a sophomore-level distinction. What you do need cold:
  • DA is concerted — one step, three arrows, no intermediate, single TS.
  • DA is stereospecific syn — substituents on a cis dienophile stay cis on the ring; trans stays trans. No flip mid-reaction.
  • Diene must be s-cis (rotated into the U shape). s-trans fails.
  • Dienophile prefers an EWG (CN, C=O, NO₂) — that lowers the LUMO so the diene's HOMO can match.
  • Endo is kinetic, exo is thermodynamic — that's it. Don't memorize the secondary orbital overlap argument.
The interactive below is well-built and useful for visual learners — just don't get bogged down on endo vs exo for the test.
Diels-Alder Animator · interactive rebuild
Step through the [4+2] cycloaddition with proper curly arrows. Toggle s-cis vs s-trans to see why s-trans fails. Toggle endo vs exo to see the kinetic preference. Hover the dienophile to highlight the EWG that lowers the LUMO.
Frame:
Diene:
Stereo:
The Diels-Alder Reaction — the 3-arrow concerted cycloaddition
Three curved arrows, one concerted step
All three arrows move at the same time around the 6-atom ring being formed. No intermediate. No stopping. 2 new σ bonds form · 2 π bonds break · 1 π bond shifts.
Alkene dienophile vs. Alkyne dienophile
Alkene dienophile
Dienophile has 1 π bond. All 3 of the diene's π electrons get used up on forming the ring.
Bond bookkeeping: 3 π in → 1 π + 2 σ out. Net: lose 2 π, gain 2 σ. Energetically favorable (σ bonds are stronger).
Alkyne dienophile
Dienophile has 2 π bonds. One is used in the reaction; the other survives in the product.
Bond bookkeeping: 4 π in (2 from diene + 2 from alkyne) → 2 π + 2 σ out. The alkyne's "second" π doesn't participate — it just sits there through the whole reaction.
The single test-day question to drill
DAT pattern: "Diene + X → ?" where X is either alkene or alkyne. Count double bonds in the product: alkene dienophile ⇒ 1 C=C (cyclohexene); alkyne dienophile ⇒ 2 C=C's (1,3-cyclohexadiene). That's the whole question. You don't need to draw the 3 arrows under time pressure — count π bonds in and π bonds out.
The 4 rules that cover every DAT Diels-Alder question
1. Diene must be s-cis. Cyclic dienes (cyclopentadiene, furan) are locked s-cis → super-reactive. Acyclic dienes sit s-trans at rest and have to rotate; steric blockers that prevent rotation kill the reaction.
2. Dienophile usually has an EWG (C=O, CN, NO₂). EWG lowers its LUMO → faster. Ethylene reacts slowly; maleic anhydride is the standard fast dienophile.
3. Stereospecific — cis stays cis, trans stays trans. Substituents on a cis dienophile end up cis on the ring; trans stays trans. The reaction is syn/suprafacial on both partners — no atoms flip sides during the single concerted step.
4. Endo preference. When there's an EWG on the dienophile, it prefers the endo (pointing under the new ring) position over exo. Kinetic product, not thermodynamic.
Chair Conformations — Axial vs. Equatorial
The one rule you need
Big groups prefer equatorial. When a substituent is axial, it crashes into the two other axial H's on the same side of the ring (1,3-diaxial interaction). Equatorial position points "out" and avoids this clash. For a ring flip, the winning chair has the largest group equatorial.
Cis/trans in chairs
On a cyclohexane, cis = both substituents on the same side of the ring (one up, one up — or one down, one down); trans = opposite sides. After a ring flip, every axial becomes equatorial and vice versa — but cis/trans never changes. Memorize: 1,4-cis has 1 ax + 1 eq; 1,4-trans has both eq (or both ax). Trans-1,4-di-tert-butylcyclohexane is the stablest configuration because both t-Bu's can be equatorial at once.
Hub 03

Alkynes — double trouble

Alkynes are two π bonds stacked. Most of their reactions are the alkene reactions done twice (or stopped halfway). The exam-unique twists are terminal alkyne acidity (pKa ≈ 25) and the tautomerization of enols to ketones after hydration.

Plate IV — The Alkyne Hub
Starting material: 1-butyne. Watch which reactions stop at the alkene (Lindlar, Na/NH₃) and which go all the way to alkanes (H₂/Pt).
1
Lindlar (cis) vs Na/NH₃ (trans) — Alkyne Reduction to Alkene
Syn cis · Anti trans
▾
Both reagents stop at the alkene (not alkane).
Lindlar's catalyst (Pd on CaCO₃ poisoned with Pb + quinoline): syn delivery of H₂ from the metal surface → cis-alkene.
Na/NH₃(l) at −33 °C (dissolving metal): radical anion pathway → trans-alkene (anti addition).
H₂ / Pd-C goes ALL the way to alkane — don't stop at the alkene.
R–C≡C–R' + H₂ / Lindlar → cis-R–CH=CH–R'
R–C≡C–R' + Na / NH₃(l) → trans-R–CH=CH–R'
Coach mnemonic — C = Cis
The C in Catalyst (Lindlar) = Cis. Na/NH₃ gives the other one — trans. That's the whole memory trick.
2-butyne → cis-2-butene (Lindlar) vs trans-2-butene (Na/NH₃)
2-legacy
Dissolving Metal Reduction → trans-Alkene (merged into card 1)
Anti · trans
▾
Na (or Li) in liquid NH₃ reduces alkyne to trans-alkene through a radical anion → vinyl anion → protonation sequence. Anti addition.
R–C≡C–R' + Na / NH₃(l)  →  trans-R–CH=CH–R'
1
e⁻ transfer
Na donates electron → radical anion.
2
Protonation
NH₃ protonates the radical anion → vinyl radical (trans, most stable).
3
2nd e⁻ / proton
Another Na donates e⁻ → vinyl anion → protonation → trans-alkene.
3
Acid-Catalyzed Hydration (Hg²⁺) → Methyl Ketone
Markov · keto
▾
H₂O adds Markov across the alkyne (with HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ catalyst) → enol → tautomerizes to the more stable ketone. Terminal alkynes give methyl ketones.
R–C≡CH  →H₂O / H₂SO₄ / HgSO₄  R–C(OH)=CH₂  ⇌  R–CO–CH₃
Keto–enol tautomerization
Enol (C=C–OH) rapidly flips to keto (C(=O)–C–H) under acid or base. Keto is almost always the stable tautomer. Don't leave an enol as your final product.
4
Hydroboration–Oxidation → Aldehyde
anti-Markov
▾
For terminal alkynes, R₂BH (disiamylborane, bulky B) adds anti-Markov. Oxidative workup gives an enol that tautomerizes → aldehyde.
R–C≡CH  →1. R₂BH · 2. H₂O₂/OH⁻  R–CH=CH–OH  ⇌  R–CH₂–CHO
Markov vs anti-Markov on terminal alkynes
Hg/H₂O → methyl ketone (O on internal C). R₂BH/H₂O₂ → aldehyde (O on terminal C). The DAT loves making you pick between these two.
5
Addition of HX (1 or 2 eq)
Markov
▾
1 equiv HX → vinyl halide (Markov). 2 equiv HX → geminal dihalide (both X's on the same carbon — the more substituted one).
R–C≡CH + 2 HX  →  R–CX₂–CH₃
6
Acetylide Formation + Alkylation
C–C bond
▾
Terminal alkyne has pKa ≈ 25 → deprotonated by NaNH₂ (or Grignards, n-BuLi) to give an acetylide nucleophile. That acetylide does SN2 on a 1° alkyl halide or methyl halide to forge a new C–C bond.
R–C≡CH  →NaNH₂  R–C≡C⁻  →R'–CH₂Br  R–C≡C–CH₂R'
Why 1° alkyl halides only
Acetylides are also strong bases. With 2° or 3° alkyl halides they cause E2 (elimination) instead of SN2. Memorize: acetylide + methyl/1° → SN2 works; 2°/3° → E2 only.
7
Ozonolysis of Alkynes
Cleavage
▾
O₃ cleaves an alkyne to give two carboxylic acids (or CO₂ from a terminal ≡CH). Same positional logic as alkene ozonolysis.
R–C≡C–R'  →1. O₃ · 2. H₂O  R–COOH + R'–COOH
Two reductions on the same internal alkyne — cis vs trans alkene
Same starting 2-butyne in both columns. Lindlar's poisoned Pd surface delivers both H atoms to the same face → cis alkene. Na/NH₃(l) goes through a vinyl radical that prefers the trans geometry before the second H arrives → trans alkene. Both stop cleanly at the alkene; neither over-reduces.
Decision widget
Lindlar vs Na/NH₃ — cis vs trans alkene
highest-yield DAT pair
LindlarH₂ / Pd-CaCO₃-Pb-quinoline
Poisoned Pd — just active enough for one addition, then dies
Syn delivery of H₂ on metal surface → cis-alkene
Can't over-reduce to alkane
→ cis
vs
Dissolving MetalNa / NH₃(liq)
Radical anion pathway — e⁻ from Na, then H from NH₃
Vinyl radical prefers trans geometry → trans-alkene
Also won't over-reduce (alkene isn't reduced)
→ trans
Mnemonic: Lindlar = Lazy cis. Na/NH₃ = "NerAns" trans (goofy but memorable). Seriously though: Lindlar makes Cis; sodium gives Trans. Both are stereospecific — neither converts one alkene geometry into the other.
Alkyne takeaways
  • Lindlar → cis. Na/NH₃ → trans. The single most-tested pair in alkyne questions.
  • Terminal alkyne hydration: Hg/H₂O → methyl ketone (Markov); R₂BH then H₂O₂ → aldehyde (anti-Markov).
  • Terminal alkynes have acidic Hs (pKa ≈ 25) → deprotonate with NaNH₂ to get a nucleophilic acetylide, which builds C–C bonds via SN2 on 1° alkyl halides.
  • Everything else is just "the alkene reaction, done twice."
Practice
Alkyne Practicecis/trans · hydration · acetylide · 5 questions
0/5
12-butyne is treated with Na in liquid NH₃. The product is:
Explanation
C is correct. Dissolving metal reduction (Na/NH₃) gives the trans-alkene through a vinyl-anion intermediate that preferentially adopts the less-crowded trans geometry. For cis-alkene, use Lindlar's catalyst (H₂/Pd-CaCO₃-Pb-quinoline).
21-hexyne + H₂O / HgSO₄ / H₂SO₄ gives:
Explanation
B is correct. Markov hydration puts OH on the more substituted C (C2) → enol → tautomerizes to methyl ketone. Terminal alkyne + Hg/H₂O always gives the methyl ketone. For the aldehyde (option A), you'd need R₂BH then H₂O₂ (anti-Markov). D is wrong because enols always flip to the keto form.
3To synthesize 3-methyl-1-butyne from 1-butyne and a methyl halide, use:
Explanation
D is correct. NaNH₂ deprotonates the terminal alkyne (pKa ≈ 25) → acetylide anion, which SN2's on CH₃I. NaOH (pKaH = 16) is too weak to deprotonate the alkyne. The acetylide only works with 1°/methyl alkyl halides — 2°/3° give E2.
4Ozonolysis of 3-hexyne (CH₃CH₂-C≡C-CH₂CH₃) with oxidative workup gives:
Explanation
A is correct. Alkyne ozonolysis cleaves all the way to carboxylic acids (unlike alkene ozonolysis which typically gives aldehydes/ketones). Each C of the former C≡C becomes a -COOH. For a terminal alkyne, the =CH end becomes CO₂.
5You want to make propanal (CH₃-CH₂-CHO) from propyne (CH₃-C≡CH). Use:
Explanation
C is correct. Hydroboration of a terminal alkyne with a bulky borane (R₂BH) puts B on the terminal C (anti-Markov). H₂O₂/NaOH converts B-C to C-OH → enol → tautomerizes to the aldehyde. Option A (Hg/H₂O) is Markov → gives the ketone (acetone here), not aldehyde.
Hub 04

Substitution vs Elimination — the big decision

The DAT loves to hand you an alkyl halide with a nucleophile/base and ask "what happens?" Four possible paths: SN1, SN2, E1, E2. Which one depends on four variables: substrate · nucleophile/base · solvent · temperature. Master the decision tree and you'll never get this wrong again.

Pattern shortcuts for this hub
Plate V · Companion · Interactive walk-through
Let's walk a single problem all the way to the verdict
Four prompts — substrate, nucleophile/base, solvent, temperature. Each step draws the species in question; the verdict renders as a full reaction card with stereochemistry, regio, and worked examples.
Choose a substrate to begin.
Plate V — The SN/E Decision Tree (reference view)
Full static tree for reference. Use the interactive wizard above to walk through a specific problem; use this view to see every path at once.
1
SN2 — Backside Attack
Concerted · inversion
▾
Nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group in a single step → inversion (Walden). Rate depends on both Nu and R–X.
Nu⁻ + R–X  →  R–Nu + X⁻  (inversion at stereocenter)
Methyl or 1° substrate (2° marginal · 3° blocks) Strong Nu (CN⁻, I⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻, RO⁻) Polar aprotic solvent (DMSO, DMF, acetone)
Worked example (S)-2-bromobutane + NaCN/DMSO → (R)-2-cyanobutane. CN⁻ attacks from the back face; in one concerted step C-Br breaks while C-CN forms → 100% inversion at the reacting carbon.
Why doesn't SN2 work on a 3° substrate?
Backside attack requires the Nu to come in opposite the leaving group. On 3°, that face is blocked by three R groups. Steric crowding kills the SN2 transition state; 3° substrates go SN1, E1, or E2 instead.
Practice
Which substrate undergoes SN2 fastest with NaI in acetone?
Answer: CH₃Br · zero steric hindrance at the reacting C → fastest backside attack.
Stereo lock
SN2 always inverts the configuration at the reacting C (Walden umbrella flip). Use it to deliberately invert a chiral center.
Play mechanism · 3 views Tier 2
Step Mode
SN2 Mechanism — Walden Inversion(S)-2-bromobutane + OH⁻ → (R)-2-butanol · one concerted step · 3 views
1/3
Substrate
Methyl > 1° >> 2° >>> 3° (3° blocks it)
Nucleophile
Strong (CN⁻, I⁻, RS⁻, RO⁻, N₃⁻)
Solvent
Polar aprotic (DMSO, DMF, acetone)
Stereochem
Inversion at C (100%)
Deep dive · why backside attack is mandatory Tier 3
Why backside attack is mandatory — Nu must align with the σ* antibonding orbital
WALDEN INVERSION Nu⁻ σ-bonding (filled) C H H H LG Nu would have to push into a FILLED σ orbital — Pauli forbidden also blocked by the H/H/H "umbrella" already on that face SN2 inversion is not a preference — it's the only geometrically + electronically allowed path.
The C–LG bond has a σ-bonding orbital (filled, electrons in it) on the LG side and a σ* antibonding orbital (empty, hungry for electrons) pointing the opposite way — directly behind the C, opposite the LG.

Backside attack: Nu's lone pair lines up with the σ* lobe → fills it → new C–Nu bond forms → C–LG breaks. The 3 other substituents on C must flip through the central plane to the opposite face → Walden inversion, like an umbrella flipping inside out.

Frontside attack would require the Nu to push into the filled σ orbital — that's a 4-electron interaction, Pauli-forbidden. Plus the existing H/H/H "umbrella" is already in the way. There is no valid TS, so this never happens.

Consequence: SN2 always gives 100% inversion at the reacting carbon. Used to deliberately invert chiral centers.
2
SN1 — Cation, then Trap
Stepwise · racemic
▾
X leaves first, forming a flat carbocation, which a weak nucleophile traps from either face → racemization. Rearrangements are possible.
R–X  →  R⁺ + X⁻  →Nu  R–Nu (racemic)
3° substrate (or benzylic / allylic) Weak Nu — usually the solvent (H₂O, ROH) Polar protic solvent
Worked example (CH₃)₃C-Br + H₂O → (CH₃)₃C-OH. The 3° cation forms first (rate-determining); water attacks either face → racemic if the C is chiral. Loss of H⁺ gives the neutral alcohol.
Why doesn't SN1 work on a primary substrate?
The intermediate would be a 1° carbocation — too unstable to form. SN1 needs a stable cation: 3° > benzylic/allylic > 2°. Methyl and 1° substrates are forced to go SN2 instead.
Practice
Which substrate solvolyzes fastest with H₂O?
Answer: (CH₃)₃CBr · 3° cation is most stable → fastest ionization → fastest SN1.
Rearrangement alert
Any 2° cation adjacent to a 3° or benzylic C can hydride-shift. Always check the cation's neighbors before finalizing the product.
Play mechanism · 3 frames Tier 2
Step Mode
SN1 Mechanism · solvolysis of t-butyl bromide3° substrate · planar cation · 50/50 face attack → racemization · 3 frames
1/3
Deep dive · why SN1 racemizes Tier 3
Why SN1 racemizes — the planar cation has no stereochemical memory
An SN2 reaction inverts a chiral center 100% of the time because the nucleophile is forced to attack from the back. SN1 has no such constraint: once the cation forms, the C is sp² hybridized with three substituents in a plane and an empty p-orbital sticking up and down. The nucleophile sees both lobes of that p-orbital equally and attacks each with ~50% probability.

Consequence: if the starting material was a single enantiomer (say, R), the product is a racemic mixture of R and S — no optical activity, no stereochemical memory. That's why SN1 is the textbook example of "loss of stereochemistry."

In practice the ratio drifts slightly from 50/50 because the leaving group (Br⁻ in this example) lingers near one face of the cation as it forms (the "ion pair") — but the dominant outcome is racemization.
3
E2 — Anti-Periplanar Elimination
Concerted · Zaitsev
▾
Strong base grabs a β-H while the leaving group departs, forming a π bond in one concerted step. Requires the H and X to be anti-periplanar (180°). Usually gives the most substituted alkene (Zaitsev).
H–C–C–X + B⁻  →  C=C + B–H + X⁻
2° or 3° substrate (1° marginal) Strong base (NaOEt, NaOH, NaH) H + LG must align 180° (anti-periplanar)
Worked example 2-bromo-2-methylbutane + NaOEt → 2-methyl-2-butene (Zaitsev). Base removes the β-H that gives the most-substituted alkene; the H and Br must be anti to each other in the same step. One concerted bond shuffle.
Why does cyclohexane E2 sometimes refuse to give Zaitsev?
On a cyclohexane chair, both H and LG must be axial to be anti-periplanar. If the leaving group is locked equatorial (because of a bulky neighbor), the only available β-H may be the "wrong" one geometrically — you get the less-substituted (non-Zaitsev) alkene by force. Stereo trumps Zaitsev.
Practice
2-bromobutane + bulky base (t-BuO⁻) gives mostly:
Answer: 1-butene · t-BuO⁻ is too bulky to reach the internal β-H, so it grabs the terminal β-H instead → less-substituted (Hofmann) alkene.
Bulky-base trap
Strong base ≠ small base. t-BuO⁻ and LDA override Zaitsev because they can only reach the less-hindered β-H. Always check base size before predicting the alkene.
Coach note · meet Naomi
NaOMe is "Naomi." NaOEt is her twin sister "Nioet" — ethyl instead of methyl. Same family: small, strong base in a protic solvent. Default reaction is E2 — Zaitsev, more substituted alkene — because she is small enough to grab whatever β-H sits anti to the leaving group. In rare cases she will do SN2, but default to E2 when you see her. You will also see Naomi in enolate reactions deprotonating the alpha hydrogen. "Basic bitch, she loves eliminating shit. That's her thing."
Coach note · the anti-periplanar requirement
E2 has a strict geometric requirement: the leaving group and the β-H being eliminated must be anti-periplanar — 180° across from each other. If the bromine is on a wedge, the H you eliminate has to be on a dash. If they are not already lined up, rotate the back carbon until they are. On a cyclohexane chair, that means BOTH the LG and the β-H must be axial — and on locked chairs (with bulky equatorial groups), only certain face combinations satisfy this. The DAT loves to test this with locked t-butyl cyclohexanes where one diastereomer can do E2 and the other can't.
Deep dive · Hofmann exception + stereo lock Tier 2
Hofmann exception
With a bulky base (t-BuO⁻, LDA), the base grabs the less hindered (less substituted) β-H → less substituted alkene (Hofmann). Same for quaternary ammonium salts (Hofmann elimination).
Stereospecific
On cyclohexanes, both H and LG must be axial for E2. If the only H that's anti to X is the wrong one stereo-wise, you'll get a non-Zaitsev alkene.
4
E1 — Cation then β-H loss
Stepwise · Zaitsev
▾
Like SN1, but a weak base removes a β-H from the carbocation instead of the Nu trapping it. Same cation → Zaitsev alkene.
R–X  →  R⁺  →base  alkene (Zaitsev)
3° substrate (or stable cation) Weak base — solvent or alcohol Heat (Δ) drives elimination over substitution
Worked example 2-bromo-2-methylpropane heated in EtOH → 2-methylpropene + HBr. Br leaves first → 3° cation; ethanol acts as a weak base, taking a β-H → C=C π bond. Zaitsev (most-substituted) alkene wins.
How is E1 different from SN1 if both go through the same cation?
Same intermediate, different fate. SN1: weak Nu (often the same solvent) attacks the cation → substitution product. E1: a weak base (usually the conjugate base of the solvent) takes a β-H instead → alkene. Heat shifts the balance toward E1; cool conditions favor SN1.
Practice
tert-butyl bromide is heated in ethanol. The major product is:
Answer: 2-methylpropene · heat + 3° substrate + weak base = E1 dominates over SN1. Zaitsev gives the most-substituted alkene.
Rearrangement risk
E1 goes through a free carbocation — same hydride/methyl shift risks as SN1. Always check whether a 1,2-shift gives a more stable cation before predicting the alkene.
5
Competition: SN1 vs E1 vs SN2 vs E2
Decision
▾
Apply this 4-question filter in order:
1. Is the substrate 3°?
Yes SN2 dead. Strong base → E2. Weak Nu, heat → E1/SN1 (mix).
No go to Q2.
2. Is the base strong (pKa of its conjugate acid, BH⁺, > ~16)?
Yes + bulky E2 (Hofmann).
Yes, small E2 if 2°, SN2 if 1°.
3. Is there a strong nucleophile but weak base (CN⁻, I⁻, RS⁻)?
Yes SN2 (for 1° and 2°).
No go to Q4.
4. Weak Nu + protic solvent + heat?
Yes on 2°/3° SN1 + E1 mix.
No reaction probably doesn't go.
Substrate summary
SubstrateSN2SN1E2E1
MethylYesNoNo (no β-H)No
1°YesNoYes (bulky base)No
2°YesYesYesYes
3°NoYesYesYes
Benzylic/allylicYesYesYesYes
SN/E takeaways
  • Strong base → E2. Good nucleophile (not base) → SN2. Bulky base → Hofmann. No base, heat, protic solvent → SN1/E1.
  • 3° substrates can't do SN2 (too hindered). 1° substrates can't do SN1/E1 (cation too unstable).
  • SN2: inversion. SN1: racemic. E2: anti-periplanar. E1: Zaitsev, mixed E/Z.
  • Polar aprotic solvents (DMSO, DMF, acetone) supercharge SN2. Polar protic solvents (H₂O, ROH, AcOH) favor SN1/E1.
Practice
SN/E PracticePick the dominant pathway · 5 questions
0/5
1(R)-2-bromobutane is treated with NaI in acetone. The major product is:
Explanation
C is correct. NaI in acetone is textbook SN2 conditions: I⁻ is a strong nucleophile, acetone is polar aprotic. 2° substrate + SN2 → inversion. (R) starting material → (S) product. No cation forms, so no racemization (B). I⁻ isn't basic enough to do E2 (D).
2tert-butyl bromide is heated in ethanol. The major product is:
Explanation
B is correct. 3° substrate + weak nucleophile (EtOH) + protic solvent + heat = classic SN1/E1 conditions. You get a mix of the substitution product (tert-butyl ethyl ether, via SN1) and the elimination product (isobutylene, via E1). 3° blocks SN2 entirely.
32-bromo-2-methylbutane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol. The major product is:
Explanation
A is correct. Potassium tert-butoxide is a bulky strong base → forces E2 via Hofmann (removes the most accessible β-H, giving the LESS substituted alkene). Zaitsev (B) would win with a smaller base like EtO⁻ or OH⁻. SN2 (C) is dead on a 3° substrate.
4Which combination would give the FASTEST SN2 reaction?
Explanation
D is correct. Perfect SN2 = methyl substrate (smallest, fastest) + strong nucleophile (CN⁻) + polar aprotic solvent (DMSO — doesn't H-bond the nucleophile, so it stays reactive). A is 3° (SN2 forbidden). B and C use protic solvents that slow SN2. D checks every box.
5An E2 elimination of cis-1-bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane with NaOEt:
Explanation
C is correct. E2 requires anti-periplanar geometry. In cis-1-bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane, the bulky tert-butyl locks the ring so Br is equatorial. Axial H's are not anti to equatorial Br — no H satisfies anti-periplanar. The reaction is very slow. (The trans isomer, with Br axial, reacts normally.) This is the classic "locked chair" trap.
Hub 05

Alcohols — the Swiss Army Knife

Alcohols can become alkyl halides (substitution), alkenes (dehydration), ethers (Williamson), carbonyls (oxidation), or esters (Fischer). They're the molecular crossroads. The OH group is a bad leaving group, so most alcohol reactions start by converting OH to something better: protonation, tosylation, or a P/S reagent.

Alcohol Oxidation Decision Tree · pick substrate + reagent
Click a substrate (1° / 2° / 3°) and a reagent (PCC / Jones / Swern). The decision tree highlights the path and shows the product. The trap: PCC stops at the aldehyde for 1°; Jones overshoots to the carboxylic acid.
Substrate
Reagent
Pattern shortcuts for this hub
Plate VI — The Alcohol Hub
Starting material: 1-propanol. Six outflow routes; most start by converting the terrible OH leaving group into a usable one.
1
Acid-Catalyzed Dehydration → Alkene
E1 · Zaitsev
▾
Conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ + heat. 3° > 2° >> 1° (1° rarely works, and when it does it's usually E2). Gives Zaitsev alkene; watch for rearrangements (E1 via cation).
R₂CH–C(OH)R'₂  →H₂SO₄ · Δ  alkene (Zaitsev) + H₂O
Step Mode
E1 Dehydration Mechanism2-methyl-2-butanol → 2-methyl-2-butene · cation intermediate · Zaitsev · 3 steps
1/3
Rearrangement trap — the cation walks before it eliminates
The naïve answer for E1 of 3-methyl-2-butanol: lose H₂O at C2, β-H from C1 → 3-methyl-1-butene (terminal, monosubstituted).

The real answer: H₂O leaves at C2 → 2° cation. A 1,2-hydride shift from the adjacent C3 (which is 3°, has 3 R groups) gives a 3° cation (~17 kcal/mol more stable). E1 is rate-limited by ionization, so the cation has plenty of time to rearrange before any β-H is grabbed. Elimination from the 3° cation gives 2-methyl-2-butene — a trisubstituted alkene (Zaitsev squared).

Always ask: can a 1,2-H or 1,2-CH₃ shift produce a more stable cation? If yes, it does, and the final alkene comes from the new position. The same trap applies to SN1 reactions on 2° substrates next to a 3° C.
2
R–OH → R–X (HX, SOCl₂, PBr₃)
Conversion
▾
Three flavors:
• HX: protonate OH, then Nu attacks. For 3° goes SN1 (fast, rearranges). For 1°/2° with HBr goes SN2, but rearrangements possible on 2°.
• SOCl₂ (+ pyridine): gives R–Cl. Mechanism converts OH into chlorosulfite (excellent LG), then Cl⁻ attacks. No rearrangement.
• PBr₃: gives R–Br. Similar activation, no rearrangement.
R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂ + HCl
R–OH + PBr₃ → R–Br + HOPBr₂
When to pick which
If the problem has a stereocenter and you can't afford a racemization or rearrangement → use SOCl₂ or PBr₃. For 3° alcohols → HX works cleanly (cation already preferred).
3
Tosylation (TsCl/pyridine)
Activation
▾
Tosyl chloride converts OH into a tosylate (–OTs), an excellent leaving group. Critically, this conversion happens without touching the C → retention of configuration. Next step (SN2 with Nu) then inverts.
R–OH → R–OTs → R–Nu (overall inversion, if SN2)
The tosylate trick
Whenever you see "the product should have opposite stereochem from the starting alcohol," think 1. TsCl/pyridine · 2. Nu⁻ (SN2). This is how you do clean stereo-inversion on an alcohol.
4
Oxidation of 1° and 2° Alcohols
Redox
▾
The key "stops and goes":
• PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate, anhydrous): 1° → aldehyde (stops there). 2° → ketone.
• Jones / CrO₃ / H₂CrO₄ / K₂Cr₂O₇: 1° → all the way to carboxylic acid. 2° → ketone.
• 3° alcohols: no oxidation (no α-H to lose).
R–CH₂–OH  →PCC  R–CHO   vs   R–CH₂–OH  →Jones  R–COOH
DAT pattern
If the problem says "oxidize without over-oxidation" or uses anhydrous conditions, it's PCC. If it says "acidic chromate" or shows CrO₃/H₂SO₄/H₂O, it's Jones → full oxidation.
Coach note · Chromium Jones
Chromium Jones — that's how it is. He is a strong oxidizer, top of the food chain. Primary alcohol → carboxylic acid. Secondary alcohol → ketone (nothing left to oxidize once you make the C=O — the carbonyl carbon has no H to lose). Tertiary alcohol → no reaction at all (no α-H on the C-OH carbon, nothing to remove). If you ever doubt yourself on this one, remember: it is not your job to redo organic chem, it is your job to spot the reagent and pick the product.
5
Williamson Ether Synthesis
SN2
▾
Deprotonate the alcohol with a strong base (NaH or Na metal) → alkoxide R–O⁻. Then SN2 on a 1° or methyl alkyl halide → ether. Use 2°/3° → E2.
R–OH  →NaH  R–O⁻  →R'–CH₂Br (SN2)  R–O–CH₂R'
Which side of the ether gets the alkyl halide?
Always pick the path where the alkyl halide is less hindered (methyl/1°). If both pieces are 3°, Williamson will not work.
6
Fischer Esterification (preview)
To ester
▾
Alcohol + carboxylic acid + H⁺ catalyst → ester + water. Reversible — drive with excess alcohol or by removing water. Full mechanism is covered under the Carboxylic Acids hub.
R–OH + R'–COOH  ⇌H⁺  R'–CO–O–R + H₂O
Two oxidants on the same primary alcohol — stop at aldehyde or push to acid
Same starting 1-propanol in both columns. PCC is anhydrous, so the aldehyde never picks up water to form the hydrate that further oxidation requires — it stops there. Jones is aqueous chromic acid, so the aldehyde becomes a hydrate, which presents a new C–H to the Cr(VI) and is oxidized one rung higher to a carboxylic acid.
Decision widget
PCC vs Jones — which oxidation?
DAT favorite trap
PCCPCC / CH₂Cl₂
Anhydrous (no water around to form hydrate)
1° alcohol → aldehyde · stops there
2° alcohol → ketone
3° alcohol → no reaction (no α-H)
→ aldehyde
vs
JonesCrO₃ / H₂SO₄ / H₂O
Aqueous acidic — water is part of it
1° alcohol → carboxylic acid · goes all the way
2° alcohol → ketone (same as PCC)
3° alcohol → no reaction
→ carboxylic acid
The trick: 2° alcohols give the same ketone either way — PCC vs Jones only matters for 1°. When the DAT asks "which oxidant stops at the aldehyde?" the answer is PCC (anhydrous) because the hydrate intermediate that Jones can over-oxidize never forms.
Alcohol takeaways
  • The OH must be activated before it leaves: protonate, tosylate, or reagent-convert with SOCl₂/PBr₃.
  • PCC = stop at aldehyde. Jones = go to carboxylic acid. 3° alcohols: no oxidation.
  • SOCl₂ and PBr₃ do NOT rearrange. HX on a 2° alcohol often does.
  • Williamson ether: deprotonate, then SN2 on 1°/methyl R–X.
  • Tosylation = free retention-then-inversion trick for stereo control.
