Alcohol PracticeOxidation · conversion · stereochem · 5 questions
0/5
11-butanol is treated with PCC in CH₂Cl₂. The product is:
Explanation
B is correct. PCC is a mild, anhydrous oxidant — it oxidizes 1° alcohols only as far as the aldehyde (no water around to form the hydrate → can't over-oxidize to COOH). A (butanoic acid) would require Jones or hot KMnO₄. C is wrong position. D is wrong — PCC works.
2(R)-2-butanol is converted to 2-chlorobutane. To get the (S) product cleanly, use:
Explanation
C is correct. Two-step "tosylate then SN2": TsCl makes the tosylate with retention (no bond to C broken), then Cl⁻ does SN2 on R–OTs with inversion. Net: retention × inversion = inversion overall → (S) product cleanly. A (HCl on 2° alcohol) goes SN1 → racemic. B (SOCl₂) gives Cl but no inversion. D gives Br, not Cl.
3Williamson ether synthesis of ethyl tert-butyl ether requires:
Explanation
D is correct. Williamson is an SN2 — it needs the alkyl halide to be 1° or methyl. In A, ethyl bromide (1°) works cleanly. In B, tert-butyl bromide (3°) + strong base → E2 gives isobutylene (elimination), no ether. Always make the Williamson by putting the alkyl halide on the less hindered side of the target ether.
42-methylcyclohexanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄. The major alkene is:
Explanation
A is correct. E1 dehydration gives the Zaitsev (most substituted) alkene. From 2-methylcyclohexanol, the cation is 2° on C1; it could also shift to 3° but doesn't need to (β-H elimination already gives the trisubstituted alkene). Losing the H on C2 → 1-methylcyclohexene (3 substituents on C=C). Losing on C6 → 3-methylcyclohexene (only 2 substituents), which is minor.
5Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄/acetone) oxidizes:
Explanation
C is correct. Jones is the aqueous acidic chromate oxidant — it fully oxidizes 1° alcohols to carboxylic acids (via aldehyde hydrate intermediate, then further oxidation) and 2° alcohols to ketones (no H left on the carbonyl C — nothing to oxidize further). 3° alcohols don't react.
Hub 06

Ethers & Epoxides — the strained ring twist

Ethers are boring — they're inert under most conditions. Epoxides are the opposite: strained three-membered rings open readily with both nucleophiles and electrophiles. The direction of attack flips between acid and base — master that flip and you've mastered this hub.

Plate VII — Ether & Epoxide Reactions
Ethers are mostly inert. Epoxides split into two reactions depending on conditions — this flip is the hub's centerpiece.
1
Ether Cleavage (HI, HBr)
Acidic
▾
Only strong HX (HI > HBr) cleaves ethers. Mechanism: protonate O, then I⁻ (great nucleophile) attacks. 1° goes SN2 at the less substituted carbon. 3° goes SN1, breaking on the more substituted side.
R–O–R' + 2 HI → R–I + R'–I + H₂O (excess HI)
or R–O–R' + HI → R–I + R'–OH (1 eq)
Two openings on the same unsymmetric epoxide — Markov vs anti-Markov
Same starting 2,2-dimethyloxirane in both columns. Acid protonates O first, so the TS has cation-like δ+ on the more-substituted carbon — H₂O attacks there (Markov). Base/Nu⁻ runs as straight SN2; sterics drive Nu to the less substituted carbon (anti-Markov). Both are anti (backside).
2
Epoxide — Acidic Ring Opening
Markov · anti
▾
Protonate the O → protonated epoxide (O⁺). Nucleophile attacks the more substituted C because the TS has cation-like character there. Still backside → anti.
epoxide + H₃O⁺  →  anti diol (Nu/OH on more substituted C)
1
Protonation
H⁺ protonates the oxygen → positively charged three-membered ring.
2
Nu attacks more substituted C
The more substituted C has more positive character (better cation). H₂O (or other Nu) attacks it backside. Ring opens.
3
Deprotonate
Remove H⁺ → neutral anti diol.
3
Epoxide — Basic (Nu⁻) Ring Opening
anti-Markov · anti
▾
Nucleophile (RO⁻, CN⁻, R–MgX, RLi, OH⁻) attacks the less substituted C directly (classic SN2 sterics) → anti product. Works because of ring strain (epoxides are unique among ethers).
epoxide + Nu⁻ → anti product, Nu on less substituted C, OH on other
Grignard + epoxide
Hugely useful: R–MgX + ethylene oxide → R–CH₂–CH₂–OH. Adds a two-carbon hydroxyethyl unit to any Grignard. Exam favorite.
Ether/epoxide takeaways
  • Ethers are inert except under harsh HX (HI, HBr) which cleaves them.
  • Epoxides open readily because of ring strain. Acid → Markov. Base/Nu → anti-Markov. Both give anti (backside).
  • Grignard + ethylene oxide is the standard way to tack two carbons and an OH onto a Grignard.
Practice
Ether & Epoxide PracticeThe acid vs base flip · 5 questions
0/5
12-methyl-2-(1-methylethyl)oxirane (an epoxide with one quaternary-like C and one CH-Me C) is opened with H₃O⁺. The nucleophile H₂O attacks:
Explanation
B is correct. Under acid, the protonated epoxide has cation-like character on the more-substituted C (better stabilized cation). Water attacks there (Markov-like). This is the opposite of basic opening (where SN2-like sterics drives Nu to the less substituted C).
2Same epoxide as above, opened with NaOMe. The methoxide attacks:
Explanation
C is correct. Under base/Nu⁻ conditions, the reaction is purely SN2-like: no cation, so sterics dominates → Nu hits the less hindered carbon. Both acidic and basic openings give anti (backside attack), but regiochemistry flips.
3Diethyl ether (CH₃CH₂-O-CH₂CH₃) is treated with 1 equiv HI at high temperature. The product(s) are:
Explanation
A is correct. HI is one of the few reagents that cleaves ethers (I⁻ is a great nucleophile; O gets protonated). With 1 equiv, you get the alkyl iodide + alcohol. With excess HI, the alcohol gets converted to a second alkyl iodide too (answer B would require excess).
4To add a 2-carbon hydroxyethyl chain to a molecule via Grignard, the best partner is:
Explanation
D is correct. R-MgBr + ethylene oxide opens the ring at the less-hindered carbon, adding -CH₂-CH₂-OH to the Grignard → a 1° alcohol two carbons longer. A adds one carbon to a 1° alcohol; C adds one carbon to a 2° alcohol. Diethyl ether (B) is just the solvent — inert.
5An epoxide derived from cis-2-butene is opened with aqueous acid. The product is:
Explanation
B is correct. mCPBA gives syn epoxidation (cis alkene → cis epoxide). Then acidic ring opening is anti → overall: cis alkene + syn epoxidation + anti opening → anti diol = racemic (R,R)/(S,S). This is the canonical "cis alkene gives racemic diol via epoxide" result. (For comparison: cis alkene + OsO₄ would give meso diol because OsO₄ is syn.)
Hub 07

Aromatic — Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution

Benzene is a nucleophile (electron-rich π system), but it refuses to add because that would destroy aromaticity. Instead, it substitutes: electrophile attacks → arenium ion → loses H⁺ → aromatic again. Five core reactions, plus directing effects that decide where a second group lands.

Coach note · the recognition shortcut
If you see a ring, think EAS. That is the family. Electrophilic aromatic substitution covers a whole bunch of reactions on benzene — and you do not have to know every carbocation intermediate or every resonance step. You just have to recognize: ring + something getting added = EAS. It looks like addition, but really, it is substitution — a hydrogen on the ring is what gets kicked off so the ring can stay aromatic. The whole family is Thomas's favorite; maybe that helps you flag it on test day.
Pattern shortcuts for this hub
Plate VIII — The EAS Hub
Starting material: benzene. All 5 core reactions follow the same 3-step arenium ion mechanism — only the E⁺ changes.
Director Sorter · drag-and-drop drill
Tier 1 muscle memory. Drag each substituent tile into the bucket where its directing behaviour belongs. The halogen tier is the trap — halogens are deactivators (lone pair too far from the ring to fully donate) but still o/p directors (the lone pair wins on the directing question, the inductive pull wins on the rate question).
Round 1 Sort 16 substituents into 5 buckets 0 / 16 placed
Score: 0 / 16
Why each bucket directs the way it does
  • Strong activators (–NH₂, –OH, –OR): the lone pair on N/O resonance-donates into the ring. The σ-complex resonance contributors place negative density at ortho and para — that's where the next E⁺ lands. Lone-pair donation outweighs the small inductive pull, so they're also rate-accelerators (activators).
  • Weak activators (–NHCOR, –alkyl, –vinyl): still o/p, but donate via hyperconjugation (alkyl) or partial resonance (vinyl, amide where the carbonyl pulls some N density away). Slower than strong activators but same regiochemistry.
  • Halogens (–F, –Cl, –Br, –I): the trap. Lone pair can resonance-donate (so o/p direction wins) — but the σ-bond is so polarized that inductive withdrawal dominates the rate. Net: o/p director AND deactivator.
  • Weak deactivators (–CHO, –COR, –COOR): π-system pulls electrons out of the ring through resonance. The σ-complex with + at ortho or para is destabilized (the + lands next to another already-electron-poor C). E⁺ prefers meta, where the resonance contributors don't put + adjacent to the EWG.
  • Strong deactivators (–NO₂, –CN, –SO₃H): same logic as weak deactivators but with much stronger withdrawal. Meta director, severe rate slowdown — sometimes 10⁵× slower than benzene.
Where Does It Land? · click the carbon the new group attacks
Tier 2 prediction game. Pick a substrate, click the C where the next electrophile (Br⁺ from Br₂/FeBr₃) ends up. The reveal panel explains the σ-complex resonance logic — for activators, the contributor with + on the ipso C (bearing the donor) is stabilized; for deactivators, that contributor is destabilized so E⁺ avoids o/p and lands at meta.

— + Br₂ / FeBr₃ → ? click the C where Br lands

Tier 3. The same two reagents in different orders give different products. Pick a target, click reagent tiles to fill the steps in sequence, then click Run sequence to walk through what each step actually produces. The two introductory puzzles use the SAME reagents but require opposite orderings — that contrast is the whole point.
Pick a puzzle Drag the reagents into the right sequence
