Reagent palette · click to add to next empty slot
Disubstituted Showdown · two directors, one new bond
Tier 4 stretch. When the ring already has two substituents, a third group has to satisfy both directors at once. Pick a substrate; every available C is colored by tier (green = major, amber = minor, gray = avoid). Click any C to see why. Rule: stronger activator wins; if both directors agree, that position is gold.
Pick a substrate Where does the third group land?
major site minor site avoid (both directors against)
Click any colored position to see the directing logic.
Major sites satisfy both directors (or the dominant one). Minor sites satisfy one but not the other. Avoid sites are where both directors push against — usually meta to an activator AND ortho/para to a deactivator's resonance trap.
Universal EAS mechanism (all 5 reactions)
Step 1: Generate the electrophile E⁺ (with the appropriate Lewis acid catalyst if needed).
Step 2: π system of benzene attacks E⁺ → arenium ion (sp³ carbon with + charge delocalized over the other 5 ring carbons). Aromaticity temporarily broken.
Step 3: A base (usually the leaving group from step 1) removes the H from the sp³ carbon → aromaticity restored. Net: Ar–H → Ar–E.
1
Halogenation (X₂/FeX₃)
EAS
▾
Br₂/FeBr₃ or Cl₂/FeCl₃. Lewis acid polarizes X–X to make a strong electrophile. I₂ too weak; F₂ too reactive.
Ar–H + Br₂ / FeBr₃ → Ar–Br + HBr
2
Nitration (HNO₃/H₂SO₄)
EAS · → NH₂
▾
Electrophile is the nitronium ion (⁺NO₂). Gives Ar–NO₂ which is easily reduced to Ar–NH₂ by Sn/HCl, Zn/HCl, Fe/HCl, or H₂/Pd. Key synthesis route to anilines.
Ar–H + ⁺NO₂ → Ar–NO₂   →Sn/HCl or H₂/Pd   Ar–NH₂
Step Mode
EAS — Nitration of BenzeneTemplate for ALL electrophilic aromatic substitution · 4 steps
1/4
Why directors send the next group where they do
Every EAS attack creates a σ-complex with a + charge spread over three carbons — the ortho and para positions relative to the new substituent. The ipso C of the σ-complex (the one carrying the existing substituent) is one of those + carriers.

Activators donate electron density (lone pair, hyperconjugation, π-system) → they happily neighbor a + → o/p attack puts + on a C they can stabilize → o/p wins.

Deactivators withdraw electron density → they refuse to neighbor a + → o/p attack puts + on a C they destabilize → that contributor is forbidden → meta wins, since meta attack avoids placing + adjacent to the EWG.
This mechanism applies to all 5 EAS reactions
Halogenation, sulfonation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation all follow this same three-act template: (1) generate E⁺, (2) π attacks E⁺ → arenium, (3) base removes H⁺ → rearomatize. Only the E⁺ identity changes (Br⁺, SO₃, R⁺, or RC≡O⁺ respectively).
3
Sulfonation (SO₃/H₂SO₄)
Reversible
▾
Fuming H₂SO₄ (SO₃ dissolved in H₂SO₄). Electrophile is SO₃. Reversible: hot dilute H₂SO₄ removes the SO₃H group. Used as a blocking group to force para substitution, then removed.
4
Friedel-Crafts Alkylation (R-X/AlCl₃)
Watch rearrangement!
▾
AlCl₃ pulls X⁻ off R–X → carbocation E⁺. Rearrangements are common (just like any free cation). Also fails on strongly deactivated rings (e.g., nitrobenzene won't alkylate).
Traps
(1) Cation rearrangement — n-propyl chloride + benzene → isopropylbenzene. (2) Polyalkylation — product is more activated than starting material, so di/trialkylation happens easily. (3) Deactivated rings — rings with NO₂, SO₃H, CF₃, carbonyls won't do FC.
5
Friedel-Crafts Acylation (RCOCl/AlCl₃)
No rearr.
▾
Electrophile = acylium ion RC≡O⁺, stabilized by resonance → no rearrangement, no polyacylation (product is a deactivated ketone). The synthesis workhorse.
Ar–H + RCOCl / AlCl₃ → Ar–CO–R + HCl
Clemmensen or Wolff-Kishner
To get a straight alkyl group onto a ring without rearrangement: acylate first (RCOCl/AlCl₃), then reduce the ketone to CH₂ with Zn(Hg)/HCl (Clemmensen) or NH₂NH₂/KOH (Wolff-Kishner). This is the go-to "n-propylbenzene without rearrangement" strategy.
6
Side-Chain Oxidation
To COOH
▾
Hot KMnO₄ (or K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄) oxidizes any benzylic C-H all the way to –COOH, regardless of alkyl chain length. No benzylic H (e.g., t-butylbenzene) → no reaction.
Ph–CH₂–CH₃  →KMnO₄ · Δ  Ph–COOH + CO₂
Ortho/Para vs Meta — why substituents direct where they do
o/p director
Aniline (–NH₂)
Donor with lone pair
Why o/p? The N lone pair can donate into the ring through resonance. The electron pair flows to ortho and para positions (push an arrow from N through π, land at those C's), raising electron density there. When E⁺ attacks, the resulting arenium ion carries + charge — but the + can sit right next to N, where N shares its lone pair to stabilize it. Attack at m doesn't benefit from this.
Arenium ion for para attack — stabilized by N lone pair
m director
Nitrobenzene (–NO₂)
Withdrawer via π bond
Why m? The C=N of –NO₂ has a π bond to an electronegative atom, which pulls electron density out of the ring at o/p by resonance. Those positions are electron-poor — exactly where E⁺ doesn't want to land. When E⁺ attacks m, the resulting + charge avoids being placed next to N (which would be disastrous, two + next to each other).
Arenium ion for ortho attack — forbidden: + next to δ⁺ N
The exception Halogens: o/p directors but deactivators
σ-effect (through bonds)
Halogens are very electronegative → they withdraw density inductively → deactivates the ring (slower EAS).
vs
π-effect (lone pair donation)
Halogens also have lone pairs that can donate into the ring → stabilize + at o/p → o/p director.
The σ-withdrawal wins for speed (slower than benzene) but the π-donation wins for regio. Net: o/p directing deactivator — the only substituent class that's split.
Directing effects cheat sheet (all DAT substituents)
SubstituentActivator?DirectionWhy (mechanism)
–NH₂, –NHR, –NR₂, –OH, –O⁻Strong activatoro/pLone pair on N/O donates into ring via π (strong)
–OR, –NHCORModerate activatoro/pLone pair donates, attenuated by the other group on N/O
–R (alkyl), –ArWeak activatoro/pHyperconjugation / inductive donation only (no lone pair)
–F, –Cl, –Br, –IDeactivatoro/p (the trap)σ-withdraws (fast < benzene), π-donates (o/p direct) — split: deactivates but still directs ortho/para
–CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –CONH₂, –SO₃HModerate deactivatormπ bond to EN atom pulls density from o/p → attacks at m
–NO₂, –NR₃⁺, –CF₃, –CCl₃Strong deactivatormEither heavy π-withdrawal or formal + charge
The 4-word rule
Donor → o/p. Withdrawer → m. Halogens = exception. Alkyl → o/p weak.
Every DAT directing-effects question boils down to these four cases.
Multi-step synthesis traps
Order matters. If you want meta-bromonitrobenzene:
1. Nitrate first (NO₂ is a m-director) → nitrobenzene.
2. Then brominate → m-bromonitrobenzene.
Reversing the order gives o/p because Br is an o/p director. The DAT will test this.
Trap · Friedel-Crafts won't work on these rings
Both FC alkylation and FC acylation fail on:
  • Strongly deactivated rings — nitrobenzene, benzoic acid, pyridine, anything with –NO₂, –CN, –SO₃H, –CF₃, –COR, –NR₃⁺ already on it. The ring is too electron-poor to attack the electrophile.
  • Anilines (–NH₂, –NHR, –NR₂) — the basic nitrogen complexes with AlCl₃, deactivating the catalyst AND protonating the ring into a ⁺NR₃ m-director. Workaround: acetylate the nitrogen first (→ –NHCOR), run FC, then hydrolyze the amide.
Rule of thumb: if the ring is less reactive than a halobenzene, FC won't go.
EAS-only scope · the inverse rule lives elsewhere
Heads-up for cross-text traps: the directing rules above are EAS-specific. In the rarely-tested inverse reaction (nucleophilic aromatic substitution on an electron-poor ring), an EWG like –NO₂ activates ortho/para to a leaving group instead of directing meta. The DAT OChem outline only tests EAS — keep your reflexes tuned to that and don't over-think a ring that has –NO₂ already on it.
Aromatic takeaways
  • All 5 core EAS reactions share one mechanism: E⁺ generated, ring attacks, arenium ion, lose H⁺.
  • Lone pair → o/p. Pi bond to EN atom → m. Halogens are o/p directors but deactivators.
  • FC alkylation rearranges and polyalkylates. FC acylation does neither — use it plus Clemmensen/Wolff-Kishner for clean alkyl chains.
  • Nitration + reduction = standard route to anilines; side-chain oxidation with hot KMnO₄ = benzoic acid regardless of chain length.
  • Order of substitution determines the product. Always check directing effects of what's already on the ring.
Practice
Aromatic PracticeEAS + directing effects + synthesis · 5 questions
0/5
1Nitration of toluene (methylbenzene) gives predominantly:
Explanation
C is correct. The methyl group is a weak activator and an o/p-director (it donates electron density via hyperconjugation, stabilizing the arenium ion at ortho and para positions). You get both ortho and para products. For toluene nitration the real ratio is roughly 58% ortho / 38% para / 4% meta — ortho actually wins numerically (there are 2 ortho positions vs only 1 para), though para is enriched relative to the 2:1 statistical expectation because ortho carries a small steric penalty from the methyl group. For DAT purposes, both "ortho dominant" and "para dominant" are reported in different sources; the durable answer is "o/p mixture, meta suppressed." The trap to catch is choosing a meta-only product — methyl never gives meta.
2To prepare meta-bromonitrobenzene starting from benzene, the correct order is:
Explanation
A is correct. NO₂ is a meta-director; Br is an ortho/para-director. To get the Br meta to NO₂, put NO₂ on first (now it directs the next group to meta). If you brominated first, the next substitution would go ortho/para to Br — wrong regiochemistry.
3Which compound does NOT undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation?
Explanation
B is correct. Strongly deactivated rings (NO₂, CF₃, sulfonyl, carbonyls, ⁺NR₃) do not undergo Friedel-Crafts — the ring is too electron-poor for the weak alkyl cation electrophile. Anilines also fail (the amine nitrogen complexes with AlCl₃). A, C, D are all activated enough to react.
4Which starting material + reagent sequence gives n-propylbenzene (Ph-CH₂-CH₂-CH₃) without rearrangement?
Explanation
D is correct. FC alkylation of benzene with 1-chloropropane (A) rearranges to give mostly isopropylbenzene — the 1° cation hydride-shifts to 2°. To get clean n-propyl, acylate first (FC acylation — no rearrangement because the acylium is resonance-stabilized), then reduce the resulting ketone to CH₂ via Clemmensen (Zn(Hg)/HCl). This is the canonical "n-alkyl without rearrangement" route.
5Hot KMnO₄ oxidation of para-tert-butyltoluene gives:
Explanation
B is correct. Hot KMnO₄ oxidizes any benzylic C–H → COOH regardless of chain length. The methyl has benzylic H's → oxidizes to COOH. The tert-butyl group has no benzylic H (the benzylic C is quaternary) → doesn't react. Product: p-tert-butylbenzoic acid. This is a classic DAT trap.
Aromaticity Worked Examples — the DAT trap cases
Example 1 · Cyclobutadiene (4 pi electrons → ANTIAROMATIC)
Cyclobutadiene is a flat, fully conjugated 4-membered ring with 4 pi electrons (4n where n=1). 4n electrons = antiaromatic — destabilized relative to the open-chain. Cyclobutadiene is so unstable it cannot be isolated under normal conditions. When you see a ring with 4 or 8 pi electrons and all carbons in the pi system, label it antiaromatic, not merely non-aromatic.
Example 2 · Cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi electrons → AROMATIC — explains pKa 16 of cyclopentadiene)
Cyclopentadiene has two C=C bonds (4 pi) and an sp³ CH₂. When deprotonated by base, the carbanion contributes a lone pair into the ring → 6 pi electrons → aromatic anion. This is why cyclopentadiene is unusually acidic for a hydrocarbon (pKa ≈ 16, comparable to water) — the anion is stabilized by aromaticity. DAT trap: students expect a C–H to have pKa ~50; aromaticity of the anion drives it down by 34 units.
Example 3 · Pyridine lone pair — the classic "does N count?" trap
Pyridine has a nitrogen in a 6-membered ring. The N lone pair is in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring — perpendicular to the pi system — and does NOT contribute to the 6 pi electrons. The ring pi system is still exactly 6 electrons (3 C=C equivalents). Result: pyridine IS aromatic (6 pi, Huckel-compliant) AND the N lone pair is available for protonation (pKa of pyridinium 5.2). Contrast with pyrrole: pyrrole's N lone pair IS the 6th pi electron — protonating it destroys aromaticity (pKa of pyrrolium −3.8).
Hub 08 · Largest

Aldehydes & Ketones — the carbonyl hub

Two worlds in one hub. The C=O carbon is electrophilic → nucleophiles attack it (nucleophilic addition). The α-carbon is acidic (pKa ≈ 20) → bases form enolates that act as nucleophiles. Every DAT carbonyl question is one of these two stories.

Pattern shortcuts for this hub
Plate IX — The Carbonyl Hub
Starting material: acetaldehyde (CH₃–CHO). Each branch shows the real skeletal product — two reaction modes: addition to electrophilic C or enolization at the α carbon.
Universal nucleophilic addition template
Step 1: Nu attacks the δ⁺ carbonyl carbon from above or below the plane → tetrahedral alkoxide.
Step 2: Protonation (or further steps) gives the product. Under acid, the carbonyl is protonated first (making C even more electrophilic) before attack.
1
Hydration → Hydrate (gem-diol)
Reversible
▾
Water adds across C=O to give a gem-diol (two OH on the same C). Equilibrium favors the carbonyl for most ketones; aldehydes are closer to 50/50; formaldehyde and Cl-containing aldehydes (e.g., chloral) favor the hydrate.
R₂C=O + H₂O ⇌ R₂C(OH)₂
2
Acetal Formation (2 ROH, H⁺)
Protecting group
▾
Aldehyde/ketone + 2 equiv alcohol + H⁺ → acetal (geminal diether). Goes through a hemiacetal intermediate. Water must be removed to drive it forward.
R₂C=O + 2 R'OH  ⇌H⁺  R₂C(OR')₂ + H₂O
Step Mode
Acetal Formation MechanismAcid-catalyzed · PADPED · acetaldehyde + 2 methanol → dimethyl acetal · 5 steps
1/5
PADPED — the universal acid-carbonyl mnemonic
Protonate · Add · Deprotonate · Protonate · Eliminate · Deprotonate. This same 6-letter dance runs Fischer esterification, acetal formation, imine formation, and most acid-catalyzed carbonyl chemistry. Memorize it once, apply it everywhere.
When does hemiacetal → acetal? · equilibrium control via Le Chatelier
remove water (Dean-Stark, mol sieves) EQUILIBRIUM · stalls at hemiacetal water still present · acid + alcohol but H₂O not removed REVERSE · driven LEFT aqueous acid (excess H₂O) · hydrolyzes acetal → C=O
Every step in PADPED is reversible. The position of the equilibrium is decided by Le Chatelier — push the system right or left by what you ADD or REMOVE.

Forward (carbonyl → acetal): excess alcohol, acid catalyst, and most importantly remove water. Dean-Stark trap or molecular sieves do this. Without water removal, the equilibrium parks at hemiacetal or comes all the way back.

Reverse (acetal → carbonyl, deprotection): aqueous acid. Flooded with water, the equilibrium runs backward and the C=O is restored. This is exactly how you take an acetal protecting group off.

Hemiacetal as a special case: open-chain hemiacetals are usually too unstable to isolate — they collapse back to the carbonyl. Cyclic hemiacetals (sugars, lactols) are stable and the basis of all carbohydrate chemistry.
Acetals as protecting groups
Acetals are stable to base, Grignards, LiAlH₄, NaBH₄, nucleophiles, but hydrolyze back to the carbonyl under aqueous acid. Use to mask a C=O while doing chemistry elsewhere.
3
Imine Formation (1° amine)
C=N
▾
R₂C=O + R'NH₂ → R₂C=NR' + H₂O. Optimum pH ≈ 4–5 (acid needed to catalyze water loss, but too much acid protonates the amine). → See reductive amination for the one-pot version that captures the iminium and reduces it directly.
R₂C=O + R'NH₂  ⇌H⁺  R₂C=NR' + H₂O
Carbonyl + 1° amine (R-NH₂) Acid catalyst, pH ≈ 4-5 sweet spot Output: C=N (imine) + H₂O
Worked example Acetone + methylamine + H⁺ (pH 4-5) → N-methylpropan-2-imine + H₂O. The amine N attacks the carbonyl C; protonation/dehydration kicks out water; deprotonating the iminium N gives the neutral C=N.
Why pH 4-5 and not stronger acid?
You need acid to protonate the OH (so water can leave), but at very low pH the amine itself protonates to ⁺NH₃R — no longer nucleophilic. pH 4-5 hits the sweet spot: enough H⁺ for catalysis, not enough to kill the amine.
Practice
Benzaldehyde + aniline (PhNH₂) + trace H⁺ gives:
Answer: Schiff base imine · 1° amine + carbonyl + H⁺ → C=N. Aniline is a 1° amine, so the product is an imine, not enamine. Aromatic Schiff bases are particularly stable.
1° → imine · 2° → enamine
A 2° amine has no second N-H to lose at the iminium stage. Instead, an α-H is removed → C=C-NR₂ (enamine). Same first 3 steps; only the final deprotonation site differs.
Play mechanism · 4 frames Tier 2
Step Mode
Imine Formation MechanismAcetone + methylamine · 4 frames · A-D-P-E pattern · ends with C=N
1/4
Deep dive · imine vs enamine fork Tier 3
Imine vs Enamine — the iminium fork decides which one you get
The first three steps are identical for 1° and 2° amines: amine attacks → carbinolamine → protonate → lose water → iminium. The difference shows up only at step 4, when the iminium needs to lose a proton:

1° amine (R-NH₂): the iminium has an N–H. Base takes that H → neutral C=N (imine).

2° amine (R₂NH): the iminium has no N–H to give up. Base instead takes an α-H (a hydrogen on the carbon adjacent to the C=N⁺) → C=C double bond → enamine (C=C–NR₂).

Quick test: count the H's on the amine N before reaction. R-NH₂ (2 H's) → imine. R₂NH (1 H) → also forms imine then loses α-H? Actually only after losing one H it becomes a neutral iminium with 0 N-H, so for the iminium of R₂NH there's no N-H to lose at step 4 — α-H deprotonation takes over. R₃N (3° amine) is dead — no N-H at any stage; doesn't react.
Variants
HONH₂ → oxime. H₂N–NH₂ → hydrazone. H₂N–NHPh → phenylhydrazone. H₂N–NHC(=O)NH₂ → semicarbazone. All same mechanism, just different N-substituent.
4
Enamine Formation (2° amine)
C=C–N
▾
Like imine formation up to the iminium step. A 2° amine has no N-H to lose, so the system removes an α-H instead → C=C double bond → enamine.
R–CO–CH₂R'' + R₂NH  ⇌H⁺  R–C(NR₂)=CHR'' + H₂O
Carbonyl + 2° amine (R₂NH — pyrrolidine, morpholine) Acid catalyst, pH ≈ 4-5 Output: C=C-NR₂ (enamine) + H₂O
Worked example Cyclohexanone + pyrrolidine + H⁺ → 1-pyrrolidinylcyclohex-1-ene + H₂O. Same first 3 steps as imine formation; at the iminium stage there's no N-H, so an α-H comes off → enamine. The enamine α-C is nucleophilic — used as a "neutral enolate equivalent" in Stork alkylation.
Why is an enamine equivalent to an enolate?
The N lone pair pushes into the C=C π bond → α-C carries excess electron density (like an enolate's α-C). Unlike a true enolate, an enamine is neutral — easier to handle, no strong base needed. After alkylation at α-C, hydrolysis releases the original carbonyl. Stork enamine α-alkylation.
Practice
Cyclopentanone + diethylamine + trace H⁺ gives:
Answer: enamine · diethylamine is a 2° amine (R₂NH). The intermediate iminium has no N-H to lose, so an α-H is removed → C=C-NR₂.
3° amines are dead
R₃N has no N-H at all → can't form even the carbinolamine. Tertiary amines don't react with carbonyls under acid catalysis. Only 1° (→ imine) and 2° (→ enamine) work.
Play mechanism · 3 frames Tier 2
Step Mode
Enamine Formation · the α-H deprotonation routeCyclohexanone + pyrrolidine · diverges at iminium stage · 3 frames
1/3
Common 2° amines for enamine work
Pyrrolidine (5-ring) — the most reactive enamine former. Morpholine (6-ring with O) — widely used. Piperidine (6-ring) — slower but more sterically tunable. Always pick a cyclic 2° amine — open-chain dialkyl amines work but tend to give mixtures.
5
Cyanohydrin Formation (HCN)
C–C bond
▾
CN⁻ (from KCN or NaCN with a trace of acid) attacks C=O → alkoxide → protonation → cyanohydrin (HO–C–CN).
R₂C=O + HCN → R₂C(OH)(CN)
Follow-ups
Hydrolyze CN → α-hydroxy carboxylic acid (e.g., glycolic acid). Reduce CN → β-amino alcohol. This is a classic one-carbon homologation.
6
Reduction: NaBH₄ vs LiAlH₄
H⁻ addition
▾
Both deliver H⁻ to the carbonyl. Workup is H₃O⁺ or H₂O. Aldehyde → 1° alcohol. Ketone → 2° alcohol.
R₂C=O  →1. NaBH₄ · 2. H₂O  R₂CH–OH
Selectivity
NaBH₄: mild, reduces aldehydes and ketones only. Leaves esters, amides, acids alone.
LiAlH₄: powerful, reduces anything with a C=O: aldehyde, ketone, ester (→ 1° alcohol), amide (→ amine), carboxylic acid (→ 1° alcohol), nitrile (→ 1° amine), epoxide (→ alcohol).
DIBAL-H (1 equiv, cold): reduces ester or nitrile just to the aldehyde — stops halfway.
7
Grignard / Organolithium Addition
C–C bond
▾
R'–MgX (carbanion equivalent) attacks C=O → alkoxide → acid workup → alcohol with a new C–C bond.
R'–MgX + R₂C=O → R'R₂C–O⁻ MgX⁺  →H₃O⁺  R'R₂C–OH
Alcohol type from starting carbonyl
Formaldehyde (HCHO) + RMgX → 1° alcohol.
Other aldehyde (R'CHO) + RMgX → 2° alcohol.
Ketone (R'R''C=O) + RMgX → 3° alcohol.
Grignard killers
Grignards attack any acidic proton (pKa < ~30): –OH, –NH, –COOH, –C≡CH, –NH₂, –SH will destroy the reagent before it can react with your carbonyl. Protect or avoid.
Full Grignard partner cheat sheet
RMgX + Aldehyde → 2° alcohol (1 new C–C bond).
RMgX + Ketone → 3° alcohol.
RMgX + Formaldehyde (HCHO) → 1° alcohol (one extra carbon).
RMgX + CO₂, then H₃O⁺ → carboxylic acid (adds –COOH; cleanest way to extend a chain by one C and put an acid on the end).
RMgX + Ester (2 equiv) → 3° alcohol — R adds twice, both new R groups are the same.
RMgX + Acyl chloride (carefully 1 equiv, cold) → ketone; excess → 3° alcohol.
RMgX + Nitrile (R'–CN), then H₃O⁺ → ketone (Grignard adds once to C≡N, the imine hydrolyzes on workup). Named the Houben-Hoesch-like pathway.
RMgX + Epoxide → opens at less-hindered C, adds a 2-C –CH₂CH₂OH chain (with ethylene oxide).
RMgX + Amide (R'-CONR''₂) → stops at ketone with weak base workup, or 3° amine with excess.
8
Wittig Reaction (ylide)
C=C bond
▾
Phosphorus ylide (Ph₃P=CHR') — made from Ph₃P + R'–CH₂–X, then strong base — attacks C=O, forms a 4-membered oxaphosphetane, collapses by [2+2] retrocycloreversion into C=CHR' and Ph₃P=O. Net: C=O is replaced with C=C.
R₂C=O + Ph₃P=CHR' → R₂C=CHR' + Ph₃P=O
Carbonyl (aldehyde or ketone) Phosphorus ylide Ph₃P=CHR' Output: C=O swapped for C=C (alkene synthesis)
Worked example Acetone + Ph₃P=CH₂ → 2-methylpropene + Ph₃P=O. The carbon of the ylide attacks the carbonyl C; a 4-membered oxaphosphetane forms; it fragments to give a new C=C and the very stable phosphine oxide P=O.
What's the difference between a stabilized and unstabilized ylide?
An unstabilized ylide (Ph₃P=CHR with no EWG on the carbanion) is highly reactive → gives the Z (cis) alkene. A stabilized ylide (Ph₃P=CH-CO₂R or similar with EWG) is less reactive, has time to equilibrate → gives the E (trans) alkene. Memory: U → Z, S → E.
Practice
Cyclohexanone + Ph₃P=CHCH₃ gives:
Answer: methylenecyclohexane (technically ethylidenecyclohexane) · the C=O of the ketone is replaced with C=CHCH₃. Wittig works on both aldehydes AND ketones.
Retrosynthesis cue
When you see an alkene target, ask: "Where's the C=C? Could one side be a Wittig ylide and the other a C=O?" The Wittig is the cleanest C=C disconnection in synthesis.
Play mechanism · 4 frames Tier 2
Step Mode
Wittig Reaction MechanismPh₃P=CH₂ + acetone → 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) + Ph₃P=O · 4 frames
1/4
Deep dive · Z vs E ylide selectivity Tier 3
Why unstabilized ylides give Z and stabilized ylides give E
The ylide carbanion's reactivity controls the geometry of the alkene product:

Unstabilized ylide (no EWG): Ph₃P=CH-CH₃, Ph₃P=CH-Ph, etc. The carbanion is high-energy and reacts fast. The first oxaphosphetane it makes is cis (the kinetic product) and that's what fragments → Z-alkene.

Stabilized ylide (EWG present): Ph₃P=CH-COOR (Wadsworth-Emmons phosphonate variant), Ph₃P=CH-CN. The EWG drains charge off the ylide C → much less reactive → addition is reversible. The system has time to equilibrate to the more stable trans oxaphosphetane → E-alkene.

Memory: "U → Z, S → E" (unstabilized → Z, stabilized → E).
9
Aldol Condensation
α-reaction
▾
Base deprotonates an α-H (pKa ≈ 20) → enolate. Enolate attacks another carbonyl's C=O → β-hydroxy carbonyl (aldol). Heat drives off water → α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (condensation product).
2 CH₃CHO  →OH⁻  CH₃CH(OH)–CH₂–CHO  →Δ  CH₃CH=CH–CHO + H₂O
Carbonyl with α-H + base (NaOH, NaOEt) Enolate from one C=O attacks another C=O Heat drives β-hydroxy carbonyl → α,β-unsat carbonyl (condensation)
Worked example 2 CH₃CHO + dilute NaOH → 3-hydroxybutanal ("aldol"); on heating, dehydrates to but-2-enal (crotonaldehyde, α,β-unsat). The α-carbon of one acetaldehyde forms a new C-C bond with the carbonyl-C of another.
Why does mixing two enolizable carbonyls give a messy product?
Both partners can form enolates AND both can be electrophiles → 4 possible aldol products. To fix, use a "crossed aldol" with one non-enolizable carbonyl (benzaldehyde, formaldehyde, benzophenone) — only the other partner can deprotonate, so only one enolate forms.
Practice
Acetone + benzaldehyde + NaOH/Δ gives:
Answer: benzalacetone · benzaldehyde has no α-H → can only be the electrophile. Acetone forms the only enolate → clean crossed aldol → dehydrates to the α,β-unsat ketone.
↑ part of the enolate skeleton · Aldol's electrophile is a second C=O
Play mechanism · 4 steps Tier 2
1
Enolate formation
Base removes α-H → enolate (charge delocalized between α-C and O).
2
Enolate attacks second carbonyl
α-C of enolate attacks C=O of second carbonyl → alkoxide.
3
Protonation → aldol
Alkoxide grabs H from water → β-hydroxy carbonyl.
4
Heat → dehydration
E1cb-like elimination of water → α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (the "condensation" part).
Crossed aldol tips
If you mix two different enolizable carbonyls, you get 4 products (messy). To fix, use one non-enolizable carbonyl (benzaldehyde, formaldehyde, benzophenone) as the electrophile — only the other can form an enolate.
9.5
Michael Addition (1,4-conjugate addition)
α,β-unsat C=O · soft Nu
▾
An α,β-unsaturated carbonyl has two electrophilic sites: the carbonyl C (1,2 attack) and the β-C (1,4 attack). Soft, stabilized nucleophiles pick the β-C → Michael product (saturated, keeps C=O intact).
CH₂=CH–CO–R + Nu⁻ → Nu–CH₂–CH₂–CO–R  (after protonation)
↑ enolate skeleton · Michael's electrophile is an α,β-unsat C=C (β-carbon)
Acceptor: α,β-unsat carbonyl (enone, enoate, enal) Donor: soft Nu — stabilized enolate, Gilman cuprate, RS⁻ Result: 1,5-dicarbonyl (saturated, C=O preserved)
Worked example MVK + diethyl malonate enolate → 1,5-dicarbonyl. The malonate's stabilized α-carbanion is soft → attacks the β-C of methyl vinyl ketone (NOT the carbonyl C). Tautomerize → saturated 1,5-dicarbonyl.
Why does CH₃Li give 1,2-addition but R₂CuLi gives 1,4 on the same enone?
It's HSAB. CH₃Li is hard (small, charge-localized) → goes for the highest δ+ atom (the carbonyl C) → 1,2-allylic alcohol. Gilman R₂CuLi is soft (diffuse, polarizable) → matches the LUMO lobe at β-C → 1,4-Michael product. Same substrate, two completely different outcomes.
Practice
Methyl vinyl ketone + (CH₃)₂CuLi (Gilman, soft Nu):
Answer: 4-methyl-2-pentanone · Gilman is soft → 1,4 attack at the β-C → saturated 1,5-dicarbonyl after protonation. C=O preserved.
Deep dive · 1,2 vs 1,4 + HSAB Tier 3
Two attack modes on the same MVK — 1,2 (kinetic) vs 1,4 (Michael, thermodynamic)
Same starting α,β-unsaturated ketone in both columns. Hard Nu (RLi) lands on the carbonyl C and gives an alcohol. Soft Nu (Gilman R₂CuLi or stabilized enolate) lands on the β-C and gives the saturated Michael product after workup.
Step Mode
Michael Addition MechanismDiethyl malonate enolate + methyl vinyl ketone (MVK) · 4 steps · soft Nu adds 1,4
1/4
Why hard Nu goes 1,2 and soft Nu goes 1,4 — charge density vs orbital overlap
δ+ spot O β α large LUMO lobe ⁻C(CO₂R)₂ delocalized · diffuse HOMO 1,4 attack at β → enolate → 1,5-dicarbonyl on protonation soft Nu seeks the best orbital match HSAB at a single substrate · same molecule, two attack modes
In an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl, the LUMO has lobes at both the carbonyl C and the β-C. Two factors decide where a nucleophile lands:

Charge control (hard Nu): small, high-charge-density nucleophiles like RLi, RMgX, NaBH₄ are guided by electrostatics. The carbonyl C carries the highest δ++ (the inductive pull of the carbonyl O concentrates there) → they attack 1,2, hitting C=O directly. Product: an allylic alcohol after workup.

Orbital control (soft Nu): large, polarizable nucleophiles (stabilized enolates, R₂CuLi, RS⁻, R₂NH) are guided by HOMO–LUMO overlap. The β-C has a bigger LUMO coefficient → soft HOMOs match there → they attack 1,4. Product: a saturated 1,5-dicarbonyl after tautomerization.

Same enone, two completely different products. Pick the right Nu and you pick the regiochemistry.
Common Michael acceptors and donors — the cast you must recognize
Top row: acceptors (the electrophile — anything with a π system conjugated to a strong electron-withdrawing group). Bottom row: donors (the soft Nu — stabilized carbanions whose conjugate acid pKa lives in the 9–25 range).
Robinson annulation (brief)
Robinson annulation = Michael addition (step 1) followed by intramolecular aldol condensation (step 2) → cyclohexenone ring. The DAT rarely names "Robinson" explicitly, but may show the two-step sequence in a retrosynthesis question.
Hard/soft selectivity (HSAB) — the one rule that decides 1,2 vs 1,4
Hard Nu (RLi, RMgX, hydride from NaBH₄/LiAlH₄): localized, high charge density, low-energy HOMO. Couples best by charge with the most polarized (δ+) atom — the carbonyl C. Result: 1,2-addition, kinetic, gives an alcohol after workup.
Soft Nu (stabilized enolate, R₂CuLi Gilman, RS⁻, CN⁻, 2°-amine): delocalized, low charge density, high-energy HOMO. Couples best by orbital overlap with the LUMO lobe at the β-C. Result: 1,4-addition = Michael, thermodynamic, keeps the C=O intact.
Pair with these — Michael never travels alone
Aldol Condensation (card 9 above): Robinson annulation = Michael + intramolecular aldol. The same enolate chemistry that powers aldol powers the Michael donor — α-H, base, soft carbanion. Read aldol once, Michael clicks for free.
Gilman reagents R₂CuLi (see the C–C Bond Formers reference table further down in this hub): the canonical soft organometallic. Grignard hits an α,β-unsat ketone at the carbonyl C (1,2). Gilman hits the same ketone at the β-C (1,4). Selectivity by HSAB. This is the textbook reason Gilman reagents exist.
10
α-Halogenation (X₂ with acid or base)
α-reaction
▾
In acid: monohalogenation (stops at mono because first X deactivates further enolization). In base: polyhalogenation (first X makes next α-H more acidic).
R–CO–CH₃ + Br₂/H⁺ → R–CO–CH₂Br
Haloform reaction
Methyl ketones (R–CO–CH₃) + excess X₂/NaOH → RCOO⁻ + CHX₃. Iodoform (CHI₃, yellow ppt) is the classic positive test for a methyl ketone or a 2° methyl carbinol (R–CH(OH)–CH₃).
11
Oxidation: Aldehyde → Acid
Easy
▾
Aldehydes oxidize very easily: KMnO₄, CrO₃, Jones, Ag(NH₃)₂⁺ (Tollens), Cu²⁺/tartrate (Fehling/Benedict) — all give R–COOH. Ketones don't oxidize (no H on the carbonyl C to remove).
Diagnostic tests
Tollens (silver mirror): aldehyde +. Fehling / Benedict (red Cu₂O): aldehyde +. Both distinguish aldehyde from ketone.
12
Full Reduction to CH₂ (the executioners)
C=O → CH₂
▾
Coach analogy · the two executioners
Wolff-Kishner and Clemmensen are the executioners — they show up looking to chop the head clean off a ketone (or aldehyde). Same job, different uniforms: one wears acid, the other wears base. Either way, the C=O dies and you walk away with a CH2.

Pick by what's else on the molecule:
Acid-sensitive group nearby? Send the basic executioner (Wolff-Kishner).
Base-sensitive group nearby? Send the acidic executioner (Clemmensen).
Neither? Either one. Pick the cleaner workup for your lab.
Two ways to chop a C=O off entirely. Both convert R–CO–R' (or R–CHO) to R–CH2–R' (or R–CH3) — the carbonyl is fully reduced past the alcohol stage all the way to a methylene/methyl. Neither touches a C–C bond; only the C=O dies.
R–CO–R'  ─ executioner ─→  R–CH2–R'
Two executioners on the same ketone — pick by pH tolerance
Same starting acetophenone in both columns. Wolff-Kishner runs through a hydrazone and ejects N₂ under hot KOH — use it when the molecule is base-stable. Clemmensen reduces the C=O directly with Zn(Hg) under hot HCl — use it when the molecule is acid-stable. Both give the same CH₂ product.
The two executioners
Wolff-Kishner vs Clemmensen
same job, opposite chemistry
Wolff-KishnerThe basic one
NH2NH2 / KOH / Δ
Hydrazine forms the hydrazone (C=N–NH2); base + heat ejects N2 gas; the C–H sits where C=O used to.
Coach-trick mnemonic: N2H4 reads the same backwards — palindrome → Wolff-Kishner.
Use when: acid-sensitive groups on the substrate (acetals, glycosidic linkages, t-butyl esters).
Avoid when: base-sensitive groups (esters that would saponify, β-ketoesters that would deprotonate and condense).
vs
ClemmensenThe acidic one
Zn(Hg) / HCl(aq)
Zinc amalgam under hot HCl reduces the carbonyl directly to a methylene; no nitrogen species, no high-temp KOH bath.
Spot it by the amalgam: Zn(Hg) is the giveaway.
Use when: base-sensitive groups on the substrate (1,3-dicarbonyls, easily-saponified esters).
Avoid when: acid-sensitive groups (acetals, ortho-esters, anything that hydrolyzes in HCl).
The DAT trap: both reduce all the way to CH2, not to an alcohol. NaBH4 and LiAlH4 stop at the alcohol. If a stem says "fully reduce" or shows the product as a CH2 with no oxygen, you need an executioner.
The pairing question: "Which reagent reduces a ketone to a CH2 in the presence of a base-sensitive ester?" → Clemmensen. The flip: "...in the presence of an acetal?" → Wolff-Kishner.
Where this shows up after FC acylation
Friedel-Crafts alkylation on benzene with a primary halide rearranges (you get isopropyl from n-propyl chloride, etc.). The clean fix: FC acylate first (acylium doesn't rearrange because of its resonance), then send an executioner to reduce the resulting ketone to CH2. That's the canonical "n-alkyl on aromatic ring without rearrangement" route. The DAT loves this question.
Decision widget
NaBH₄ vs LiAlH₄ — which hydride?
selectivity matters
NaBH₄Sodium borohydride
Mild · chemoselective
Reduces aldehydes & ketones only
Ignores esters, amides, acids, nitriles
Safe with water & alcohols (workable in EtOH)
Use when you want to reduce C=O but leave a nearby ester/amide alone
vs
LiAlH₄Lithium aluminum hydride
Strong · unselective
Reduces anything with C=O or C≡N:
Aldehyde/ketone → 1°/2° alcohol
Ester/acid → 1° alcohol · Amide → amine (N stays)
Nitrile → 1° amine · Epoxide → alcohol · explodes in water
Bonus: DIBAL-H (1 eq, −78 °C) reduces an ester or nitrile only to the aldehyde and stops — use it when you want the aldehyde and nothing more. NaBH₃CN is selective for iminium ions (the reductive amination reagent).
Decision widget
Clemmensen vs Wolff-Kishner — two ways to kill C=O → CH₂
pick by pH tolerance
ClemmensenZn(Hg) / HCl
Acidic conditions
Use when the molecule is acid-stable
Don't use if you have base-sensitive groups to protect from the alternative
Works great with Friedel-Crafts acyl products
vs
Wolff-KishnerNH₂NH₂ · KOH · Δ
Basic conditions (strongly)
Use when the molecule is base-stable
Don't use with acid-sensitive groups' opposite
Forms a hydrazone, then strong base + heat ejects N₂
Both give: C=O → CH₂ (methylene). Same product; pick by the other functional groups in your molecule. Neither works on esters, acids, or amides — only aldehydes and ketones.
Carbonyl takeaways
  • Two attack modes: Nu → electrophilic C (addition) or α-H removed → nucleophilic enolate.
  • Aldehydes > ketones in reactivity (less steric, more δ⁺). Ketones = less electrophilic but still do everything on this list.
  • NaBH₄ is chemoselective (only aldehydes/ketones); LiAlH₄ reduces anything (esters, amides, acids, nitriles).
  • Aldol = enolate + second carbonyl → β-hydroxy carbonyl, which dehydrates to α,β-unsaturated product.
  • Imine with 1° amine; enamine with 2° amine. Both via carbinolamine.
  • Wittig swaps C=O for C=C. Clemmensen/Wolff-Kishner remove C=O entirely → CH₂.
Practice
Carbonyl Practice5 questions covering addition, reduction, Wittig, aldol
0/5
1Which reagent converts methyl benzoate (PhCOOCH₃) to benzaldehyde (PhCHO) in one step?
Explanation
B is correct. DIBAL-H (1 eq, −78 °C) reduces an ester to the aldehyde and stops — the rule: ester or nitrile → aldehyde, no further. A (LiAlH₄) would go all the way to the 1° alcohol. C (NaBH₄) doesn't touch esters. D (PCC) oxidizes alcohols, not esters.
2Acetone reacts with Ph₃P=CH₂ (a non-stabilized Wittig ylide). What is the product?
Explanation
C is correct. A Wittig reaction swaps C=O for C=CHR' (or C=CH₂ here). Acetone's C=O becomes C=CH₂ → (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ = isobutylene. The Ph₃P becomes Ph₃P=O (triphenylphosphine oxide, byproduct).
3Which compound gives a positive Tollens test (silver mirror)?
Explanation
A is correct. Tollens reagent (Ag(NH₃)₂⁺) is a mild oxidant that oxidizes aldehydes → carboxylic acids, depositing metallic silver (positive test). Ketones (B) have no C–H on the carbonyl C and don't oxidize. Alcohols (C) don't either. Ethers (D) are inert.
4In the aldol condensation of two equivalents of propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO) with catalytic NaOH, the major final product after heating is:
Explanation
D is correct. Propanal's α-carbon is deprotonated → enolate → attacks a second propanal → β-hydroxy aldehyde (A would be the answer if the problem said without heat). With heat, the β-hydroxy product loses water → α,β-unsaturated aldehyde = 2-methyl-2-pentenal. That's the full aldol condensation.
5You want to convert cyclohexanone into methylenecyclohexane (cyclohexane with =CH₂ replacing the C=O). The best one-step method is:
Explanation
B is correct. The Wittig converts C=O directly into an alkene (C=CR'). For =CH₂ specifically, use the methylene ylide Ph₃P=CH₂. Only the Wittig installs a new C=C double bond at the former carbonyl carbon.

Why the others fail: A (H₂/Pt) — molecular hydrogen on Pt doesn't reduce a simple ketone (needs a stronger reducing system like NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄). C (NaBH₄) reduces C=O → C–OH, giving cyclohexanol (alcohol, no alkene). D (Clemmensen, Zn(Hg)/HCl) also breaks the C=O — but it reduces it all the way to a CH₂ single bond, giving methylcyclohexane (saturated). That is the trap to catch: methylcyclohexane (saturated) and methylenecyclohexane (exocyclic alkene) are two different molecules. Only the Wittig keeps the double bond.
Hub 09

Carboxylic Acids & Derivatives — the reactivity ladder

Carboxylic acids (RCOOH) and their "derivatives" — acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters, amides, nitriles — share the same mechanism: nucleophilic acyl substitution. A nucleophile attacks the carbonyl, kicks out the leaving group. The only question is: which direction is thermodynamically downhill?

Plate X — The Reactivity Ladder
Arranged by the leaving group ability of each substituent. Top is easiest to kick out, bottom is nearly impossible. Going down is spontaneous; up needs activation.
1
Fischer Esterification
Reversible · PADPED
▾
R–COOH + R'OH + H⁺ → ester + H₂O. Reversible; drive with excess R'OH or distill off water. Mechanism is the classic PADPED: Protonate, Add, Deprotonate, Protonate, Eliminate, Deprotonate.
R–COOH + R'OH  ⇌H⁺  R–COOR' + H₂O
Step Mode
Fischer EsterificationAcetic acid + methanol · full PADPED · 4 consolidated steps
1/4
Fischer vs Saponification
Fischer uses H⁺ catalysis and goes through a tetrahedral intermediate — reversible. Saponification uses OH⁻ as a stoichiometric base and also goes through a tetrahedral intermediate — but the final carboxylate product is unreactive (RCOO⁻), so it's irreversible. Same molecular choreography; opposite thermodynamics.
2
Saponification (ester + NaOH)
Irreversible · base · single addition-elimination
▾
Base hydrolysis of an ester. Irreversible because the carboxylate product is locked — the resonance-stabilized RCOO⁻ is too unreactive to re-form the ester.
R–COOR' + NaOH  →aq · Δ  R–COO⁻ Na⁺ + R'OH
Substrate: ester (R-CO-OR') Reagent: NaOH (or KOH), aqueous, heat Mechanism: single addition-elimination · IRREVERSIBLE
Worked example Methyl acetate + NaOH/Δ → sodium acetate + methanol. Hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl C; tetrahedral intermediate collapses, kicking out methoxide; the resulting carboxylic acid gets deprotonated by another NaOH → carboxylate (locked).
Why is saponification irreversible while Fischer esterification is reversible?
The final step in saponification is deprotonation of RCOOH by hydroxide — irreversible because pKa(RCOOH ≈ 5) ≪ pKa(H₂O = 16). The carboxylate is locked. Fischer doesn't have this lock — its products (RCOOH + R'OH + H⁺) can all re-attack each other.
Practice
Ethyl benzoate + aqueous NaOH/Δ gives:
Answer: sodium benzoate + ethanol · NaOH cleaves the ester (addition-elimination), then deprotonates PhCOOH to its sodium salt. To get benzoic acid you'd acidify on workup (H₃O⁺).
Stoichiometric, not catalytic
Unlike acid-catalyzed Fischer, NaOH is consumed in saponification — one equivalent per ester. The base is the reagent, not a catalyst.
Play mechanism · 4 frames Tier 2
Step Mode
Saponification of methyl acetateOH⁻ + ester · single addition-elimination · proton transfer locks the carboxylate · 4 frames
1/4
Deep dive · why irreversible vs Fischer Tier 3
Why this is irreversible — the carboxylate is a dead end
The carboxylate (RCOO⁻) is not just unreactive — it's structurally protected. Resonance spreads the negative charge equally over both oxygens, so neither O is a real nucleophile target and the central C carries no usable δ⁺. An incoming alkoxide (R'O⁻) sees a fully-delocalized anion and bounces. The ester carbon, which was electrophilic, has been chemically retired. That is what irreversibility looks like: the well-trapped product cannot re-enter the mechanism. Compare the Fischer card above — there, the final deprotonation regenerates a neutral ester that can be re-protonated and run backward.
Decision widget
Fischer esterification vs Saponification
acid catalysis (rev) vs base promotion (irrev)
FischerRCOOH + R'OH + H⁺
Acid drives a reversible equilibrium that lives near 50:50 unless you push it.
vs
SaponificationR–COOR' + NaOH
Base consumes the ester one-way — the carboxylate sits permanently on the product side.
Axis Fischer esterification Saponification
Catalyst / driver H⁺ (catalytic — H₂SO₄ or HCl, regenerated each cycle). OH⁻ (stoichiometric — NaOH/KOH is consumed; not a catalyst).
Reversibility Reversible. Sits at equilibrium; the same mechanism runs backward as acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis. Irreversible. Carboxylate (RCOO⁻) is delocalized and unreactive — no path back to ester.
Conditions Neat or in alcohol solvent, heat (Δ), often excess R'OH or a Dean–Stark trap to remove H₂O. Aqueous NaOH (or KOH), heat (Δ). No reagent excess needed; reaction completes on its own.
Mechanism type Acid-catalyzed addition–elimination. Six-step PADPED sequence with proton transfers wrapping the addition and the elimination. Base-promoted addition–elimination. Three mechanistic moves (add, eliminate, deprotonate) — no protonation steps before or during C–O bond changes.
DAT trap Le Chatelier question. To shift the equilibrium toward ester, add R'OH or remove H₂O. Equilibrium math is the test. No Le Chatelier. The trap is conflating the two reactions: students put H⁺ on a saponification or call it reversible. Read the conditions first.
Same choreography, opposite thermodynamics. Both pass through a tetrahedral intermediate. The difference is what closes the door at the end: Fischer regenerates a neutral ester (can run backward), saponification deprotonates the acid to a carboxylate (cannot). When the conditions list NaOH/aq, heat, the answer is one-way; when they list H⁺/ROH, heat, you are looking at an equilibrium and Le Chatelier is on the table.
Where the name comes from — soap-making
"Saponification" is from the Latin sapo, soap. The original reaction was animal fat (a triglyceride) + lye (NaOH or KOH), giving glycerol and three equivalents of the sodium salt of a long-chain fatty acid — that salt is soap. The hydrophobic R chain dissolves grease; the carboxylate head dissolves in water. With NaOH you get hard bar soap; with KOH you get softer liquid soap. Modern industrial soap-making is the same mechanism, scaled.
DAT pattern · always read for the conditions
Acid (H⁺ / ROH, Δ)?  Fischer esterification (forward) or acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis (reverse) — same mechanism, equilibrium can be pushed either way.
Base (NaOH or KOH, aq, Δ)?  Saponification. One-way only. The product is the carboxylate salt; isolating the free acid takes a workup acidification.
The trap: students conflate the two and apply Le Chatelier to saponification. The mechanism question reduces to a single tell — does the final step regenerate H⁺ (Fischer, reversible) or deprotonate the acid to RCOO⁻ (saponification, irreversible)?
Where this connects in the rest of the course
Fischer esterification — card 1 of this hub. Same tetrahedral intermediate, opposite thermodynamic fate. Read the two cards back-to-back.
NAS reactivity ladder — top of this hub (Plate X). Saponification fits the nucleophile attacks acyl C, leaving group departs template; the only twist is that the proton transfer at the end pulls the product off the ladder permanently.
Carbonyl ox/red ladder — Hub 05 (Carbonyls). Saponification doesn't change the carbon's oxidation state — it stays at the COOH/RCOO⁻ level. Compare with LiAlH₄ on an ester, which drops two rungs to the alcohol.
3
Acid Chloride Formation (SOCl₂)
Activation
▾
R–COOH + SOCl₂ (or PCl₃, PCl₅) → R–COCl + SO₂ + HCl. The acid chloride can then react with anything: water, alcohols, amines, ring (FC acylation), H⁻ reducers, R₂Cu (→ ketone).
R–COOH + SOCl₂ → R–COCl + SO₂ + HCl
4
Acid Chloride → Anything
Universal
▾
R–COCl is the "king" of carbonyls. Reactions:
• + H₂O → R–COOH (+ HCl)
• + R'OH → ester R–COOR'
• + NH₃ or R₂NH → amide R–CONR'₂ (need 2 equiv — the second neutralizes HCl)
• + R'COO⁻ → anhydride
• + LiAlH₄ → 1° alcohol ; + LiAlH(OtBu)₃ → aldehyde (stops halfway)
• + R'₂CuLi (Gilman) → ketone (stops at ketone)
• + benzene/AlCl₃ → aryl ketone (FC acylation)
5
Amide Hydrolysis
Harsh
▾
Amides are the most stable carbonyl derivative — requires hot, concentrated acid or base to hydrolyze. Products: carboxylic acid (or carboxylate) + amine (or ammonium salt).
R–CONR'₂  →H₃O⁺ · Δ  R–COOH + HNR'₂
6
LiAlH₄ Reduction of COOH/Ester/Amide/Nitrile
Redox
▾
The LiAlH₄ reductions to memorize:
• R–COOH → R–CH₂OH (1° alcohol)
• R–COOR' → R–CH₂OH + R'OH
• R–CONR'₂ → R–CH₂–NR'₂ (amide becomes amine, not an alcohol — the N stays)
• R–CN → R–CH₂–NH₂ (nitrile to 1° amine)
• R–NO₂ → Not reduced by LiAlH₄ (use H₂/Pd or Sn/HCl)
7
Decarboxylation
β-keto / malonic
▾
Carboxylic acids don't decarboxylate under normal conditions. But β-keto acids and malonic acids (β-diacids) lose CO₂ on gentle heat via a cyclic 6-membered TS that forms an enol.
R–CO–CH₂–COOH  →Δ  R–CO–CH₃ + CO₂
Malonic ester synthesis
CH₂(COOR)₂ → deprotonate with NaOR → alkylate with R'X → saponify → β-diacid → decarboxylate → RCH₂COOH. Synthetic tool to make substituted acetic acids. Same idea with acetoacetic ester for methyl ketones.
Carboxylic acid takeaways
  • Reactivity ladder: acid chloride > anhydride > acid ≈ ester > amide. Going "down" is easy; going "up" requires making the acid chloride first.
  • Fischer (H⁺, ROH) is reversible; saponification (NaOH) is irreversible — locks as carboxylate.
  • LiAlH₄ reduces everything: acid/ester → 1° alcohol; amide → amine (N stays); nitrile → 1° amine.
  • Amides are the most stable → require hot concentrated acid/base to hydrolyze.
  • β-keto and β-diacids decarboxylate on heat — the key to malonic/acetoacetic ester syntheses.
Practice
Acids & Derivatives PracticeReactivity ladder + reduction · 5 questions
0/5
1Rank in order of increasing reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution: ester, amide, acid chloride, anhydride.
Explanation
C is correct. The ladder (least → most): amide < ester < anhydride < acid chloride. Reactivity tracks the leaving-group ability: NR₂⁻ (terrible) < RO⁻ < RCOO⁻ < Cl⁻ (excellent). This ordering is why you can always convert "down" easily, but need to activate (make the acid chloride first) to climb up.
2Methyl propanoate (CH₃CH₂COOCH₃) is treated with excess LiAlH₄, then H₂O. The product is:
Explanation
B is correct. Excess LiAlH₄ reduces esters all the way to two alcohols: the acyl side → 1° alcohol (propanoic acid → 1-propanol) and the alkoxy side → its alcohol (methanol). A is what you'd get with 1 eq DIBAL-H at –78 °C.
3To synthesize N-methylbenzamide from benzoic acid, the best sequence is:
Explanation
A is correct. Carboxylic acid + amine directly gives an ammonium carboxylate salt, not an amide. You need to activate the acid first (most commonly as the acid chloride via SOCl₂). Then R–COCl + 2 R'NH₂ → amide + R'NH₃⁺Cl⁻ (the second equiv neutralizes HCl).
4Diethyl malonate is treated with NaOEt, then 1-bromopropane, then aqueous NaOH, then heat (decarboxylation). The final product is:
Explanation
C is correct. Malonic ester synthesis: (1) NaOEt removes the acidic α-H between the two esters. (2) The enolate does SN2 on n-propyl bromide → monoalkylated malonate. (3) Saponify both esters → malonic-type diacid. (4) Heat → decarboxylation of the β-diacid → one COOH drops off as CO₂. Net: you've added a propyl group and ended with a substituted acetic acid = CH₃CH₂CH₂–CH₂–COOH = pentanoic acid.
5Saponification of an ester vs. Fischer esterification differ in that:
Explanation
D is correct. Fischer (H⁺, ROH) hydrolyzes/esterifies reversibly — you drive equilibrium with excess reagent or by removing water. Saponification (NaOH) is irreversible because the final product is the unreactive carboxylate anion (RCOO⁻) — there's no way back. Mechanistically also different: Fischer = PADPED, saponification = single addition-elimination.
Hub 10

Amines — nitrogen chemistry

Amines are basic (pKa of R₃NH⁺ ≈ 10) and nucleophilic. They're tough to make cleanly by direct alkylation (over-alkylation) — so DAT-tested methods use a trick: go through an azide, phthalimide, or nitrile, or use reductive amination.

Amine Basicity Ranker · live drill
Pick the more basic amine. The wizard walks the reasoning: more electron density on N = more basic. Alkyl groups push electrons toward N (boost). Aryl/EWG groups pull electrons away (kill). Ring conjugation = N lone pair delocalized into ring = much weaker base.
Basicity ranking principles
• More alkyl groups on N = more basic (alkyl donors push electrons toward N). Trialkyl > dialkyl > monoalkyl > NH₃ in gas phase.
• Aryl amines are MUCH weaker (lone pair partially delocalized into the ring; aniline pKa of conjugate acid ≈ 4.6 vs cyclohexylamine ≈ 10.6).
• Pyridine vs pyrrole: pyridine\'s N lone pair is in an sp² orbital perpendicular to the ring → still basic (pKa 5.2). Pyrrole\'s lone pair IS the aromatic π system → not basic at all (protonation destroys aromaticity).
• Amides are NOT basic — the N lone pair conjugates into the C=O.
Pattern shortcuts for this hub
Plate XI — Amine Synthesis & Reactions
Six syntheses feed in on the left; four reactions branch out on the right. Direct RX + NH₃ is avoided — it over-alkylates.
1
Azide Synthesis (cleanest 1° amine)
SN2 · reduce
▾
R–X + NaN₃ (SN2) → R–N₃, then LiAlH₄ (or H₂/Pd) reduces N₃ → NH₂. No over-alkylation because N₃ is not nucleophilic once installed.
R–X → R–N₃ → R–NH₂
2
Gabriel Synthesis
Phthalimide
▾
Potassium phthalimide (a nitrogen nucleophile tied into a ring) does SN2 on R–X → N-alkylphthalimide. Hydrazinolysis (NH₂NH₂) kicks out the amine. Gives only 1° amines.
Limitation
Works only on 1° alkyl halides (SN2). 3° gives E2 with the bulky phthalimide anion.
3
Reductive Amination
Imine → amine
▾
C=O + R'NH₂ → imine → reduce in situ with NaBH₃CN (selective, doesn't touch the carbonyl) → 2° amine. Most versatile way to extend an amine by one alkyl group cleanly. → See imine formation for the mechanism that makes the iminium NaBH₃CN reduces.
R₂C=O + R'NH₂  →NaBH₃CN, pH 4-5  R₂CH–NHR'
Step Mode
Reductive Amination MechanismAcetone + methylamine + NaBH₃CN · imine then H⁻ · 3 steps
1/3
Why NaBH₃CN works one-pot — iminium beats C=O for hydride attack
Two carbonyl-like species coexist in the flask: the starting C=O (acetone) and the iminium (after the amine condenses + H⁺ adds to N). Both have a δ+ carbon, but the iminium carries a formal positive charge — its LUMO is dramatically lower in energy.

NaBH₃CN is mild on purpose. The –CN group withdraws electron density from B, weakening the B–H bond enough that hydride won't attack the relatively neutral C=O. But the iminium's much hotter δ+ C is an easy target → H⁻ delivers there → 2° amine.

Why pH 4–5? Below pH 4, the free amine protonates fully → no nucleophile, no imine forms. Above pH 5, no acid, no iminium, no electrophile. The 4–5 window is where the reaction actually runs: enough H⁺ to make the imine and protonate it, not enough to kill the amine before condensation.
Why NaBH₃CN, not NaBH₄?
NaBH₄ is hot enough to reduce C=O directly → kills the starting acetone before any imine can form. NaBH₃CN is the cooler version that survives long enough for the imine to assemble first.
4
Hofmann Elimination
Quat ammonium · less subst. alkene
▾
Excess CH₃I + Ag₂O / Δ on a 1° or 2° amine → E2 elimination via a bulky –N⁺(CH₃)₃ leaving group → less-substituted (Hofmann) alkene. The bulky leaving group is what forces the regio away from Zaitsev; that's the only DAT-relevant detail.
R–NH₂  →1. xs CH₃I 2. Ag₂O · Δ  alkene (Hofmann) + N(CH₃)₃
5
Diazonium Chemistry (ArNH₂ + NaNO₂/HCl)
Aryl only
▾
Aryl amines (ArNH₂) + NaNO₂/HCl at 0 °C → aryl diazonium salt (Ar–N₂⁺). Powerful because N₂ is a spectacular leaving group. Reactions:
• + CuCl → Ar–Cl. + CuBr → Ar–Br. + CuCN → Ar–CN. (Sandmeyer)
• + KI → Ar–I. + H₃PO₂ → Ar–H (removes the N₂ entirely).
• + H₂O/Δ → Ar–OH (phenol).
• + Ar'–OH (coupling) → azo dye Ar–N=N–Ar'.
6
Strecker Amino Acid Synthesis
aldehyde → amino acid
▾
Aldehyde or ketone + NH₃ + HCN (or NH₄Cl + KCN) → alpha-amino nitrile. Acid hydrolysis (H₃O⁺) converts the nitrile to a carboxylic acid → alpha-amino acid. DAT context: "synthesize this amino acid from this aldehyde."
RCHO + NH₃ + HCN → RCH(NH₂)CN  →H₃O⁺, Δ  RCH(NH₂)COOH
Strecker: acetaldehyde → alanine (2 steps)
DAT context
When a DAT question asks you to synthesize an amino acid from an aldehyde, think Strecker: add NH₃ + HCN to get the aminonitrile, then hydrolyze to the amino acid.
Amine takeaways
  • Direct alkylation of NH₃ with R–X over-alkylates → use azide, Gabriel, nitrile, or reductive amination to get clean 1° amines.
  • Reductive amination (C=O + amine + NaBH₃CN) adds one R group cleanly — best general method for 2°/3° amines.
  • Hofmann elimination (exhaustive methylation, Ag₂O/Δ) = less substituted alkene.
  • Aryl amines + NaNO₂/HCl at 0 °C = diazonium → swap N₂ for almost anything (Sandmeyer, OH, H, aryl coupling).
  • Amides reduce to amines with LiAlH₄ (N stays, C=O goes).
Practice
Amine PracticeSynthesis · reactions · diazonium · 5 questions
0/5
1The cleanest way to prepare n-butylamine from 1-bromobutane is:
Explanation
C is correct. The azide synthesis: R–X + NaN₃ gives R–N₃ (an azide, which is NOT nucleophilic once installed, so no over-alkylation). Reduce with LiAlH₄ → clean 1° amine. A and B give a mess of 1°/2°/3°/4° amines (over-alkylation). D is an elimination, not a synthesis.
2Aniline is treated with NaNO₂ / HCl at 0 °C, then CuBr. The product is:
Explanation
B is correct. This is the Sandmeyer reaction. At 0 °C, NaNO₂/HCl converts ArNH₂ to the aryl diazonium salt (Ar–N₂⁺). CuBr replaces N₂ with Br (N₂ is a phenomenal leaving group). The amine group becomes Br — net Ar–NH₂ → Ar–Br = bromobenzene.
3N,N-dimethylcyclohexylamine is treated with excess CH₃I, then Ag₂O with heat. The major product is:
Explanation
A is correct. Hofmann elimination: excess CH₃I exhaustively methylates the amine → quaternary ammonium iodide. Ag₂O converts the counterion to hydroxide. Heating induces E2 with the bulky –N⁺(CH₃)₃ leaving group → less substituted alkene (Hofmann product) + (CH₃)₃N. From cyclohexyl, the only possible alkene is cyclohexene.
4Benzamide (PhCONH₂) is reduced with LiAlH₄. The product is:
Explanation
D is correct. LiAlH₄ reduces amides to amines (not alcohols!) — the nitrogen stays on the carbon. PhCONH₂ → PhCH₂NH₂ (benzylamine). This is different from ester/acid reduction, where the heteroatom leaves as the alcohol/acid. Common DAT trap: students confuse amide reduction with ester reduction.
5Gabriel synthesis is used to prepare 1° amines. Which is the correct reagent sequence on 1-bromobutane?
Explanation
B is correct. Gabriel: potassium phthalimide is a nitrogen nucleophile with only ONE N-H to lose. It does SN2 on R–X (works for 1° and methyl), giving N-alkyl phthalimide. Hydrazine (NH₂NH₂) then cleaves it to release the primary amine + phthalhydrazide. This is the classic "one-and-done" 1° amine synthesis. A is the nitrile route (valid but different). D uses the wrong reductant — azide (N₃⁻) is reduced by LiAlH₄ or H₂/Pd, not NaBH₄.
Tier III · Advanced

Lab techniques — IMFs, separations, qualitative tests

The DAT tests practical lab knowledge: which solvent for recrystallization, which IMF gives the highest BP, which extraction reagent pulls a carboxylic acid out of an ether layer, what color a positive Tollens test produces. Below: the IMF strength ladder, animated separatory funnel for acid-base extraction, TLC plate explorer, and the five qualitative-test cards you must memorize.

Coach lock Like dissolves like. Polar plate + nonpolar solvent → polar sticks low. Acid-base extractions exploit pKa.
Intermolecular-Force Strength Ladder
Stronger IMFs = higher BP/MP, lower vapor pressure. Branched isomers have LOWER BPs than straight chains (less surface area = less dispersion contact).
Acid-Base Extraction Funnel
Click a reagent to wash the ether layer. The corresponding compound deprotonates (or protonates) and migrates to the aqueous layer. Recover by neutralizing the aqueous and back-extracting.
Mixture in ether: PhCOOH + PhOH + PhNH₂
TLC Plate Explorer
Polar silica plate + nonpolar developing solvent. Polar compounds adsorb to the plate (low Rf). Nonpolar compounds ride the solvent up (high Rf).
Rf = (distance traveled by spot) / (distance to solvent front). Always 0 to 1.
Column chromatography uses the same physics with gravity flow: most nonpolar elutes first (washes down fastest); most polar last.
Qualitative Tests · the six you must know
Each card has its own animated micro-experiment. Press Run test to watch the substrate react with the reagent — the visual transitions, the substrate sketch updates, and the positive-result color reveals at the bottom.
Ag(NH₃)₂⁺ · NaOH (aq)
Tollens' test
Targets: aldehyde (mild oxidation) — silver-mirror reaction
Substrate + reagent · click run
Silver mirror on flask wall
PositiveAldehydes (RCHO) — donate the C-H to Ag⁺, get oxidized to RCOO⁻
NegativeKetones — no H on the carbonyl C to lose
Edge caseFormic acid (HCOOH) is weakly positive: the H on the carbonyl C still acts as an "aldehyde C-H"
DAT trap A solution that turns Tollens-positive doesn't necessarily contain an aldehyde — formic acid (and α-hydroxy ketones via tautomerization) can give weak positives. Confirm with Fehling/Benedict and IR (RCHO has C-H stretch ~2720 cm⁻¹).
Hub 08 · Carbonyl oxidation
Cu²⁺ · tartrate (Fehling) · citrate (Benedict)
Fehling / Benedict test
Targets: aldehyde + reducing sugars (glucose, fructose, maltose, lactose)
Glucose · Cu²⁺ + tartrate
Brick-red Cu₂O precipitate
PositiveGlucose, maltose, lactose — open-chain form has a free aldehyde at the anomeric C
PositiveFructose — base tautomerizes the α-hydroxy ketone to glucose via 1,2-enediol
NegativeSucrose — both anomeric carbons locked in the glycosidic bond, no free aldehyde
DAT trap The chelator (tartrate / citrate) is just a solubilizer for Cu²⁺ at high pH — it does NOT change which substrates react. Fehling vs. Benedict differ only in chelator and shelf life; both give the same brick-red Cu₂O.
Hub 12 · Tautomerization
I₂ · NaOH (excess)
Iodoform test
Targets: methyl ketones · CH₃CHO · CH₃CH(OH)R (methyl carbinol)
2-butanone · α-iodination 0/3
Yellow CHI₃ precipitate
PositiveMethyl ketones (R-CO-CH₃) — α-Hs replaced by I three times, then ⁻OH cleaves CHI₃
PositiveEthanol and methyl-2° alcohols (RCH(OH)CH₃) — first oxidized to a methyl ketone in situ
NegativeMethanol, 1° alcohols beyond ethanol, 3° alcohols, ethyl ketones — no methyl-α geometry
DAT trap Ethanol is positive (oxidizes to acetaldehyde, then triple-iodinated). Methanol is negative (no α-carbon to halogenate). Acetone and 2-butanone are positive; 3-pentanone is negative.
Hub 12 · α-halogenation
AgNO₃ in ethanol (SN1)
Silver nitrate test
Targets: alkyl halides — rate tracks carbocation stability (3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃)
RX + Ag⁺ → R⁺ + AgX↓
White / cream / yellow AgX precipitate
Fast3° alkyl halides, allylic, benzylic — precipitate forms within seconds at room temp
Slow2° alkyl halides — precipitate forms on warming; 1° needs prolonged heat
No reactionMethyl halides, vinyl halides, aryl halides — cannot form a stable carbocation
DAT trap The precipitate color identifies the halogen: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream/pale-yellow, AgI is yellow. AgF does NOT precipitate (F⁻ is too small/strongly hydrated). Vinyl/aryl halides give NO precipitate — the cation would be sp² at the leaving-group carbon.
Hub 06 · SN1 reactivity
Br₂ in CCl₄ (or CH₂Cl₂) · dark
Bromine decolorization
Targets: alkenes & alkynes — electrophilic addition via bromonium ion
Cyclohexene + Br₂ (red-brown)
Red-brown → colorless
PositiveAlkenes (anti-addition through bromonium) — color disappears within seconds
PositiveAlkynes — add 1 or 2 equivalents of Br₂; both fade the color
NegativeAlkanes & arenes in the dark — benzene is too aromatic to add (needs FeBr₃ for substitution, which doesn't decolorize the same way)
DAT trap Use CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂ in the dark — never run this test under UV light or with alkanes present. Light initiates a radical chain that ALSO consumes Br₂ (with HBr evolution), giving a false positive on alkanes. The dark condition isolates the addition pathway.
Hub 03 · Alkene addition
CrO₃ · H₂SO₄ in acetone
Jones test
Targets: 1° & 2° alcohols, aldehydes — strong oxidation to acid / ketone
Cr⁶⁺ orange · ROH ready
Orange Cr⁶⁺ → green Cr³⁺
Positive1° alcohol → carboxylic acid (RCH₂OH → RCOOH); aldehyde → carboxylic acid
Positive2° alcohol → ketone (RR'CHOH → RR'C=O)
Negative3° alcohols, ethers, ketones — no α-H on the C-OH carbon (3°), or already at maximum oxidation state
DAT trap Jones over-oxidizes 1° alcohols past the aldehyde to the acid because acetone+H₂SO₄ is not anhydrous. To stop at the aldehyde, use PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in dry CH₂Cl₂ — milder, no water present.
Hub 07 · Alcohol oxidation
Tollens vs Fehling/Benedict — both detect aldehyde, but differ in result
Both reagents are mild oxidants that turn an aldehyde into a carboxylate, getting themselves reduced in the process. Aldehyde C is the only carbonyl carbon with an H to lose — that's why ketones don't respond.

· Tollens uses Ag(NH₃)₂⁺ → reduces to Ag⁰ metal deposited as a shiny silver mirror on the flask wall.
· Fehling / Benedict uses Cu²⁺ (chelated by tartrate in Fehling, citrate in Benedict — the chelator just keeps Cu²⁺ in solution at high pH) → reduces to Cu⁺ as brick-red Cu₂O precipitate.

Mechanism is the same in both: aldehyde donates 2 electrons (and 2 H⁺) to the metal ion. The metal ion accepts those electrons and drops out as a visible solid.
Reducing sugars · why fructose reacts even though it's a ketone
A "reducing sugar" is a sugar with a free anomeric (hemiacetal) carbon — open-chain form has an aldehyde or α-hydroxy ketone. Glucose, maltose, and lactose all open to an aldehyde → positive on both Tollens and Fehling/Benedict.
Fructose is a ketose, but it tautomerizes (via the 1,2-enediol intermediate) to glucose under the basic conditions of these tests → also positive. Same for mannose ↔ glucose interconversion.
Sucrose is NOT a reducing sugar — both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond → no free aldehyde or ketone in equilibrium → negative on both tests.
Ketones in general (acetone, 2-butanone) cannot lose an H from the carbonyl C and stay negative.
Distill
Simple distillation works when two liquids differ in BP by ≥25 °C. Fractional distillation uses a packed column (more theoretical plates) when BPs are closer.
Recrystallize
Hot dissolve, slow cool. Need a solvent the compound is highly soluble in HOT and barely soluble in COLD. Pure crystals nucleate while impurities stay dissolved. If no crystals form on cooling, scratch the glass or add a seed crystal.
Chromatography
GC separates by boiling point (lowest BP elutes first). TLC + column separate by polarity (polar sticks to silica). Memorize: polar plate, nonpolar solvent → polar = low Rf.
Practice
Lab Techniques PracticeDAT-style · 5 questions
0/5
1You shake a mixture of an organic acid (RCOOH) and a neutral hydrocarbon in a separatory funnel with aqueous NaHCO₃. Where does the organic acid go?
Explanation
A is correct. NaHCO₃ (mild base, pKa(H₂CO₃) ≈ 6.4) deprotonates carboxylic acids (pKa ~4.5) but NOT phenols (pKa ~10) or alcohols (pKa ~16). The carboxylate anion RCOO⁻ Na⁺ is water-soluble and stays in the aqueous layer. The neutral hydrocarbon stays in the organic layer. This is the SELECTIVE extraction principle: use a base that's strong enough for one functional group but not others. Stronger base (NaOH) deprotonates phenols too; weaker base (NaHCO₃) only gets carboxylic acids.
2On a TLC plate, a polar compound and a nonpolar compound are eluted with a nonpolar solvent. Which has the HIGHER Rf?
Explanation
B is correct. TLC silica gel is POLAR. Polar compounds STICK to the polar stationary phase (low Rf). Nonpolar compounds elute with the mobile phase (high Rf). Rule of thumb: "like dissolves like" — the polar compound bonds to the polar silica and lags behind; the nonpolar compound rides with the nonpolar solvent up the plate. To raise a polar compound's Rf, use a more polar solvent (or a less polar stationary phase like alumina or reversed-phase silica).
3A student wants to identify whether an unknown is an aldehyde or a ketone. Which qualitative test is selective for aldehydes ONLY?
Explanation
C is correct. TOLLENS REAGENT is selective for ALDEHYDES — it oxidizes them to carboxylates while REDUCING the Ag⁺ to metallic silver, producing the famous silver mirror on the test tube. Ketones lack the aldehyde C–H bond, can't be oxidized at the carbonyl, and give a negative test. (A) Jones reagent oxidizes BOTH aldehydes (→ acid) and 1° alcohols and 2° alcohols (→ ketone); not selective. (B) Br₂/CCl₄ tests for alkenes/alkynes. (D) Lucas tests alcohol class (1° vs 2° vs 3°).
4You have three colorless liquids of similar boiling point (~80 °C): hexane (nonpolar), ethanol (H-bonding alcohol), and 1-iodopropane. Which would have the HIGHEST boiling point?
Explanation
B is correct. Even though all three have similar boiling points (~80 °C in this hypothetical), the principle being tested is IMF strength. ETHANOL has H-BONDING (O–H), which is the strongest IMF in this comparison. Hexane has only London dispersion. 1-iodopropane has dipole-dipole + London (iodine is heavy and polarizable, which helps). So if we ranked IMF strength: ethanol > 1-iodopropane > hexane. In real life: ethanol BP = 78 °C, 1-iodopropane = 102 °C, hexane = 69 °C — actually iodopropane wins due to massive polarizability of iodine. But the DAT-style 'pick the H-bonder for highest BP' is usually the intended answer when comparing similar-mass molecules. The IMF ranking is: H-bond > dipole-dipole > London. (For the DAT: if you see H-bonding, that's almost always the highest-BP option.)
5You want to separate two liquids that boil 5 °C apart. Which technique is appropriate?
Explanation
A is correct. Rule of thumb: SIMPLE distillation works when BPs differ by > 25 °C; FRACTIONAL distillation is required when BPs differ by less than that. Two liquids only 5 °C apart need the additional theoretical plates a fractionating column provides — vapor repeatedly condenses and re-evaporates, enriching with the lower-boiling component at each step. (C) Recrystallization separates solids. (D) Extraction requires a chemistry difference (acid vs base vs neutral, or polar vs nonpolar), not just a small BP difference.
Practice
Nomenclature PracticeDAT-style · 5 questions
0/5
1IUPAC name for (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH(OH)CH₃?
Explanation
B is correct. The chain is 5 carbons (pentane). The OH is the principal characteristic group, so it gets the LOWEST possible locant. Number from the OH-bearing end: C1 = CH₃, C2 = CH(OH), C3 = CH₂, C4 = CH(CH₃), C5 = CH₃. So OH at 2, methyl at 4 → 4-methylpentan-2-ol. (C) "2-methyl-pentan-4-ol" numbers from the wrong end (gives the OH a higher locant). The rule: principal characteristic group gets lowest locant, then substituents next.
2The compound CH₃-CH=CH-CHO (4 carbons, C=C between C2 and C3, aldehyde at C1) is named:
Explanation
A is correct. The aldehyde C is always C1 (the highest-priority group gets the lowest locant). So C1=CHO, C2=CH, C3=CH, C4=CH₃, with the C=C between C2 and C3 → but-2-enal. Common name: crotonaldehyde (also called 2-butenal). (B) numbers from the wrong end. (C) is a different molecule (methacrolein). (D) "enol" would mean an alcohol on an alkene (not an aldehyde).
3The molecule CH₃-CH(Br)-CH=CH-CH₃ (5 carbons, Br on C2, C=C between C3 and C4) — which is its proper E/Z designation if the methyl groups on C3 and C4 are on opposite sides?
Explanation
C is correct. Number from the end nearer the C=C: C1=CH₃, C2=CH, C3=CH, C4=CHBr, C5=CH₃. C=C between C2-C3 → pent-2-ene. Br on C4 → 4-bromo. So name is 4-bromopent-2-ene. With the methyls on opposite sides of the double bond, geometry is E (entgegen, opposite). E/Z is assigned via CIP priorities on EACH end of the double bond. (A) E vs Z is the geometry — opposite sides = E. (B/D) numbering is wrong (the C=C should get the lowest locant).
4For naming a compound that contains BOTH an alcohol AND a ketone, which takes priority as the principal characteristic group (the suffix)?
Explanation
D is correct. IUPAC functional-group priority order (highest to lowest, for "suffix" purposes): carboxylic acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > ether > alkene/alkyne > halide. So a compound with both a ketone and an alcohol is named as a HYDROXY-KETONE: the ketone is the suffix (-one), the alcohol becomes a "hydroxy-" prefix. Example: 4-hydroxypentan-2-one, not 2-oxo-pentan-4-ol. The locant rule applies WITHIN the rule (lowest locant goes to the higher-priority group, which is the ketone here).
5Which two compounds are constitutional isomers of each other?
Explanation
B is correct. CONSTITUTIONAL isomers (also called structural isomers) have the same molecular formula but DIFFERENT CONNECTIVITY — different atoms bonded to different atoms. Ethanol (CH₃CH₂-OH) and dimethyl ether (CH₃-O-CH₃) are both C₂H₆O but with completely different bonding: ethanol is C–C–O–H, ether is C–O–C. (A) n-butane and isobutane are also constitutional isomers — but the QUESTION asks which is the BEST example or the option specifically. (C) cis/trans = geometric (stereo)isomers. (D) (R) and (S) = enantiomers. Note A is actually also constitutional isomers; the cleanest "non-trick" answer depends on the question wording — both B and A would be correct, but B is the more textbook example because they have different functional groups (alcohol vs ether) rather than just different chains.
Tier III · Advanced (final)

Alpha & condensation chemistry

A hydrogen on the carbon next to a carbonyl ("alpha-H") is unusually acidic — pKa ~20 vs ~50 for normal C–H — because its conjugate base (the enolate) is resonance-stabilized. This unlocks five major reactions: alpha-halogenation/haloform, aldol condensation, Claisen condensation, β-decarboxylation, and the acetoacetic/malonic ester syntheses. The DAT loves all of them.

Coach lock Alpha-H is acidic. Enolate is the nucleophile. Aldol stitches one carbonyl to the alpha of another.
Boss · toughest group The α-Chemistry Boss · one pattern, many electrophiles
Students dread α-chemistry because it has eight reactions that look different. They are not different. Every one of them is the same three-step skeleton — the only thing that changes is what attacks the enolate. Master the skeleton once, then learn the eight electrophiles.
The 8 reactions · what's the electrophile? Tier 2
01 Aldol
E = aldehyde / ketone (C=O)
Enolate attacks the C=O of a second carbonyl → β-hydroxy carbonyl. Heat dehydrates → α,β-unsaturated carbonyl ("aldol condensation").
02 Claisen
E = ester (C=O with –OR leaving)
Like aldol but the second carbonyl is an ester. The –OR group leaves after attack → β-keto ester. Critical: use NaOR matching the ester (NaOEt with –OEt).
03 Michael 1,4
E = α,β-unsaturated C=C (β-carbon)
Soft enolate attacks the β-carbon of an enone (1,4-addition, NOT the C=O directly). Product: 1,5-dicarbonyl. Hard nucleophiles (RLi) go 1,2 instead.
04 α-Halogenation
E = X–X (Cl₂, Br₂, I₂)
Enolate displaces a halide from X–X → α-halo carbonyl. In acid, mono-halogenation; in base, often poly-halogenates → leads to haloform.
05 Haloform
E = X₂ (3×) then HO⁻ cleaves
Triple α-halogenation of a methyl ketone, then HO⁻ cleaves the C–C bond between carbonyl and CX₃ → carboxylate + CHX₃ (haloform). DAT trap: only methyl ketones do this.
06 Malonic alkylation
E = R–X (alkyl halide)
Diethyl malonate's α-H (pKa 13) is much more acidic than a normal carbonyl. Enolate displaces R–X (SN2) → alkyl-malonate. Hydrolysis + heat (β-decarbox) yields a substituted acetic acid.
07 Acetoacetic alkylation
E = R–X (same as malonic)
Same logic as malonic but starting from ethyl acetoacetate (one ester is replaced with a methyl ketone). After hydrolysis + decarbox, the product is a methyl ketone, not a carboxylic acid.
08 β-Decarboxylation
"E" = heat (loss of CO₂)
The "workup" step in malonic / acetoacetic syntheses. β-keto acid or β-diacid + heat → 6-membered cyclic TS expels CO₂ and yields an enol → tautomerizes to ketone. Doesn't fit the 3-step pattern; it's the finishing step that makes those syntheses irreversible.
Decision drill · 8 questions Tier 3
Tool 1 — Keto-Enol Tautomerism
Acetone has three alpha-Hs. Deprotonating one gives the enolate (resonance-stabilized). Re-protonating on O gives the enol form. Re-protonating on C gives back the keto form. Enol/keto are tautomers (different connectivity), not resonance contributors.
Tool 2 — Aldol Condensation (4 steps)
Two acetaldehyde molecules + dilute NaOH. The enolate of one attacks the carbonyl carbon of the other. Protonation gives the β-hydroxy aldehyde ("aldol"). With heat, dehydration gives the α,β-unsaturated carbonyl — the "condensation" part.
↑ this is the universal 3-step enolate skeleton · Aldol's electrophile is a second C=O
Tool 3 — Claisen Condensation
Same idea as aldol but with esters. Two ethyl propanoates + NaOEt. The ester enolate attacks the carbonyl C of the second ester; the OEt of the second leaves; product is a β-keto ester. Critical: use the alkoxide that matches the ester (NaOEt for ethyl ester, NaOMe for methyl ester) — otherwise you transesterify.
↑ same 3-step enolate skeleton · Claisen's electrophile is an ester (with –OR leaving group)
Tool 4 — β-Decarboxylation (6-membered TS)
A β-keto acid loses CO₂ on heating via a 6-membered cyclic transition state. The carboxyl OH H-bonds to the β-carbonyl O; concerted electron flow releases CO₂ and gives the enol, which tautomerizes to the ketone. This is step 5 of acetoacetic/malonic ester syntheses.
Why only β-keto acids? A simple acid (e.g., propanoic) cannot decarboxylate easily — there's no β-carbonyl to accept the H-bond and stabilize the enol intermediate. Without that 6-ring TS, CO₂ loss is too high in energy.
Tool 5 — Malonic Ester Synthesis · the 5-step ladder
Diethyl malonate is the workhorse: an α-H sandwiched between two esters drops to pKa ≈ 13, which means NaOEt can fully deprotonate it. From there: alkylate, hydrolyze, and decarboxylate. The output is always a substituted acetic acid.
↑ same 3-step enolate skeleton · Malonic's electrophile is an alkyl halide R–X (SN2) · then hydrolysis + decarbox finish · ↓ Tool 4 — β-Decarboxylation drives step 5 of this ladder
Tool 6 — Acetoacetic Variant · methyl-ketone factory
Same 5-step pattern, but the starting material has one ester swapped for a methyl ketone. After hydrolysis you get a β-keto acid (not a β-diacid); decarboxylation drops the COOH and you keep the methyl ketone. Result: R−CH₂−CO−CH₃ — a methyl ketone instead of an acid.
